lessons.title: What Signals and Systems Are
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing on the roof of your building in Dhaka during Eid. You shout 'Eid Mubarak!' to your friend on the next roof. Your voice leaves your mouth as tiny pushes in the air. The air carries those pushes, the wind adds some noise, a passing bus adds more noise, and finally your friend's ears pick up something a bit weaker and a bit messier than what you said. Your voice is a signal. The air between the roofs is a system. This whole course is about exactly this picture: something carries information, something else changes it, and we want to describe both with clear rules.

What a signal is: A signal is any quantity that changes with time, or with position, and carries some information. Your voice is air pressure changing with time. The temperature in Rajshahi through a day is a signal. The price of a share on the Dhaka Stock Exchange is a signal that changes every few seconds. A heartbeat recording in a hospital, called an ECG, is a voltage changing with time. A photo is also a signal, but its brightness changes with position (left-right and up-down) instead of time. In maths we write a signal as a function, like x(t), where t is time and x(t) is the value at that moment.

Why we call it a function: Think of a signal as a table that answers one question: 'At this moment, what is the value?' At t = 0 seconds the temperature is 26 degrees, at t = 3 hours it is 29 degrees, and so on. A function is just a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. So a signal is a function of time. This is helpful because everything you learned about functions in calculus now works on signals: you can add them, multiply them, shift them, and draw their graphs.

What a system is: A system is anything that takes a signal in and gives a signal out. We draw it as a box with an arrow going in, called the input x(t), and an arrow coming out, called the output y(t). A loudspeaker is a system: electrical signal in, sound out. A microphone is the reverse. A mobile phone's noise-cancelling chip is a system: noisy voice in, clean voice out. The volume knob is a very simple system: it multiplies the signal by a number. Even your ears and brain form a system that turns air pressure into understanding.

The box picture: The magic of the box picture is that we often do not care what is inside. We only care about the rule connecting input to output. If I tell you 'this box doubles whatever goes in', you can predict every output without opening the box. Write it as y(t) = 2x(t). If the box adds an echo half a second later at half strength, write y(t) = x(t) + 0.5x(t - 0.5). The rule is the system. Most of this course is about finding such rules, studying their properties, and predicting outputs.

A tiny worked example: Suppose a box follows the rule y(t) = 3x(t) + 1. If the input at some moment is 2, the output is 3 times 2 plus 1, which is 7. If the input is 0, the output is 1. Now suppose a second box follows the rule y(t) = x(t - 2). This box simply delays the signal by 2 seconds. Whatever went in at time 5 comes out at time 7. Delays like this appear everywhere: in phone calls, in echoes inside a mosque, and inside every computer chip.

Why this course matters: Almost everything modern runs on signals. When you talk on a phone, your voice becomes an electrical signal, then a list of numbers, then radio waves, then numbers again, then sound. At every step a system is working on a signal. Music apps compress songs, cameras clean up blurry photos, WiFi routers fight noise, hospitals filter ECG readings, and Google Maps smooths GPS positions. Engineers who design any of this use the ideas in this course every day.

Why CSE students need it: You might think signals belong to electrical engineers only. But computer science now handles huge amounts of sound, images, video and sensor data. Speech recognition, like the voice typing on your phone, starts with signal processing. Image filters in Instagram are systems acting on 2D signals. Machine learning models that read ECGs or detect earthquakes use features made with Fourier transforms. Networking and data communication depend on how signals travel through cables and air. Later courses like Digital Signal Processing, Data Communication, Computer Networks, Multimedia and Embedded Systems all build on this one.

What engineers did before: Long ago, people built radios and telephones by trial and error. They knew which parts to connect but often could not predict exactly how a new circuit would behave. In the early 1800s, Joseph Fourier showed that complicated waves can be built by adding simple sine waves. Over the next century, engineers turned this idea and the work of others like Laplace into a toolbox. By the 20th century, telephone, radio and radar engineers had a clear theory: describe signals, describe systems, then predict the result with maths instead of guessing. That theory is what you are learning now.

Two big views of a signal: There are two ways to look at a signal. The first is the time view: what value does it have at each moment? That is the graph you would see on an oscilloscope. The second is the frequency view: which pure tones, or sine waves, are mixed inside it, and how strong is each one? That is like the bars that jump up and down on a music player's equaliser. Both views describe the same signal, just like a cake can be described by its shape or by its recipe. Much of this course is about moving between these two views.

The recipe analogy: Think of a song as a cake. The time view is the finished cake you can see and touch. The frequency view is the recipe: so much bass, so much middle sound, so much high treble. If you want less bass, it is much easier to change the recipe than to scrape bits off the finished cake. Filters work the same way. They are easiest to understand in the frequency view, where you just turn down certain ingredients.

Where the analogy breaks: A real recipe loses information about how the cake was baked. The frequency view of a signal does not lose anything. If you know the full frequency recipe, including a detail called phase, you can rebuild the exact signal. So it is more like a perfect recipe that tells you everything, even the order of the steps.

Continuous and discrete signals, a preview: Some signals exist at every moment, like your voice in the air. These are continuous-time signals, written x(t). Others exist only at separate moments, like the temperature written down once every hour. These are discrete-time signals, written x[n] with square brackets, where n is a whole number counting the samples. Computers can only store discrete lists of numbers, so turning x(t) into x[n] is one of the most important steps in modern technology. The next lesson explains this in detail.

The star of the course, LTI systems: There are endless kinds of systems, and most are hard to study. But one family is both very common and very easy to analyse: Linear Time-Invariant systems, or LTI systems. 'Linear' roughly means that if you double the input, the output doubles, and if you add two inputs, the outputs add. 'Time-invariant' means the system behaves the same today as tomorrow. For LTI systems, one single test response, called the impulse response, tells you everything. You will spend many lessons on this idea, because it powers filters, echoes, circuits and much more.

The main tools you will learn: You will learn convolution, a way to compute the output of an LTI system from its impulse response. You will learn the Fourier series and Fourier transform, which give the frequency view. You will learn the sampling theorem, which says how fast you must sample a signal so a computer does not mess it up. You will learn the Laplace transform for continuous systems and the Z-transform for discrete systems, which help you check whether a system is stable, meaning it does not blow up.

Real-life example 1, a phone call from Sylhet to Dhaka: Your aunt in Sylhet speaks. Her phone's microphone turns air pressure into a voltage signal. A chip samples that voltage thousands of times a second, turning it into numbers, x[n]. A compression system removes parts the ear will not miss, so fewer numbers need to be sent. A modulation system puts the numbers onto radio waves. The tower and network carry it to Dhaka, adding a little delay and noise. Your phone undoes the steps and a speaker system turns numbers back into sound. Every arrow in that chain is a signal, and every box is a system.

Real-life example 2, a fitness band: A fitness band on your wrist shines light into your skin and measures how much bounces back. The amount changes slightly with each heartbeat, so the light reading is a signal. But your arm also moves while you walk, which adds a big wobbly signal on top. A filter system removes the slow wobble and the fast noise, leaving the heartbeat rhythm. Another system counts the peaks per minute and shows, say, 78 beats per minute. Without signals and systems, the band would show random numbers.

Common mistakes: Students often think a signal must be electrical. It does not: temperature, prices and pixel brightness are all signals. Another mistake is thinking a system must be a physical machine. A line of code like y = (x + previous_x) / 2 is also a system, an averaging one. Some students also mix up the input and output arrows when drawing block diagrams. Always label x for input and y for output, and keep time as the variable inside the brackets.

What exams ask: Early exam questions ask you to define a signal and a system with examples, to name examples of continuous and discrete signals, and to draw a simple block diagram. A typical short question: 'Give two examples each of a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional signal.' Answer: voice and ECG are one-dimensional (they depend only on time), while a photo and a fingerprint scan are two-dimensional (they depend on two position values).

How to study this course: Draw everything. Every time you see a formula like y(t) = x(t - 2), draw x(t) and then draw y(t) next to it. The pictures will build your intuition much faster than memorising rules. Also, keep connecting to everyday things: your WiFi, your music, your phone camera. Each new idea in this course is hiding inside those gadgets.

Recap: A signal is a function that carries information, usually changing with time. A system is a rule that turns an input signal into an output signal. We can look at a signal in time or in frequency. Linear time-invariant systems are the main characters because one response describes them completely. Over the next lessons you will learn to classify signals, test system properties, compute outputs with convolution, look at spectra with Fourier, sample safely, and check stability with Laplace and Z transforms.
key_points: A signal is a quantity that changes with time or position and carries information, written as a function like x(t).
A system is a rule that takes an input signal x and produces an output signal y, drawn as a box with arrows.
Signals can be one-dimensional (voice, ECG, temperature) or two-dimensional (images).
Continuous-time signals are written x(t); discrete-time signals, which computers store, are written x[n].
A signal can be viewed in time (value at each moment) or in frequency (which sine waves it contains).
Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems are the main focus because one test response, the impulse response, describes them fully.
The main tools ahead are convolution, Fourier series and transforms, sampling, the Laplace transform and the Z-transform.
lessons.tip: For every formula in this course, draw the input and the output side by side. A quick sketch catches most mistakes and builds real intuition.
lessons.task: List 6 signals you met today (for example, your phone's battery level over the day, the call to prayer, room temperature). For each, write what changes, what it changes with (time or position), and one system that acts on it.

quiz.q: Which of these is a two-dimensional signal?
quiz.explain: A photo's brightness depends on two position values (horizontal and vertical), so it is a 2D signal. The others depend only on time.

quiz.q: A system follows y(t) = 3x(t) + 1. If the input is 2, what is the output?
quiz.explain: 3 times 2 is 6, plus 1 gives 7.

quiz.q: What does the system y(t) = x(t - 2) do?
quiz.explain: Whatever entered at time t - 2 comes out at time t, so everything appears 2 seconds later.

quiz.q: Which notation is used for a discrete-time signal?
quiz.explain: Square brackets with an integer n mark a discrete-time signal, a list of samples.

quiz.q: Why are LTI systems the main focus of the course?
options: They are the only systems that exist
One test response, the impulse response, describes them completely
quiz.explain: For linear time-invariant systems, knowing the impulse response lets you predict the output for any input.

lessons.title: Continuous vs Discrete, Analog vs Digital
lessons.content:
Think about a cricket match on TV. The ball flies smoothly through the air; at every tiny moment it has a position. But the TV camera does not record every moment. It takes, say, 50 pictures every second. When the third umpire checks a run-out, he steps through those pictures one by one. Between two pictures, he simply does not know where the bat was. The real flight of the ball is a continuous signal. The camera's pictures are a discrete signal. This lesson is about the difference, and about why computers can only work with the second kind.

Continuous-time signals: A continuous-time signal has a value at every instant of time, including all the in-between moments like t = 1.5 seconds, t = 1.51, t = 1.5104, and so on forever. We write it as x(t), with round brackets, and t can be any real number. The voltage across a capacitor, the height of a swing, the air pressure of a sound wave and the temperature in a room are all continuous-time signals. When we plot one, we draw a smooth unbroken line.

Discrete-time signals: A discrete-time signal has values only at separate, countable moments. We write it as x[n], with square brackets, where n is an integer: ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, .... There is no x[1.5]; it simply does not exist. Daily closing prices of a share, the number of goals per match, your marks in each class test, and the samples a phone records from a microphone are discrete-time signals. When we plot one, we draw separate vertical sticks with a dot on top, called a stem plot, one stick for each n.

Writing a discrete signal: A short discrete signal can be written as a list with an arrow or a mark showing where n = 0 is. For example, x[n] = {1, 3, 2, 5} with n = 0 at the first value means x[0] = 1, x[1] = 3, x[2] = 2, x[3] = 5, and x[n] = 0 everywhere else. Another way is a formula: x[n] = 2n for n = 0 to 3 gives 0, 2, 4, 6. Always be clear about where n = 0 is, because shifting it changes the signal.

Sampling, from continuous to discrete: The most common way to get a discrete signal is sampling. We measure the continuous signal at equally spaced moments. The gap between samples is called the sampling period, T (or Ts), and the number of samples per second is the sampling rate or sampling frequency, fs = 1/T. The rule is simply x[n] = x(nT). If T = 0.001 seconds, then fs = 1000 samples per second, and x[3] is the value of x(t) at t = 0.003 seconds.

A sampling example: Let x(t) = 5t, a straight line rising 5 units each second. Sample it with T = 0.5 seconds. Then x[0] = x(0) = 0, x[1] = x(0.5) = 2.5, x[2] = x(1) = 5, x[3] = x(1.5) = 7.5. The discrete signal is 0, 2.5, 5, 7.5, ... . We kept the values at those moments and threw away everything in between. For a straight line that is no loss, because we can join the dots. But for a wiggly signal, if we sample too slowly, we can miss the wiggles completely. The sampling theorem, later in the course, tells us exactly how fast is fast enough.

Amplitude: continuous or discrete: So far we talked about time. Now think about the value itself, the amplitude. If the amplitude can take any real value in a range, like 2.5371 volts, it is continuous in amplitude. If it can only take certain fixed levels, like whole numbers 0 to 255, it is discrete in amplitude. Time and amplitude are two separate questions, so we get four combinations.

The four kinds: First, continuous time and continuous amplitude: this is an analog signal, like the real voltage from a microphone. Second, discrete time and continuous amplitude: a sampled signal before rounding, like readings written to many decimal places. Third, continuous time and discrete amplitude: like the output of a staircase circuit that jumps between fixed levels but can jump at any moment. Fourth, discrete time and discrete amplitude: this is a digital signal, a list of numbers from a fixed set. Computers store only this fourth kind.

Quantization: Turning a continuous amplitude into one of a fixed set of levels is called quantization. It is like rounding to the nearest allowed value. Suppose a sensor gives values from 0 to 1 volt and we allow only 4 levels: 0, 0.33, 0.67 and 1. A reading of 0.4 becomes 0.33, a reading of 0.9 becomes 1. The difference, here 0.07 and 0.1, is called quantization error. It behaves like a little noise added to the signal. More levels means smaller error.

Bits and levels: Each level is stored as a binary number. With b bits you get 2 to the power b levels. 1 bit gives 2 levels, 8 bits give 256 levels, 16 bits give 65,536 levels. Music CDs use 16 bits per sample, which is why they sound clean. Old telephone systems used 8 bits per sample. Each extra bit doubles the number of levels and halves the step size, which roughly adds about 6 decibels of quality, a rule of thumb you will see in later courses.

The ADC and DAC: The chip that samples and quantizes is called an analog-to-digital converter, or ADC. Every phone, laptop microphone, digital thermometer and camera sensor has one. The chip that goes the other way, turning numbers back into a smooth voltage for a speaker, is a digital-to-analog converter, or DAC. A simple DAC holds each value until the next sample arrives, giving a staircase, and then a smoothing filter rounds off the corners. The whole chain is: analog in, ADC, computer work, DAC, analog out.

Why computers need discrete digital signals: A computer's memory has a finite number of cells, and each cell holds a fixed number of bits. A continuous signal has infinitely many moments and each value has infinitely many decimal places, so it can never fit. Only a finite list of numbers, each from a finite set, can fit. That is why every song on your phone, every photo and every video is a digital signal.

Why digital is so popular: Digital signals have big advantages. Copies are perfect: copy a file a thousand times and it stays the same, while an old cassette tape got worse with each copy. Digital signals resist noise: if a 0 is sent as 0 volts and a 1 as 5 volts, a little noise of 0.3 volts does not change which one it is. Digital processing is flexible: the same chip can be a filter today and an echo remover tomorrow, just by changing the program. Data can be compressed, encrypted and checked for errors.

Why analog still matters: The real world is analog. Sound, light, temperature and radio waves are continuous. So every digital system needs analog parts at its edges: microphones, antennas, amplifiers. Also, sampling and quantization lose some information if done carelessly. Engineers must choose a sampling rate and number of bits that are good enough for the job without wasting memory.

Discrete signals that were never continuous: Not all discrete signals come from sampling. The number of bKash transactions each hour, the number of students in each class, or the daily rainfall count are naturally discrete. There is no 'in-between' value to sample. The tools for discrete-time signals work for both kinds, which is why they are so useful in computing.

Storage cost, a worked example: How much memory does one minute of CD-quality stereo music need before compression? There are 44,100 samples per second, 16 bits per sample and 2 channels (left and right). That is 44,100 times 16 times 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second. Divide by 8 to get bytes: 176,400 bytes per second. Multiply by 60 seconds: about 10.6 million bytes, roughly 10 megabytes per minute. That is why compression formats like MP3 and AAC were invented: they shrink this to around 1 megabyte per minute by throwing away sounds the ear hardly notices.

Real-life example 1, a voice message on WhatsApp: You hold the button and say 'Ammu, ami ashchi'. The microphone makes an analog voltage. The phone's ADC samples it, often 16,000 or more times per second for voice, and quantizes each sample to 16 bits. Now you have a digital signal: a long list of numbers. A compression program shrinks it, the app sends it, and your mother's phone uses a DAC and speaker to turn it back into sound. Between the two phones, only numbers travelled.

Real-life example 2, a digital weighing scale in a shop: When the shopkeeper in Karwan Bazar puts potatoes on a digital scale, the load cell gives a tiny analog voltage that depends on weight. An ADC samples it several times per second and quantizes it, say to steps of 5 grams. The display shows 1.235 kg, not 1.23461 kg, because of quantization. The scale may also average the last few samples to stop the number from jumping around. That averaging is a small system acting on a discrete signal.

How fast do real systems sample? Different jobs need different rates. Telephone-quality voice has traditionally used 8,000 samples per second, which is enough to understand words but makes music sound flat. Music CDs use 44,100 samples per second, because human hearing reaches up to about 20,000 hertz and the sampling rate must be a bit more than double the highest frequency you want to keep. A room thermostat might sample only once per second, because temperature changes slowly. An ECG machine often samples a few hundred times per second, enough for the sharp spikes of a heartbeat. The lesson is simple: sample fast enough for the fastest change you care about, and no faster, or you waste memory and battery.

Common mistakes: Students often say 'discrete means digital'. Not quite: discrete refers to time, digital means discrete time and discrete amplitude. Another mistake is writing x[1.5] or x(n) carelessly. Square brackets are only for integer indices. Also, do not confuse the sampling period T (seconds between samples) with the sampling frequency fs (samples per second); they are reciprocals. If fs = 8000 Hz, T = 1/8000 = 0.125 milliseconds.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: 'Classify these as continuous or discrete, analog or digital', 'A signal x(t) = 3t is sampled at fs = 4 Hz; write the first four samples' (answer: 0, 0.75, 1.5, 2.25), 'How many levels does a 10-bit ADC have?' (answer: 1024), and 'Draw the block diagram of a digital processing system' (ADC, processor, DAC, with filters at both ends).

Recap: Continuous-time signals x(t) exist at every instant; discrete-time signals x[n] exist only at integer steps. Sampling makes x[n] = x(nT) with fs = 1/T. Amplitude can also be continuous or discrete; quantization rounds it to 2 to the power b levels for b bits. Analog means continuous in both, digital means discrete in both, and computers can only store digital signals. ADCs and DACs connect the analog world to the digital one.
key_points: Continuous-time signals x(t) have a value at every instant; discrete-time signals x[n] exist only at integer n.
Sampling takes values at equal gaps: x[n] = x(nT), with sampling rate fs = 1/T.
Quantization rounds amplitude to fixed levels; b bits give 2^b levels and the rounding difference is quantization error.
Analog means continuous time and amplitude; digital means discrete time and amplitude.
An ADC turns analog into digital; a DAC turns digital back into analog.
Digital signals copy perfectly, resist noise and can be processed by programs, but the real world at the edges is analog.
Some discrete signals, like hourly transaction counts, are naturally discrete and never came from sampling.
lessons.tip: Make a 2 by 2 table with time (continuous/discrete) on one side and amplitude (continuous/discrete) on the other, and put an example in each box. It clears up most confusion in this topic.
lessons.task: Take x(t) = sin of (2π t), one full wave each second. Sample it by hand with T = 0.25 s for n = 0 to 4 and round each value to the nearest of the levels -1, 0, 1. Plot both the samples and the original wave on paper.

quiz.q: A signal is sampled with T = 0.002 seconds. What is the sampling frequency?
quiz.explain: fs = 1/T = 1/0.002 = 500 samples per second.

quiz.q: How many quantization levels does an 8-bit ADC have?
quiz.explain: b bits give 2^b levels, so 2^8 = 256.

quiz.q: Which signal is digital?
options: Discrete in time and discrete in amplitude
Continuous in time, discrete in amplitude
Discrete in time, continuous in amplitude
quiz.explain: A digital signal is a list of samples (discrete time), each taking one of a fixed set of values (discrete amplitude).

quiz.q: x(t) = 4t is sampled with T = 0.5 s. What is x[3]?
Which is a natural advantage of digital signals?
options: Copies are perfect and small noise does not change the stored bits
quiz.explain: Digital data can be copied exactly, and noise smaller than the gap between levels does not change which value was stored.

lessons.title: Classifying Signals
lessons.content:
When you sort clothes after washing, you make piles: shirts here, socks there, school uniform on the bed. Sorting does not change the clothes, but it makes everything faster later. Engineers sort signals in the same way. Once you know a signal is periodic, or even, or an energy signal, you instantly know which tools work on it and which shortcuts you can use. This lesson gives you the main piles: deterministic or random, periodic or not, even or odd, causal or not, and energy or power.

Deterministic signals: A deterministic signal is one whose value at every time is known exactly, usually from a formula or a table. x(t) = 3 cos(2t) is deterministic: ask me the value at t = 1 and I can compute it. A recorded song, once recorded, is also deterministic because every sample is stored. Most of this course works with deterministic signals because they are easiest to analyse.

Random signals: A random signal cannot be predicted exactly before it happens. The hiss of a radio between stations, tomorrow's rainfall in Chattogram, or the exact noise in a sensor reading are random. We can describe them only with averages and probabilities, like 'the noise is usually between -0.1 and +0.1 volts'. Probability and statistics, which you studied earlier, are the tools for these. Here we will mostly mention random signals when we talk about noise.

Periodic signals, continuous time: A signal x(t) is periodic if there is a positive number T such that x(t + T) = x(t) for every t. In words: the graph repeats itself every T seconds. The smallest such T is the fundamental period, T0. The fundamental frequency is f0 = 1/T0 in hertz, or ω0 = 2π/T0 in radians per second. For x(t) = cos(4t), the period is 2π/4 = π/2 seconds, about 1.57 seconds. A signal that never repeats, like a single clap or e^(-t), is aperiodic.

Sum of two periodic signals: Is x(t) = cos(2πt) + cos(3πt) periodic? The first part has period 1 second, the second has period 2/3 second. The sum repeats when both parts repeat together, which happens at the least common multiple of the periods. Multiples of 1 are 1, 2, 3, ...; multiples of 2/3 are 2/3, 4/3, 2, .... The first common value is 2, so the sum is periodic with period 2 seconds. Rule: a sum of periodic signals is periodic only when the ratio of their periods is a rational number (a fraction of whole numbers). cos(t) + cos(πt) is not periodic, because the ratio of periods 2π and 2 is π, which is not a fraction of whole numbers.

Periodic signals, discrete time: In discrete time, the period N must be a positive integer: x[n + N] = x[n] for all n. This creates a surprise. The signal cos(ω0 n) is periodic only if ω0 divided by 2π is a fraction m/N of whole numbers. Then the fundamental period is the smallest such N, after reducing the fraction. Example: cos(πn/4). Here ω0/(2π) = 1/8, so N = 8. Example: cos(3πn/5). ω0/(2π) = 3/10, so N = 10. Example: cos(n). ω0/(2π) = 1/(2π), which is not a fraction of whole numbers, so cos(n) is not periodic at all, even though cos(t) is. The samples never land on exactly the same pattern again.

Why the discrete surprise happens: Think of a clock hand that moves ω0 radians at each tick. For the samples to repeat, the hand must come back to exactly the same spot after a whole number of ticks, having gone around a whole number of times. If each step is 1 radian, then no whole number of steps ever adds up to an exact whole number of turns (2π times an integer), because π is irrational. So the pattern never repeats exactly.

Even signals: A signal is even if x(-t) = x(t) for all t. Its graph is a mirror image across the vertical axis, like a butterfly's wings. cos(t), t squared, and |t| are even. In discrete time, x[-n] = x[n].

Odd signals: A signal is odd if x(-t) = -x(t). Flip it left-right, then upside down, and you get the same graph. sin(t), t, and t cubed are odd. An odd signal must be zero at t = 0, because x(0) = -x(0) forces x(0) = 0.

Every signal has even and odd parts: Here is a neat fact. Any signal can be split into an even part plus an odd part. The even part is xe(t) = (x(t) + x(-t)) / 2 and the odd part is xo(t) = (x(t) - x(-t)) / 2. Add them and the x(-t) pieces cancel, leaving x(t). Worked example in discrete time: x[n] = {1, 2, 3} at n = 0, 1, 2, and zero elsewhere. Then x[-n] has 3 at n = -2, 2 at n = -1, 1 at n = 0. Even part: at n = 0, (1 + 1)/2 = 1; at n = 1, (2 + 0)/2 = 1; at n = -1, (0 + 2)/2 = 1; at n = 2, 1.5; at n = -2, 1.5. Odd part: at n = 0, 0; at n = 1, 1; at n = -1, -1; at n = 2, 1.5; at n = -2, -1.5. Check at n = 2: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3. Correct.

Useful even/odd facts: even times even is even, odd times odd is even, even times odd is odd. Also, the area of an odd signal over a symmetric range, from -a to a, is zero, because the positive and negative halves cancel. These shortcuts save a lot of work in Fourier series, where an even signal has only cosine terms and an odd signal has only sine terms.

Causal, anti-causal and non-causal signals: A causal signal is zero for all t < 0; it starts at or after time zero, like a song that begins when you press play. An anti-causal signal is zero for all t > 0. A non-causal signal has non-zero values on both sides, like cos(t) for all time. These words will come back when we talk about causal systems, which cannot react before their input arrives.

Energy of a signal: Imagine x(t) is the voltage across a 1 ohm resistor. The power at each moment is x(t) squared, and the total energy is the area under x(t) squared. So we define the energy E as the integral of |x(t)| squared over all time. In discrete time, E is the sum of |x[n]| squared over all n. Example: x[n] = {1, 2, 3}. E = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. Example: x(t) = e^(-2t) for t ≥ 0, zero before. E = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-4t) dt = 1/4.

Power of a signal: Some signals go on forever, like cos(t), so their total energy is infinite. For these we use average power: the energy per unit time, averaged over a very long window. For a periodic signal, average over one period is enough. For x(t) = A cos(ω0 t), the average of cos squared over a period is 1/2, so the power is A squared over 2. For A = 4, P = 8. For the unit step u(t), which is 1 for t ≥ 0, averaging over a window from -T to T gives half the time at value 1, so P = 1/2.

Energy signals and power signals: An energy signal has finite, non-zero energy; its average power is then zero. Short pulses and decaying signals like e^(-2t)u(t) are energy signals. A power signal has finite, non-zero average power; its energy is then infinite. Periodic signals and the unit step are power signals. Some signals are neither: the ramp x(t) = t for t ≥ 0 grows forever, so both its energy and its power are infinite. A signal cannot be both, because finite energy forces zero power.

A DT worked example: x[n] = (1/2)^n for n ≥ 0, zero before. Energy = sum of (1/4)^n from n = 0 to infinity. This is a geometric series with ratio 1/4, so the sum is 1/(1 - 1/4) = 4/3. Finite, so it is an energy signal. Compare x[n] = 2 for all n: each sample adds 4 to the energy, so energy is infinite, but the average power is 4, so it is a power signal.

Real-life example 1, the azan and the generator: Two sounds reach your window. The azan from the nearby mosque has a voice that changes with words; over a few seconds it does not repeat exactly, so it is aperiodic and, once recorded, deterministic. The diesel generator downstairs hums at a steady pitch, roughly repeating 50 times a second, almost periodic. Noise-cancelling headphones find periodic hums easy to remove, because once they learn one period, they can predict the next and cancel it. The voice is harder because it keeps changing.

Real-life example 2, a camera flash vs a tube light: A camera flash is a short burst of light that starts and ends: it has finite energy, so it is an energy signal. A tube light in a classroom runs all day; its total energy keeps growing without limit, but its average power is a fixed number, like 36 watts. That is a power signal. Electricity bills are based on energy used over time, while a bulb's rating is its power, the same split you just learned.

A quick classification drill: Take x(t) = 5 sin(3t). It is deterministic, periodic with period 2π/3, odd, non-causal (it exists for negative time too), and a power signal with power 25/2 = 12.5. Now take x[n] = (0.9)^n u[n]. It is deterministic, aperiodic, neither even nor odd, causal, and an energy signal. Practising five labels on every signal you meet makes exam questions feel easy.

Common mistakes: Students often forget that discrete sinusoids may not be periodic; always check ω0/(2π) is rational. Another mistake is calling a periodic signal an energy signal: periodic non-zero signals have infinite energy. When finding even and odd parts, people forget to include the negative-n values that appear after flipping. And remember to square the magnitude for energy, not just add the values.

What exams ask: 'Determine if x[n] = cos(πn/6) + sin(πn/4) is periodic and find its period.' The first part has N = 12, the second N = 8, the LCM is 24, so the period is 24. 'Find the even and odd parts of a given sequence.' 'Is x(t) = e^(-3|t|) an energy or power signal? Find its energy.' (Energy = 2 times integral of e^(-6t) from 0 to infinity = 2/6 = 1/3, so it is an energy signal.)

Recap: Deterministic signals are known exactly, random ones only by probability. Periodic signals repeat with fundamental period T0 or N; sums are periodic only with a rational period ratio, and cos(ω0 n) is periodic only when ω0/(2π) is rational. Every signal splits into even and odd parts. Causal signals are zero before t = 0. Energy signals have finite energy and zero power; power signals have finite power and infinite energy; some signals are neither.
key_points: Deterministic signals are known exactly at every time; random signals are described only with probability.
x(t) is periodic if x(t + T) = x(t); the smallest T is the fundamental period, and f0 = 1/T0.
A sum of periodic signals is periodic only if the ratio of periods is rational; the period is their least common multiple.
cos(ω0 n) is periodic only if ω0/(2π) is a ratio of integers, so cos(n) is not periodic.
Any signal = even part (x(t) + x(-t))/2 plus odd part (x(t) - x(-t))/2.
Energy is the integral or sum of |x| squared; power is energy per unit time averaged over a long window.
Energy signals have finite energy and zero power; power signals have finite power and infinite energy; a ramp is neither.
lessons.tip: Before any calculation, ask three quick questions about the signal: does it repeat, is it symmetric, does it die out? The answers often tell you the result before you compute it.
lessons.task: Check by hand whether cos(πn/3) + cos(πn/2) is periodic and find its period. Then write the first 13 samples (n = 0 to 12) and confirm that the pattern restarts at your answer.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental period of cos(πn/4)?
Is cos(n) (discrete time) periodic?
options: No, because 1/(2π) is not a ratio of integers
quiz.explain: The period must be an integer N with N times 1 equal to a whole multiple of 2π, which is impossible because π is irrational.

quiz.q: What is the energy of x[n] = {1, 2, 3}?
quiz.explain: E = 1 squared + 2 squared + 3 squared = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14.

quiz.q: What is the average power of 4 cos(5t)?
quiz.explain: For A cos(ω0 t), P = A squared / 2 = 16/2 = 8.

quiz.q: Which statement about x(t) = t for t ≥ 0 (a ramp) is correct?
options: It is neither an energy nor a power signal
It is a power signal with P = 1/2
quiz.explain: The ramp keeps growing, so both its total energy and its average power are infinite.

lessons.title: Operations on the Time Axis
lessons.content:
Imagine you recorded your little brother singing a rhyme on your phone. Now you play with the recording. You start it two seconds late. You play it backwards and laugh at the strange sounds. You play it at double speed so he sounds like a cartoon chipmunk, or at half speed so he sounds like a sleepy giant. You turn the volume up. Every one of these tricks is an operation on a signal, and every one can be written as a tiny change to x(t). This lesson teaches you to do them on paper, exactly and without confusion.

Two kinds of operations: Some operations change the time axis, the t inside the brackets. These are time shifting, time reversal and time scaling. Others change the value, the amplitude, outside the brackets. These are amplitude scaling, adding signals and multiplying signals. Time operations are where most students make mistakes, so we will go slowly and always check with one point.

The one-point check: Here is the most useful trick in this lesson. Pick a special point of the original signal, for example where it starts. Ask: in the new signal, at what time t does the bracket contain that special value? Solve a tiny equation, and you know where that point moved. If you do this for the start and the end of a signal, you can draw any transformed version correctly.

Time shifting: y(t) = x(t - t0). If t0 is positive, the signal moves to the right, which means it happens later. This is a delay. If t0 is negative, for example y(t) = x(t + 3), the signal moves to the left, which means it happens earlier. This is an advance. Many students expect the minus sign to move things left. Use the one-point check: suppose x(t) starts at t = 0. Then x(t - 2) starts where t - 2 = 0, which is t = 2. So it starts 2 seconds later, it moved right.

A shifting example: Let x(t) be a box, equal to 1 from t = 0 to t = 2 and zero elsewhere. Then x(t - 3) is 1 when 0 ≤ t - 3 ≤ 2, which means 3 ≤ t ≤ 5. The box moved 3 to the right. And x(t + 1) is 1 when 0 ≤ t + 1 ≤ 2, so -1 ≤ t ≤ 1. The box moved 1 to the left. Same shape, new place.

Shifting in discrete time: y[n] = x[n - n0] works the same way, except n0 must be an integer. If x[n] = {1, 2, 3} at n = 0, 1, 2, then x[n - 2] has 1 at n = 2, 2 at n = 3, 3 at n = 4. You cannot shift a discrete signal by 1.5 samples, because x[n - 1.5] would ask for values that do not exist.

Time reversal: y(t) = x(-t). This flips the signal around t = 0, like a mirror placed on the vertical axis. What happened at t = 2 now happens at t = -2. The box from 0 to 2 becomes a box from -2 to 0. Playing a recording backwards is a time reversal followed by a shift so it starts at zero again. In discrete time, x[-n] flips the sample list: {1, 2, 3} at n = 0, 1, 2 becomes 3 at n = -2, 2 at n = -1, 1 at n = 0.

Time scaling, continuous time: y(t) = x(at), with a positive. If a > 1, the signal is squeezed, or compressed: everything happens faster. If 0 < a < 1, it is stretched, or expanded: everything happens slower. One-point check with the box: x(2t) is 1 when 0 ≤ 2t ≤ 2, so 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. The box became half as wide. x(t/2) is 1 when 0 ≤ t/2 ≤ 2, so 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. Twice as wide. Playing a song at double speed is x(2t): it finishes in half the time and all pitches go up.

Time scaling in discrete time, decimation: For discrete signals, scaling is trickier, because n must stay an integer. y[n] = x[2n] keeps only every second sample: y[0] = x[0], y[1] = x[2], y[2] = x[4]. The odd samples x[1], x[3] are simply thrown away. This is called downsampling or decimation by 2. Unlike continuous scaling, information can be lost here, and you cannot always get it back.

Time scaling in discrete time, expansion: y[n] = x[n/2] only makes sense when n/2 is an integer, that is for even n. So we define y[n] = x[n/2] for even n and y[n] = 0 for odd n. From {1, 2, 3} we get {1, 0, 2, 0, 3}. This is called upsampling or expansion by 2. Later, a filter can fill those zeros with smooth in-between values, which is how audio is converted to a higher sampling rate.

Combined operations: The real exam questions combine steps, like y(t) = x(2t - 4). There are two safe orders. Method 1, shift then scale: first make x(t - 4), a shift right by 4. Then replace t with 2t to get x(2t - 4), a compression by 2. Method 2, scale then shift: write x(2t - 4) = x(2(t - 2)). First make x(2t), compressed. Then replace t with t - 2 to get x(2(t - 2)), a shift right by 2, not 4. The trap is scaling first and then shifting by 4. That gives x(2(t - 4)) = x(2t - 8), the wrong signal.

Check the combined example with the box: Using the one-point check is faster than either method. x(2t - 4) is 1 when 0 ≤ 2t - 4 ≤ 2. Add 4: 4 ≤ 2t ≤ 6. Divide by 2: 2 ≤ t ≤ 3. So the new box runs from 2 to 3. Method 1: shift right by 4 gives a box from 4 to 6; compress by 2 divides every time by 2, giving 2 to 3. Method 2: compress first gives 0 to 1; shift right by 2 gives 2 to 3. Both agree, and so does the check.

Reversal combined with shift: y(t) = x(-t + 1). Using the box: 0 ≤ -t + 1 ≤ 2. Subtract 1: -1 ≤ -t ≤ 1. Multiply by -1 and flip the inequalities: -1 ≤ t ≤ 1. The box now covers -1 to 1, and it is reversed, so what was at the start of x is now at the end. For a box you cannot see the reversal because it is symmetric, but for a ramp you could. If x(t) = t on 0 to 2, then x(-t + 1) = -t + 1 on -1 to 1: it is 2 at t = -1 and 0 at t = 1, a falling line instead of a rising one.

Amplitude operations: These are simpler because they act on values, not on time. y(t) = 3x(t) makes the signal three times taller; the volume knob does this. y(t) = -x(t) flips it upside down; this is called amplitude reversal, not time reversal. y(t) = x(t) + 2 lifts it up by 2, adding a DC offset. Adding two signals adds their values at each moment: if x1(1) = 4 and x2(1) = -1, then the sum at t = 1 is 3.

Multiplying signals: y(t) = x1(t) times x2(t) multiplies values point by point. Multiplying by a box acts like a window: it keeps x(t) inside the box and sets it to zero outside. Multiplying by the unit step u(t), which is 0 before zero and 1 after, chops off everything before t = 0. Multiplying a sound by a cosine, as we will see later, is the basic idea of modulation in radios.

Differentiation and integration: Two more operations are useful. The derivative dx/dt measures how fast the signal changes; a flat part becomes zero and a sudden jump becomes a spike. The running integral, the area under x from minus infinity up to t, adds things up over time; a box becomes a ramp that rises and then stays flat. These turn out to be simple LTI systems themselves.

Why the order matters, in plain words: Think of the bracket as a set of instructions for reading the old recording. x(2t - 4) says: 'at time t, play whatever the old recording had at time 2t - 4'. At t = 2 you play the old moment 0; at t = 3 you play the old moment 2. So the new signal plays the old one from moment 0 to 2 while the clock goes from 2 to 3. That is twice as fast and starting at 2. Thinking of the bracket as 'which old moment do I play now?' makes every combined operation easy to reason about, without memorising any order.

Real-life example 1, a cricket replay: The broadcaster shows a wicket in slow motion. That is time scaling with a < 1: x(t/4) shows the event four times slower, stretched over four times the duration. The camera records extra frames per second so the slow version still looks smooth. Then the replay shows the delivery again from the start, which is a time shift. If they show the bails flying back onto the stumps for fun, that is time reversal.

Real-life example 2, the Bangla news echo: In a big auditorium at Dhaka University, the microphone sound reaches you directly and also bounces off the back wall, arriving 0.2 seconds later at half strength. What you hear is y(t) = x(t) + 0.5x(t - 0.2): a shift, an amplitude scaling and an addition, all in one line. Sound engineers measure such delays and design systems to remove them.

Common mistakes: Thinking x(t - 2) moves left. Forgetting to divide the shift by the scale factor when scaling first. Treating x[2n] as reversible; decimation can lose samples. Mixing up -x(t), which flips up and down, with x(-t), which flips left and right. And forgetting that for x(-t + 1) the reversal changes which end of the signal is first.

What exams ask: 'Given a sketch of x(t), sketch x(2t + 1), x(-t/2 + 1) and x(t)u(1 - t).' 'Given x[n] = {1, 2, 3, 4} with n = 0 at the first value, find x[2n], x[n/2] and x[3 - n].' For x[3 - n], use the one-point method: x[3 - n] at n = 3 is x[0] = 1, at n = 2 is x[1] = 2, at n = 1 is x[2] = 3, at n = 0 is x[3] = 4. So the list reverses and sits on n = 0 to 3.

Recap: Shifting x(t - t0) delays for positive t0. Reversal x(-t) mirrors about zero. Scaling x(at) compresses for a > 1 and stretches for a < 1; in discrete time x[2n] drops samples and x[n/2] inserts zeros. For combined operations, shift then scale, or scale then shift by b/a. When in doubt, solve the inequality for where the original signal lived. Amplitude operations scale, flip, offset, add and multiply values.
key_points: x(t - t0) is a delay (shift right) when t0 > 0 and an advance (shift left) when t0 < 0.
x(-t) is time reversal, a mirror image about t = 0; -x(t) is amplitude reversal, an upside-down flip.
x(at) compresses the signal for a > 1 and stretches it for 0 < a < 1.
In discrete time, x[2n] keeps every second sample (decimation, may lose data) and x[n/2] inserts zeros (expansion).
For x(at - b): shift by b then scale by a, or scale by a then shift by b/a.
The one-point check: solve where the bracket equals the original start and end points to locate the new signal.
Multiplying by a box or by u(t) acts like a window that keeps part of a signal and zeros the rest.
lessons.tip: Never trust your eyes with combined operations. Write the original range, like 0 ≤ ... ≤ 2, put the new bracket in the middle and solve for t. It takes ten seconds and is always right.
lessons.task: Draw a ramp x(t) = t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 (zero elsewhere). Using the inequality method, sketch x(t - 1), x(2t), x(-t) and x(-2t + 2), labelling the start and end values on each sketch.

quiz.q: x(t) is non-zero only for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Where is x(t - 3) non-zero?
quiz.explain: 0 ≤ t - 3 ≤ 2 gives 3 ≤ t ≤ 5. A positive t0 is a delay, a shift to the right.

quiz.q: x(t) is a box on 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Where is x(2t - 4) non-zero?
If x[n] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} for n = 0 to 4, what is y[n] = x[2n]?
quiz.explain: y[0] = x[0] = 1, y[1] = x[2] = 3, y[2] = x[4] = 5. Odd samples are dropped.

quiz.q: Which operation plays a recording at double speed?
quiz.explain: x(2t) compresses time by 2, so the recording finishes in half the time.

quiz.q: What is the difference between x(-t) and -x(t)?
options: x(-t) flips left-right; -x(t) flips upside down
x(-t) doubles the signal; -x(t) delays it
x(-t) flips upside down; -x(t) flips left-right
quiz.explain: x(-t) is time reversal (mirror about t = 0); -x(t) is amplitude reversal (mirror about the time axis).

lessons.title: Elementary Signals: Step, Impulse, Ramp, Exponential, Sinusoid
lessons.content:
With LEGO, you can build a ship, a house or a robot, but all of them are made from a handful of basic bricks. Signals work the same way. A few simple signals act as building blocks, and almost every signal you meet can be built from them by shifting, scaling and adding. Learn these bricks well, because every later lesson uses them: the step, the impulse, the ramp, the exponential and the sinusoid.

The unit step, continuous time: The unit step u(t) is 0 for all t < 0 and 1 for t ≥ 0 (some books leave the exact value at t = 0 undefined or set it to 1/2, but it rarely matters). Think of flipping on a light switch at time zero: before, nothing; after, a steady value. The step is perfect for describing anything that suddenly turns on: a battery connected to a circuit, a motor started, a song beginning.

The unit step, discrete time: u[n] is 0 for n < 0 and 1 for n ≥ 0. Here there is no confusion about the value at zero: u[0] = 1. As a list starting at n = 0: 1, 1, 1, 1, ... forever.

Using steps as switches: Because u(t - t0) switches on at t = t0, multiplying any signal by it keeps only the part after t0. And subtracting two steps makes a box. The rectangular pulse that is 1 from t = 0 to t = 2 is u(t) - u(t - 2). Check at t = 1: u(1) = 1 and u(-1) = 0, so the result is 1. At t = 3: 1 - 1 = 0. So any 'on for a while, then off' signal can be written with two steps, which makes formulas short and exact.

The unit impulse, discrete time: The discrete unit impulse δ[n], also called the Kronecker delta, is 1 at n = 0 and 0 everywhere else. It is a single tap: one sample of value 1 in a sea of zeros. It is easy and has no mystery. δ[n - 3] is a single 1 at n = 3.

Building any discrete signal from impulses: Here is the most important idea of this lesson. Any discrete signal can be written as a sum of scaled, shifted impulses. Take x[n] = {2, 5, -1} at n = 0, 1, 2. Then x[n] = 2δ[n] + 5δ[n - 1] - δ[n - 2]. Check at n = 1: only the middle term is non-zero, giving 5. In general, x[n] = sum over k of x[k]δ[n - k]. This looks like a boring identity now, but in a few lessons it will give us convolution, the key to LTI systems.

Step and impulse in discrete time: The impulse is the difference of two steps: δ[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1]. At n = 0: 1 - 0 = 1. At n = 5: 1 - 1 = 0. And the step is the running sum of impulses: u[n] = sum of δ[k] for all k ≤ n. If n is 0 or more, that sum includes k = 0 and equals 1; if n is negative, it is 0. Difference and running sum are the discrete versions of derivative and integral.

The unit impulse, continuous time: The continuous impulse δ(t), called the Dirac delta, is stranger. Imagine a tall thin box centred at zero with width w and height 1/w. Its area is always 1. Now make w smaller and smaller: the box gets narrower and taller, but the area stays 1. The Dirac delta is the limit: zero everywhere except at t = 0, infinitely tall there, with total area 1. It is not an ordinary function, but engineers treat it as an idealised very short, very strong kick. We draw it as an arrow at t = 0 labelled with its area.

Why the impulse is useful: Real life has many short kicks: a hammer tap, a camera flash, a clap, a lightning strike. Compared with how slowly a system responds, these are so short that only their total strength (the area) matters, not their exact shape. The Dirac delta captures exactly that. If you clap in a hall and record the echoes, you have measured the hall's impulse response, which later lessons show describes the whole hall as an LTI system.

The sifting property: The most used property of δ(t) is this: the integral of x(t)δ(t - t0) over all t equals x(t0). The impulse 'sifts out' the value of x at the one place where it lives. For example, the integral of (t squared + 1)δ(t - 3) dt equals 3 squared + 1 = 10. A related property: x(t)δ(t - t0) = x(t0)δ(t - t0), because only the value at t0 matters. The discrete version is x[n]δ[n - n0] = x[n0]δ[n - n0].

Step and impulse in continuous time: The step is the running integral of the impulse: u(t) = integral of δ(τ) from minus infinity to t. Before zero, the integral has collected no area; after zero, it has collected area 1. Going the other way, the impulse is the derivative of the step: δ(t) = du(t)/dt. The step is flat everywhere except for a sudden jump at zero, and the derivative of a sudden jump of size 1 is an impulse of area 1. More generally, any jump of size J in a signal produces an impulse of area J in its derivative.

The ramp: The unit ramp r(t) = t u(t) is 0 for t < 0 and rises with slope 1 after. Its derivative is the step: dr/dt = u(t). So we have a family: integrate the impulse to get the step, integrate the step to get the ramp. In discrete time, r[n] = n u[n] gives 0, 1, 2, 3, ... from n = 0. Ramps describe things that grow steadily, like water filling a bucket from a tap.

Real exponentials: x(t) = C e^(at) with real C and a. If a > 0, it grows, like money in a savings account with compound interest. If a < 0, it decays, like a cup of tea cooling toward room temperature or a capacitor discharging. If a = 0, it is a constant. A key number is the time constant, 1/|a|: after one time constant a decaying exponential has dropped to about 37 percent of its start (e^(-1) is about 0.368).

Discrete exponentials: x[n] = C a^n. If 0 < a < 1, it shrinks: (0.5)^n gives 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, .... If a > 1, it grows. If a is negative, the sign flips every step: (-0.5)^n gives 1, -0.5, 0.25, -0.125, ..., shrinking while alternating. If |a| = 1 it neither grows nor shrinks. These discrete exponentials appear everywhere: as impulse responses of simple digital filters and as solutions of difference equations.

Sinusoids: x(t) = A cos(ω0 t + φ). A is the amplitude (the peak height), ω0 is the angular frequency in radians per second, and φ is the phase, which shifts the wave left or right. Frequency in hertz is f0 = ω0/(2π) and the period is T0 = 1/f0. Example: 3 cos(100πt) has amplitude 3, ω0 = 100π, f0 = 50 Hz and period 0.02 seconds, the same frequency as the electricity in Bangladeshi wall sockets.

Complex exponentials: Euler's formula from Math III says e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ, where j is the square root of -1 (engineers use j because i means current). So e^(jω0 t) = cos(ω0 t) + j sin(ω0 t): a point running around a circle of radius 1 at speed ω0. Its real part is a cosine and its imaginary part is a sine. And cos(ω0 t) = (e^(jω0 t) + e^(-jω0 t)) / 2. Engineers love complex exponentials because their maths is simpler than cosines: derivatives and shifts just multiply them by a number. Later you will see they pass through LTI systems unchanged in shape, which is the whole reason Fourier analysis works.

The general complex exponential: With s = σ + jω, the signal e^(st) = e^(σt)(cos ωt + j sin ωt). Its real part is a cosine wrapped in an exponential envelope. If σ < 0, the wave dies out, like a plucked guitar string fading. If σ > 0, it grows, like the howl of feedback when a microphone gets too close to a speaker. If σ = 0, it is a steady wave. This one signal includes constants, exponentials and sinusoids as special cases, and it is the heart of the Laplace transform.

Discrete sinusoids have a speed limit: Here is a big difference from continuous time. e^(jω0 n) and e^(j(ω0 + 2π)n) are exactly the same signal, because e^(j2πn) = 1 for every integer n. So a discrete frequency is only meaningful in a range of width 2π, usually from -π to π. The fastest possible oscillation is at ω0 = π: cos(πn) = (-1)^n = 1, -1, 1, -1, .... Increasing ω0 from π to 2π actually makes the signal look slower again, until at 2π it is a constant. In discrete time, 'high frequency' means near π and 'low frequency' means near 0 (or near 2π).

Real-life example 1, switching on a fan: When you switch on a ceiling fan, the voltage applied is like a step. The fan's speed does not jump; it rises along a curve like 1 - e^(-t/τ), an exponential approaching its final speed, with τ of a few seconds. When the load-shedding cuts the power, the input becomes a step downward and the speed decays exponentially toward zero. One step input, one exponential response: you will compute exactly this in the convolution lessons.

Real-life example 2, the electricity line hum: The voltage in a Bangladeshi wall socket is close to a sinusoid of about 220 to 230 volts RMS at 50 Hz, so its peak is roughly 311 to 325 volts (RMS times about 1.414). The mains is designed to be a pure sinusoid, but motors and chargers add small extra waves at multiples of 50 Hz. Engineers describe this with sums of sinusoids, and a cheap audio cable picking up a 50 Hz hum is a common headache that filters fix.

Common mistakes: Writing δ(0) = 1 for the continuous delta; it is the area that is 1, not the height. Forgetting the sifting property needs the integral (or the sum) to give a number. Thinking cos(πn) and cos(3πn) are different signals; they are identical in discrete time. Mixing up ω (radians per second) and f (hertz); remember ω = 2πf. And forgetting that u(t) - u(t - 2) is the box, not u(t - 2) - u(t).

What exams ask: 'Evaluate the integral of e^(-t)δ(t - 2) dt' (answer e^(-2), about 0.135). 'Express the given signal using steps and ramps.' 'Find the period of 5 sin(4πt + π/3)' (ω0 = 4π, so T0 = 2π/4π = 0.5 seconds). 'Write x[n] = {3, 0, -2} at n = 0, 1, 2 as a sum of impulses' (3δ[n] - 2δ[n - 2]).

Recap: The step switches things on; the impulse is a single unit kick (a sample of 1 in discrete time, area 1 in continuous time). They are linked: impulse is the derivative or difference of the step, step is the running integral or sum of the impulse, and the ramp integrates the step. Sifting picks one value of a signal. Exponentials grow or decay, sinusoids oscillate, and the complex exponential e^(st) covers them all. Discrete frequencies only matter within a 2π range, with π the fastest.
key_points: u(t) or u[n] switches on at zero; u(t) - u(t - 2) builds a box from 0 to 2.
δ[n] is 1 at n = 0 only; δ(t) is an idealised kick with zero width and area 1.
Any discrete signal is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses: x[n] = Σ x[k]δ[n - k].
Sifting: the integral of x(t)δ(t - t0) dt equals x(t0).
Impulse is the derivative (or difference) of the step; the step is the running integral (or sum) of the impulse; the ramp integrates the step.
e^(st) with s = σ + jω covers constants, growing/decaying exponentials and sinusoids; Euler gives e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ.
Discrete frequencies repeat every 2π; the fastest discrete oscillation is ω0 = π, giving (-1)^n.

quiz.explain: By the sifting property, the integral equals the function at t = 3: 9 + 1 = 10.

quiz.q: Which expression gives a rectangular pulse equal to 1 for 0 ≤ t < 2?
quiz.explain: u(t) switches on at 0 and subtracting u(t - 2) switches it off at 2.

quiz.q: What is the derivative of the unit step u(t)?
quiz.explain: The step is flat except for a jump of size 1 at zero, and that jump's derivative is an impulse of area 1.

quiz.q: Which discrete-time sinusoid oscillates fastest?
quiz.explain: Discrete frequencies repeat every 2π, and π is the fastest; cos(πn) = 1, -1, 1, -1. cos(1.9πn) looks the same as cos(0.1πn), and cos(2πn) is a constant.
