lessons.title: System Properties: Memory, Causality, Linearity, Time Invariance, Stability, Invertibility
lessons.content:
When you buy a new phone, you check a few things: does it have enough memory, is the battery stable, does the camera behave the same in the morning and at night? Engineers check systems in a similar way, using six standard questions. Is it memoryless? Is it causal? Is it linear? Is it time-invariant? Is it stable? Is it invertible? Each answer is a simple yes or no, and together they tell you what tools you may use. This lesson defines each property, shows how to test it step by step, and works through examples you will see in exams.

The golden rule of testing: To prove a property holds, you must show it works for every possible input. To prove it fails, one counterexample is enough. So when testing, first try to find a simple input that breaks the property, like a step, an impulse or a constant. If you cannot break it, then prove it in general with letters.

Memory: A system is memoryless if the output at each time depends only on the input at that same time. y(t) = 5x(t) is memoryless: to know y at t = 3 you only need x at t = 3. A resistor is memoryless: the current now depends only on the voltage now (I = V/R). A system has memory if it needs past or future inputs. y[n] = x[n - 1], a one-step delay, has memory. The accumulator y[n] = sum of x[k] for all k ≤ n remembers every past input. A capacitor has memory because its voltage depends on all the current that flowed into it before.

Memory examples worked: y(t) = x(t) squared: memoryless, since only x(t) is used. y(t) = x(t - 1) + x(t): memory, because x(t - 1) is a past value. y(t) = cos(x(t)): memoryless. y(t) = x(2t): memory, because at t = 1 it needs x(2), a different time. The test is simply: does the formula ever use the input at a time other than the current t?

Causality: A system is causal if the output at any time depends only on present and past inputs, never on future ones. Every real system that works in real time must be causal, because no machine can react to something that has not happened yet. y[n] = x[n] + x[n - 1] is causal. y[n] = x[n + 1] is not causal: it needs tomorrow's input today. A memoryless system is always causal, since it only uses the present.

Tricky causality cases: y(t) = x(-t). At t = -2, the output is x(2), a future value. So it is not causal. y(t) = x(2t): at t = 1 it needs x(2), which is in the future. Not causal. y(t) = x(t/2): at t = 2 it needs x(1), a past value, but at t = -2 it needs x(-1), which is later than -2. So it is not causal either, because causality must hold for all t, including negative times. y(t) = x(t)cos(t + 1): only x(t) is used, so it is causal, even though cos(t + 1) looks like it is 'ahead'. That cosine is a fixed function of time, not the input.

Why non-causal systems still matter: If you already have the whole recording, for example a photo or a stored song, you can process it with non-causal systems. A photo-blurring filter uses pixels on both sides, left and right. Audio editors can look ahead in the file. So non-causal is not useless; it just cannot run live.

Linearity: A system is linear if it obeys two rules. Additivity: if input x1 gives y1 and input x2 gives y2, then x1 + x2 gives y1 + y2. Homogeneity (scaling): if x gives y, then a times x gives a times y, for any number a. Combined, this is the superposition principle: a x1 + b x2 gives a y1 + b y2. Linearity is a superpower, because it lets you split a complicated input into simple pieces, solve each piece, and add the answers.

Testing linearity, y(t) = 3x(t): Input a x1 + b x2 gives 3(a x1 + b x2) = a(3x1) + b(3x2) = a y1 + b y2. Linear. Testing y(t) = x(t) squared: input 2x gives 4x squared, but 2 times the old output is 2x squared. Not equal, so not linear. Testing y(t) = t x(t): input a x1 + b x2 gives t(a x1 + b x2) = a(t x1) + b(t x2). Linear, even though t appears; t multiplies the input, it does not square it.

The zero-in zero-out test: A quick check: every linear system must give zero output for zero input. Why? Put a = 0 in homogeneity: 0 times x gives 0 times y = 0. So y(t) = 2x(t) + 3 is not linear, because zero input gives 3. This catches many exam traps. Such a system is called incrementally linear or affine: it is a linear system plus a fixed offset. Note the test only works one way: passing it does not prove linearity (x squared also gives zero for zero input).

Time invariance: A system is time-invariant if a delay at the input causes exactly the same delay at the output, and nothing else changes. In words, the system behaves the same today and tomorrow. Test: let y(t) be the output for x(t). Feed in the delayed input x(t - t0) and call the output y2(t). Then compare y2(t) with the delayed old output y(t - t0). If they are always equal, the system is time-invariant.

Testing time invariance, y(t) = x(t) + x(t - 1): Feeding x(t - t0) gives y2(t) = x(t - t0) + x(t - t0 - 1). Shifting the old output gives y(t - t0) = x(t - t0) + x(t - t0 - 1). Same, so time-invariant. Testing y(t) = t x(t): feeding x(t - t0) gives y2(t) = t x(t - t0). Shifting the old output gives (t - t0) x(t - t0). Not equal, so time-varying. The coefficient t changes with time, like an amplifier whose gain is slowly turned up.

A famous trap, y(t) = x(2t): Feeding x(t - t0) means replacing x(·) with a delayed version, so y2(t) = x(2t - t0). The shifted old output is y(t - t0) = x(2(t - t0)) = x(2t - 2t0). These differ, so time-scaling is time-varying. Similarly, y[n] = x[-n] is time-varying. The careful method is: first apply the delay to the input function, then apply the system, and compare with shifting the final formula.

Stability, BIBO: A system is BIBO stable (bounded input, bounded output) if every input that stays within some limit produces an output that also stays within some limit. Bounded means there is a number M with |x(t)| ≤ M for all t. y(t) = 5x(t) is stable: if |x| ≤ M, then |y| ≤ 5M. The accumulator y[n] = sum of all past x[k] is not stable: feed in the step u[n], which is bounded by 1, and the output is n + 1, which grows forever. y(t) = e^(x(t)) is stable: if |x| ≤ M then y ≤ e^M. y(t) = t x(t) is not stable: a constant input 1 gives output t, which grows without limit.

Why stability matters: An unstable system can turn a tiny, harmless input into an enormous output. The howl when a microphone is near a speaker is an unstable feedback loop. In an aeroplane autopilot or a building's lift controller, instability can be dangerous. Engineers always check stability first. In later lessons you will learn quick tests using the impulse response and pole positions.

Invertibility: A system is invertible if different inputs always give different outputs, so you can recover the input from the output. y(t) = 2x(t) is invertible: the inverse system is x(t) = y(t)/2. y(t) = x(t) squared is not: inputs 3 and -3 both give 9. y(t) = 0 is not: every input gives 0. The accumulator is invertible: the inverse is the first difference, x[n] = y[n] - y[n - 1]. Invertibility matters in communication, where the receiver must undo what the channel did, and in encryption, where decryption is the inverse system.

A full worked example: Test y[n] = n x[n]. Memory: uses only x[n], so memoryless. Causal: yes, since memoryless. Linear: input a x1 + b x2 gives n(a x1 + b x2) = a y1 + b y2, yes. Time-invariant: delayed input gives n x[n - n0], delayed output is (n - n0) x[n - n0], not equal, so no. Stable: constant input 1 gives output n, unbounded, so no. Invertible: at n = 0 the output is always 0 whatever x[0] is, so you cannot recover x[0]; not invertible.

Real-life example 1, the mobile banking balance: Think of your bKash balance as the output and each day's deposits and withdrawals as the input. Balance today = balance yesterday + today's change. This is an accumulator. It has memory (it depends on every past day), it is causal (no future transactions counted), linear and time-invariant (the rule is the same every day). It is not BIBO stable: if you deposit a fixed 100 taka every day, a bounded input, the balance grows without limit. Good for you, but mathematically unstable.

Real-life example 2, a photo filter on a phone: A blur filter replaces each pixel by the average of itself and its neighbours. It has memory (uses nearby positions), is non-causal in the left-right sense (uses pixels on both sides), is linear (blurring two images added together equals adding the two blurred images), is space-invariant (same rule everywhere on the image), is stable (an average of bounded values is bounded) and is usually not perfectly invertible (sharp detail lost in the blur cannot be fully recovered, especially with noise).

Common mistakes: Using one example to 'prove' linearity; you need the general proof. Forgetting that the offset in y = 2x + 3 breaks linearity. Testing time invariance by shifting the formula's t everywhere instead of shifting only the input. Saying y(t) = x(t/2) is causal because it uses the past for positive t; check negative t too. Mixing up 'bounded' with 'finite at each time'; bounded means one limit for all time.

What exams ask: A classic question gives four to six systems and asks you to fill a table with yes/no for each property, with short justifications. Practise on y(t) = x(t - 2) + x(2 - t), y[n] = x[n]x[n - 1], y(t) = sin(x(t)), y[n] = x[n] + n and y(t) = the integral of x from minus infinity to t. Write one line of reasoning per cell.

Recap: Memoryless means only the present input is used. Causal means no future inputs. Linear means superposition holds, and zero input must give zero output. Time-invariant means delaying the input just delays the output. BIBO stable means bounded inputs give bounded outputs. Invertible means the input can be recovered. Disprove with one counterexample; prove with a general argument. Systems that are both linear and time-invariant, LTI, get the rest of the course.
key_points: Memoryless: output depends only on the input at the same time; a delay or accumulator has memory.
Causal: output depends only on present and past inputs; every memoryless system is causal.
Linear: superposition a x1 + b x2 gives a y1 + b y2; zero input must give zero output, so y = 2x + 3 is not linear.
Time-invariant: delaying the input only delays the output; y(t) = t x(t) and y(t) = x(2t) are time-varying.
BIBO stable: every bounded input gives a bounded output; the accumulator is unstable because a step gives a growing ramp.
Invertible: distinct inputs give distinct outputs; y = x squared is not invertible, the accumulator is (inverse = first difference).
One counterexample disproves a property; proving it needs a general argument.
lessons.tip: Keep a list of 'killer test inputs': zero, a constant, a step, an impulse, and a negative copy of the input. Most properties can be broken in one line with one of these.
lessons.task: Make a 6-column table (memory, causal, linear, time-invariant, stable, invertible) and fill it for y[n] = x[n - 2], y[n] = 2x[n] + 1, y[n] = x[n] squared and y[n] = the average of x[n] and x[n + 1]. Write one line of reason per cell.

quiz.q: Why is y(t) = 2x(t) + 3 not linear?
options: Because zero input gives output 3, not zero
quiz.explain: Any linear system must give zero output for zero input; the +3 offset breaks this.

quiz.q: Which system is not causal?
quiz.explain: y[n] = x[n + 1] needs the next input, a future value.

quiz.q: Is y(t) = t x(t) time-invariant?
options: No, delaying the input gives t x(t - t0), not (t - t0) x(t - t0)
quiz.explain: The multiplier t changes with time, so the response to a delayed input is not just a delayed response.

quiz.q: Why is the accumulator y[n] = sum of x[k] for k ≤ n not BIBO stable?
options: A bounded step input produces an output that grows without limit
quiz.explain: With x[n] = u[n], the output is n + 1, which is unbounded.

quiz.q: Which system is invertible?
quiz.explain: x(t) = y(t)/2 recovers the input. Squaring and absolute value lose the sign; y = 0 loses everything.

lessons.title: Connecting Systems and Block Diagrams
lessons.content:
Think of a garment factory in Gazipur. Cloth goes into the cutting section, then to sewing, then to washing, then to packing. Each section is a system: something goes in, something different comes out. The whole factory is one big system made by connecting small ones. Sometimes two lines work side by side and their output is combined. Sometimes a quality checker sends faulty shirts back to an earlier step. Signals and systems are connected in exactly these ways, and engineers draw them with block diagrams. This lesson teaches you to read and build these diagrams, and shows why one special family of systems, LTI, makes connected systems easy.

Why connect systems: Big systems are too hard to design in one go. A mobile phone's audio path, for example, has a microphone, an amplifier, a filter to remove noise, an analog-to-digital converter, a compressor and more. Engineers design and test each part separately, then connect them. If we know how each part behaves and how they are connected, we can predict the whole. This is the same divide-and-conquer idea you use in programming when you break a big program into functions.

The three basic building blocks of a diagram: Most block diagrams of discrete-time systems use only three kinds of block. The adder, drawn as a circle with a plus sign, adds its inputs: if 3 and 5 come in, 8 goes out. A minus sign on one arrow means that input is subtracted. The multiplier or gain, drawn as a triangle or a box with a number like 0.5, multiplies its input by that number. The unit delay, drawn as a box labelled D or z^(-1), outputs its input one step later: if x[n] goes in, x[n - 1] comes out. For continuous-time systems, the delay is usually replaced by an integrator, a box labelled with the integral sign or 1/s.

Reading a simple diagram: Suppose x[n] goes into an adder. The adder also receives x[n] passed through a delay and a gain of 0.5. The adder output is y[n]. Then y[n] = x[n] + 0.5x[n - 1]. If x = {2, 4, 6} at n = 0, 1, 2, then y[0] = 2 + 0.5(0) = 2, y[1] = 4 + 0.5(2) = 5, y[2] = 6 + 0.5(4) = 8, and y[3] = 0 + 0.5(6) = 3. This is an echo system: each sample plus half of the previous one.

Series connection, also called cascade: In a series connection, the output of the first system becomes the input of the second. Input x goes into system 1, giving w; w goes into system 2, giving y. Example: system 1 doubles, w = 2x; system 2 adds a one-step delay, y[n] = w[n - 1]. Together, y[n] = 2x[n - 1]. A phone call path is a long cascade: microphone, amplifier, filter, converter, encoder and so on, one after another.

Does order matter in a cascade: For general systems, yes. Let system A square its input and system B double it. A then B gives 2x squared. B then A gives (2x) squared = 4x squared. Different. But for LTI systems, the order never matters: you can swap any two LTI blocks in a cascade and the overall result is the same. This is a big convenience, proved in a later lesson using convolution. It lets engineers rearrange blocks to save memory or reduce noise.

Parallel connection: In a parallel connection, the same input goes into two systems at once, and their outputs are added. y = y1 + y2. Example: system 1 is y1[n] = x[n], system 2 is y2[n] = 0.3x[n - 2]. Together y[n] = x[n] + 0.3x[n - 2]. A sound engineer adding a little reverb to a singer's voice is doing exactly this: the dry voice plus a delayed, softer copy. For LTI systems, a parallel connection is equivalent to one system whose impulse response is the sum of the two impulse responses.

Feedback connection: In a feedback connection, part of the output is sent back and combined with the input. The diagram has a loop. The simplest form: e = x - H·y and y = G·e, where G is the forward gain and H is the feedback gain, both plain numbers for now. Substituting, y = G(x - Hy), so y + GHy = Gx, giving y = (G/(1 + GH))x. This G/(1 + GH) is the famous closed-loop gain formula for negative feedback.

A feedback example with numbers: Take G = 100 and H = 0.1. Then GH = 10 and the closed-loop gain is 100/11, about 9.09. Now imagine G drifts, because the amplifier gets hot, from 100 to 50. The new gain is 50/6, about 8.33. The open amplifier changed by 50 percent, but the closed-loop system changed by only about 8 percent. That is why negative feedback is everywhere in electronics: it trades raw gain for stability and accuracy. When GH is large, the gain is close to 1/H, which depends only on the feedback part, often made with precise resistors.

Feedback with memory, recursion: In discrete time, a feedback loop usually contains a delay, because a system cannot use its own output at the same instant without causing a loop that has no answer. Example: y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n - 1]. The diagram has x going into an adder; the adder output is y; y passes through a delay and a gain of 0.5 and returns to the adder. Let x be an impulse: x[0] = 1, else 0. Assuming y[-1] = 0, we get y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0.5, y[2] = 0.25, y[3] = 0.125, and so on. A single tap produces an output that goes on forever, slowly fading. This is called an infinite impulse response, and it comes from the feedback.

Positive feedback and instability: If the feedback adds instead of subtracts, or if the loop gain is too large, things can blow up. With y[n] = x[n] + 2y[n - 1] and an impulse input, the output is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ..., doubling forever. This is the microphone howl from the last lesson in equation form. In general, for this simple loop, the output dies out when the feedback multiplier has magnitude less than 1 and grows when it is greater than 1. Later, poles will give a neat way to state this for any system.

Input-output equations: Every block diagram made of adders, gains and delays can be written as one equation linking y[n] to x[n] and their delayed versions. This is a linear constant-coefficient difference equation, such as y[n] - 0.5y[n - 1] = x[n] + x[n - 1]. In continuous time, diagrams with integrators give differential equations, such as dy/dt + 2y = x. Diagram and equation are two views of the same system: one for drawing hardware or code, one for doing maths. Lesson 12 goes deeper into both.

From diagram to code: A block diagram turns directly into a program. For y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n - 1], the code is a loop: keep a variable prev = 0; for each new input value, compute y = x + 0.5*prev, output y, then set prev = y. The delay block became one stored variable. This is how audio effects in music apps and sensor smoothers in phones are really written.

Simplifying a bigger diagram: Suppose a diagram has two branches in parallel, one with gain 2 and one with a delay followed by gain 3, and the sum then goes in series into a block with gain 0.5. Step one: the parallel part gives w[n] = 2x[n] + 3x[n - 1]. Step two: the series block halves it: y[n] = x[n] + 1.5x[n - 1]. With x = {1, 1} at n = 0, 1, we get y[0] = 1, y[1] = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 and y[2] = 1.5. Reducing a diagram one connection at a time, from the inside out, is the reliable method.

Why LTI systems are the star: Out of all possible systems, why does this course focus so much on linear time-invariant ones? Four reasons. First, many real systems are LTI, or very close to it in their normal working range: circuits of resistors, capacitors and inductors, rooms that echo, cables, simple digital filters. Second, LTI systems can be fully described by one signal, the impulse response, as the next lesson shows. Third, connected LTI systems are still LTI, so whole chains can be analysed with the same tools. Fourth, sine waves and complex exponentials pass through LTI systems keeping their frequency, only changing size and timing, which makes frequency analysis possible.

When systems are not LTI: Many real systems are non-linear (a guitar distortion pedal, a diode, a saturating amplifier) or time-varying (a mobile channel as you move, an amplifier with automatic gain control). Engineers often approximate them as LTI over a small range, like treating a curved road as straight for a few metres. The LTI toolbox still gives a strong starting point.

Real-life example 1, a public address system at a waz mahfil: The speaker's voice goes into a microphone, then an amplifier, then the loudspeakers: a cascade. Several loudspeakers placed around the field play the same signal: a parallel arrangement, and since they are at different distances, listeners hear slightly delayed copies added together. If the microphone is too close to a loudspeaker, sound loops back: a feedback path. When the loop gain passes a certain point, the familiar screech starts. Turning down the volume reduces the loop gain and stops the howl.

Real-life example 2, a water tank with a float valve: In many houses a float valve fills the roof tank. Water level is the output; inflow is controlled by the float. When the level rises, the valve closes a little, reducing inflow: negative feedback. The system settles at a fixed level instead of overflowing. Drawn as a block diagram, the tank is an integrator (water level adds up the net inflow over time) and the valve is a feedback block subtracting from the inflow.

Common mistakes: Adding outputs in a series connection; in series, one feeds the next, while in parallel they are added. Forgetting the minus sign at the adder in negative feedback. Writing y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n] instead of 0.5y[n - 1]; a feedback loop in discrete time needs a delay. Assuming any two systems can be swapped in a cascade; only LTI systems guarantee this.

What exams ask: 'Draw the block diagram of y[n] = 2x[n] - 0.25y[n - 2].' 'Find the overall input-output relation of the given connection.' 'Find the closed-loop gain when G = 50 and H = 0.2' (50/11, about 4.55). 'Show by example that the order of a cascade of non-linear systems matters.'

Recap: Block diagrams use adders, gains and delays (or integrators). In series, outputs feed inputs; in parallel, outputs add; in feedback, output returns to the input, and for negative feedback with plain gains, y = G/(1 + GH) times x. Feedback with a delay creates responses that last forever and can be unstable if the loop gain is too big. Every diagram matches a difference or differential equation and maps directly to code. LTI systems stay LTI when connected, and in a cascade their order can be swapped.
key_points: Block diagrams use three main blocks: adder, gain (multiplier) and unit delay (or integrator in continuous time).
Series (cascade): output of one feeds the next; parallel: same input, outputs are added.
Negative feedback with forward gain G and feedback gain H gives closed-loop gain G/(1 + GH), which is less sensitive to changes in G.
A discrete feedback loop needs a delay, e.g. y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n - 1], which gives an impulse response that never fully ends.
Feedback can cause instability: y[n] = x[n] + 2y[n - 1] doubles forever.
Every diagram corresponds to a difference or differential equation and can be coded as a loop with stored previous values.
Connected LTI systems are still LTI, and the order of LTI blocks in a cascade can be swapped.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet an equation, draw its block diagram; whenever you meet a diagram, write its equation. Going both ways a few times makes both feel natural.
lessons.task: Draw the block diagram of y[n] = x[n] + 0.8y[n - 1]. Then compute by hand the output for an impulse input for n = 0 to 6 and plot it as a stem plot. Repeat with 1.2 instead of 0.8 and compare.

options: The first output feeds the second system
Only the larger one is kept
quiz.explain: In a parallel connection the same input goes to both systems and their outputs are summed.

quiz.q: For negative feedback with G = 100 and H = 0.1, what is the closed-loop gain?
For y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n - 1] with an impulse input and y[-1] = 0, what is y[3]?
System A squares, system B doubles. What does A followed by B give?
quiz.explain: A gives x squared, then B doubles it: 2x squared. The other order gives 4x squared, showing order matters for non-linear systems.

options: The order of the blocks can be swapped without changing the overall result
quiz.explain: A cascade of LTI systems is LTI and the order does not matter, a result shown with convolution.

lessons.title: LTI Systems and the Impulse Response
lessons.content:
Imagine you walk into an empty, dark hall at Shilpakala Academy and want to know how it sounds. You do not need to sing every song ever written inside it. You just clap your hands once, sharply, and listen. You hear the clap, then a rush of echoes bouncing off walls, getting softer and softer. Amazingly, for a linear time-invariant system like a hall, that single clap's echo pattern tells you exactly how any song, any speech and any instrument will sound in that hall. This lesson explains why. It is the most important idea in the whole course.

What is an impulse response: The impulse response of a system is its output when the input is a unit impulse. In discrete time, we feed in δ[n], which is 1 at n = 0 and 0 everywhere else, and we name the output h[n]. In continuous time, we feed in the Dirac delta δ(t) and call the output h(t). The impulse response is like the system's fingerprint. The clap in the hall is a real-world approximation of an impulse, and the recorded echoes are an approximation of h(t).

A simple impulse response: Take the echo system y[n] = x[n] + 0.5x[n - 1]. Feed in x[n] = δ[n]. Then y[0] = δ[0] + 0.5δ[-1] = 1 + 0 = 1. y[1] = δ[1] + 0.5δ[0] = 0 + 0.5 = 0.5. y[2] = 0 + 0 = 0, and all later values are 0. So h[n] = {1, 0.5} at n = 0, 1. The system's fingerprint is: the sound itself, then half of it one step later.

Another impulse response: For the feedback system y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n - 1], starting from rest (y[-1] = 0), the impulse gives y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0.5, y[2] = 0.25, and so on, so h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]. This impulse response never quite ends; it is called an infinite impulse response, or IIR. The echo system above had a finite impulse response, or FIR, of just two samples.

The big claim: For an LTI system, if you know h[n], you can compute the output for any input at all. Not just impulses: steps, songs, speech, random noise, anything. This sounds too good to be true, so let us prove it in three small steps using only the two letters of LTI: linearity and time invariance.

Step 1, break the input into impulses: From the elementary signals lesson, any discrete signal can be written as a sum of shifted, scaled impulses. For example, x[n] = {2, 1} at n = 0, 1 is x[n] = 2δ[n] + 1δ[n - 1]. In general, x[n] = sum over k of x[k]δ[n - k]. Each term is one sample of x, sitting at its own position k, with height x[k]. The input is just a row of scaled taps.

Step 2, use time invariance: We know the response to δ[n] is h[n]. Time invariance says that if the input is delayed by k steps, the output is delayed by k steps and nothing else changes. So the response to δ[n - k] is h[n - k]. One tap at position k produces a copy of the fingerprint starting at position k.

Step 3, use linearity: Linearity has two parts. Scaling: the response to x[k]δ[n - k] is x[k]h[n - k], a copy of the fingerprint multiplied by the tap's height. Adding: the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of their responses. So the response to the whole input, sum of x[k]δ[n - k], is sum over k of x[k]h[n - k]. That is the formula: y[n] = sum over k of x[k]h[n - k].

The convolution sum: This formula is called the convolution sum, and it is written y[n] = x[n] * h[n], where the star means convolution, not multiplication. In words: every input sample launches its own scaled, shifted copy of the impulse response, and the output is all those copies added together. That is all convolution is. The name may sound scary, but the idea is 'add up the echoes from every tap'.

A first worked example: Take h[n] = {1, 0.5} and x[n] = {2, 1}, both starting at n = 0. The first input sample, 2 at k = 0, launches 2 times h starting at 0: {2, 1} at n = 0, 1. The second sample, 1 at k = 1, launches 1 times h starting at 1: {1, 0.5} at n = 1, 2. Now add position by position. n = 0: 2. n = 1: 1 + 1 = 2. n = 2: 0.5. So y[n] = {2, 2, 0.5}. You can double-check with the system's own formula y[n] = x[n] + 0.5x[n - 1]: y[0] = 2, y[1] = 1 + 1 = 2, y[2] = 0 + 0.5 = 0.5. Both methods agree.

A table to keep the copies tidy: For longer signals, write the copies in rows. Take h[n] = {1, 2, 1} and x[n] = {3, 1}. Row 1 is 3 times h starting at n = 0: 3, 6, 3. Row 2 is 1 times h starting at n = 1, so write a blank under n = 0 and then 1, 2, 1. Now add each column: n = 0 gives 3, n = 1 gives 6 + 1 = 7, n = 2 gives 3 + 2 = 5, n = 3 gives 1. So y[n] = {3, 7, 5, 1}. Notice the output has 2 + 3 - 1 = 4 samples. This 'rows of copies' table is the safest hand method, and the next lesson builds on it.

Why this is powerful: For the echo system, we already had a formula, so convolution looked like extra work. But often we do not have a formula; we have only measurements. Audio engineers record the impulse response of a famous concert hall once, store h[n] as a list of numbers, and then convolve any dry recording with it. The result sounds as if it was played in that hall. This is called convolution reverb and is built into many music production programs.

The continuous-time version: The same three steps work in continuous time, with the sum replaced by an integral. Any x(t) can be written as an integral of shifted, scaled impulses, x(τ)δ(t - τ). Each slice of input launches a scaled copy x(τ)h(t - τ). Adding them all up gives the convolution integral: y(t) = integral over τ of x(τ)h(t - τ) dτ, written y(t) = x(t) * h(t). Lesson 10 works through this carefully with pictures.

The step response: Another useful test is the step response s[n], the output when the input is the unit step u[n]. Since a step is a running sum of impulses, the step response of an LTI system is the running sum of the impulse response: s[n] = sum of h[k] for k ≤ n. For h[n] = {1, 0.5}, s[n] = 1, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5, .... In continuous time, s(t) is the running integral of h(t), and h(t) is the derivative of s(t). Engineers often measure the step response because a clean step (switching something on) is easier to produce than a perfect impulse.

Why we need both L and T: If the system were not time-invariant, a tap at position 5 might produce a different fingerprint than a tap at position 0, so one h[n] would not be enough; you would need a different response for every position. If the system were not linear, the scaled taps would not produce scaled responses, and the responses would not simply add. Both properties together make one fingerprint sufficient.

What h tells you directly: Many system properties can be read from h without any other information. If h[n] = 0 for all n < 0, the system is causal (it does not respond before the tap). If h[n] = 0 for n ≠ 0, the system is memoryless; it just multiplies by h[0]. If the sum of |h[n]| is finite, the system is BIBO stable. Lesson 11 proves these.

Measuring an impulse response in practice: A perfect impulse is impossible to make, but short sharp sounds come close: a clap, a balloon pop, a starter pistol. Modern methods play a sweep, a tone sliding from low to high frequency, and then compute the impulse response with software, because a sweep carries more energy and gives cleaner results than a single clap. Either way, the result is a list of numbers that represents the room, the speaker, or the cable.

Real-life example 1, the mosque echo: In a large mosque with hard walls, a voice from the imam's microphone reaches you directly, then from the left wall a little later, then from the dome later still, each copy weaker. That set of arrivals is the impulse response. Every syllable of the khutbah is an input tap, and what you hear is the sum of all the echoes from all the syllables: convolution. When echoes are long, syllables blur into each other, which is why carpets and soft panels, which shorten the impulse response, make speech clearer.

Real-life example 2, a blurry photo: When a camera moves slightly during a photo, each point of light becomes a short streak. That streak is the camera's impulse response in two dimensions, called the point spread function. The blurry photo is the sharp scene convolved with the streak. Photo apps that 'unblur' an image try to estimate this streak and undo the convolution, a process called deconvolution. Astronomers do the same with telescope images.

Common mistakes: Thinking the star in x * h means ordinary multiplication; it means convolution. Forgetting that the impulse response is defined with the system starting at rest, with no stored energy and zero earlier outputs. Using convolution for a system that is not LTI; it only works when both linearity and time invariance hold. And mixing up h[n - k] with h[k - n]; the impulse response is shifted to where the tap is, at position k, so it is h[n - k].

What exams ask: 'Define impulse response. Why does it completely characterise an LTI system?' Expect to write the three-step derivation. 'Find the impulse response of y[n] = x[n] - 2x[n - 1] + x[n - 2]' (answer: {1, -2, 1}). 'Given h[n] = {1, 2} and x[n] = {1, 1, 1}, find y[n]' (answer: {1, 3, 3, 2}).

A quick sanity check you can always use: the sum of all output samples equals the sum of the input samples times the sum of the impulse response samples. In the table example, the input sum is 3 + 1 = 4, the impulse response sum is 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, and the output sum is 3 + 7 + 5 + 1 = 16 = 4 times 4. If your numbers fail this test, you made an addition mistake somewhere.

Recap: The impulse response h is the output when the input is a unit impulse, with the system starting at rest. Any input is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses; time invariance turns each shifted impulse into a shifted h, and linearity scales and adds those copies. The result is the convolution sum y[n] = sum of x[k]h[n - k], or the convolution integral in continuous time. One measurement of h describes an LTI system completely, which is why it is used for room acoustics, photo deblurring and filter design.
key_points: The impulse response h[n] (or h(t)) is the output of a system at rest when the input is a unit impulse.
Any input is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses: x[n] = Σ x[k]δ[n - k].
Time invariance turns δ[n - k] into h[n - k]; linearity turns x[k]δ[n - k] into x[k]h[n - k] and lets responses add.
Convolution sum: y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n - k] = x[n] * h[n]; in continuous time, the convolution integral.
FIR systems have finite-length h; IIR systems, often with feedback, have h that never fully ends, like (0.5)^n u[n].
The step response is the running sum (or integral) of the impulse response.
One h describes an LTI system completely: causality, memory and stability can be read from it.
lessons.tip: When you convolve, say it out loud: 'each input sample launches a copy of h, scaled and shifted; then I add the copies'. If you can picture the copies, you will never get lost in the formula.
lessons.task: Find the impulse response of y[n] = x[n] + x[n - 1] + x[n - 2] (a 3-point sum). Then use the 'launch copies and add' method to find the output for x[n] = {1, 2, 3} at n = 0, 1, 2, and check your answer by plugging directly into the equation.

quiz.q: What is the impulse response of y[n] = x[n] + 0.5x[n - 1]?
quiz.explain: With x = δ, y[0] = 1 and y[1] = 0.5, and all later values are zero.

quiz.q: Which two properties are needed for the convolution formula to describe a system?
quiz.explain: Time invariance makes shifted impulses give shifted h; linearity lets us scale and add the copies.

quiz.q: h[n] = {1, 2} and x[n] = {1, 1, 1}, all starting at n = 0. What is y[n] = x[n] * h[n]?
What does the star in y[n] = x[n] * h[n] mean?
quiz.explain: In signals and systems, * between two signals means convolution.

quiz.q: The feedback system y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n - 1] has h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]. What kind of impulse response is this?
quiz.explain: The impulse response keeps going forever while shrinking, so it is an infinite impulse response.

lessons.title: Convolution Sum: Worked Methods
lessons.content:
Think of a Pohela Boishakh rally moving slowly past a row of tea stalls. Each stall's owner shouts a greeting as the rally passes, and at each moment the total noise is the sum of all the shouts from the stalls the rally is currently next to. As the rally slides along, it overlaps different stalls, and the total keeps changing. That picture of one row sliding past another, multiplying what lines up and adding it all, is exactly how convolution is computed by hand. In the last lesson you learned why convolution works. In this one you will learn to compute it quickly and correctly using three methods.

The formula again: For a discrete LTI system with impulse response h[n] and input x[n], the output is y[n] = sum over k of x[k]h[n - k]. For each output position n, you go through every k, multiply x[k] by h[n - k], and add. Because convolution is commutative, you can also write y[n] = sum over k of h[k]x[n - k]; either order gives the same answer, so pick whichever is easier.

Method 1, rows of copies: This is the method from the last lesson. Each input sample x[k] launches a copy of h, multiplied by x[k] and starting at position k. Write each copy as a row, lined up under the right positions, then add the columns. It is the most natural method and is excellent for short signals.

Rows example: x[n] = {1, 2, 3} and h[n] = {1, 1}, both starting at n = 0. Row from x[0] = 1: 1, 1 at n = 0, 1. Row from x[1] = 2: 2, 2 at n = 1, 2. Row from x[2] = 3: 3, 3 at n = 2, 3. Column sums: n = 0 gives 1; n = 1 gives 1 + 2 = 3; n = 2 gives 2 + 3 = 5; n = 3 gives 3. So y[n] = {1, 3, 5, 3}.

Method 2, flip and slide: This method follows the formula directly and is the one examiners like to see drawn. For each n, think of h[n - k] as a function of k. First flip h to get h[-k]: the list reversed and placed so its first sample is at k = 0 and the others at negative k. Then slide it by n: h[n - k] is the flipped h moved n steps to the right. Wherever the slid h overlaps x, multiply the pairs and add. Each value of n is one position of the slide.

Flip and slide example, same signals: Flip h = {1, 1} to get 1 at k = -1 and 1 at k = 0. For n = 0, the flipped h sits on k = -1, 0. Overlap with x only at k = 0: 1 times 1 = 1. So y[0] = 1. For n = 1, it sits on k = 0, 1: overlap gives 1 times 1 + 2 times 1 = 3. For n = 2, it sits on k = 1, 2: 2 + 3 = 5. For n = 3, it sits on k = 2, 3: only k = 2 overlaps, giving 3. For n = 4, no overlap, so 0. Same answer, {1, 3, 5, 3}, as it must be.

Why flip at all: The flip comes from the h[n - k] in the formula. Physically, think of time: the input sample from long ago (small k) has had more time to travel through h, so it meets the later part of h. The most recent sample meets the start of h. Flipping lines up the newest input with h[0] and the oldest with the tail of h. Once you see it this way, flipping feels natural rather than like a strange rule.

Method 3, the multiplication trick: Here is a lovely shortcut. Convolving two finite lists is exactly like multiplying two numbers in long multiplication, but without carrying. Write x = 1 2 3 and h = 1 1. Multiply: 1 2 3 times 1 gives 1 2 3; shifted one place, 1 2 3 times 1 gives 1 2 3. Add the columns without carrying: 1, 2 + 1, 3 + 2, 3 = 1, 3, 5, 3. Even easier example: 12 times 13 is 156, and {1, 2} convolved with {1, 3} is {1, 5, 6}. Convolution is also exactly polynomial multiplication: (1 + 2z)(1 + 3z) = 1 + 5z + 6z squared. This connection becomes the Z-transform later.

Where does the output start and how long is it: If x is non-zero from n = a for Lx samples, and h is non-zero from n = b for Lh samples, then y is non-zero from n = a + b, and its length is at most Lx + Lh - 1. In the example, a = 0 and b = 0, so y starts at 0, and its length is 3 + 2 - 1 = 4. This is a quick check on every answer. If you get five samples for a 3-sample input and a 2-sample h, something went wrong.

A signal that starts at a negative index: Let x[n] = {1, 2} at n = -1, 0 and h[n] = {1, -1} at n = 0, 1. The output starts at -1 + 0 = -1 and has length 2 + 2 - 1 = 3. Using polynomial multiplication: (1 + 2z)(1 - z) = 1 + 2z - z - 2z squared = 1 + z - 2z squared. So y = {1, 1, -2} at n = -1, 0, 1. Always mark where n = 0 is in your answer.

The moving average: A very common h is the moving average. For three points, h[n] = {1/3, 1/3, 1/3}. Convolving with it replaces each sample by the average of itself and the two before it. Take x = {3, 6, 9, 12}. Then y[0] = 3/3 = 1, y[1] = (3 + 6)/3 = 3, y[2] = (3 + 6 + 9)/3 = 6, y[3] = (6 + 9 + 12)/3 = 9, y[4] = (9 + 12)/3 = 7, y[5] = 12/3 = 4. In the middle, where the window is full, the output is a true average. At the edges the window is partly empty, so values ramp up and down. Moving averages smooth jumpy data and are a simple low-pass filter.

Convolution with infinite signals: Some signals never end, like the step u[n] or an exponential. Then you use the formula with algebra rather than tables. Example: x[n] = u[n] and h[n] = a^n u[n] with |a| < 1. For n ≥ 0, y[n] = sum from k = 0 to n of a^k (the step makes x[n - k] = 1 only for k ≤ n). That is a geometric series: y[n] = (1 - a^(n + 1)) / (1 - a). For a = 0.5: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 1.5, y[2] = 1.75, y[3] = 1.875, approaching 2. For n < 0, y[n] = 0. This is the step response of the feedback system y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n - 1].

The geometric series formula you need: Many convolution problems end in a sum like 1 + r + r squared + ... + r^N. Its value is (1 - r^(N + 1)) / (1 - r) when r is not 1, and N + 1 when r = 1. For an infinite sum with |r| < 1, the value is 1/(1 - r). Keep these handy; they appear again in Z-transforms and stability.

Convolving two exponentials: x[n] = a^n u[n] and h[n] = b^n u[n], with a not equal to b. For n ≥ 0, y[n] = sum from k = 0 to n of a^k b^(n - k) = b^n times the sum of (a/b)^k, which by the geometric series gives (b^(n + 1) - a^(n + 1)) / (b - a). Check with n = 0: (b - a)/(b - a) = 1, and directly y[0] = a^0 b^0 = 1. Good.

Convolving with an impulse: Convolving any x with δ[n] gives x back, since δ is the identity. Convolving with δ[n - 3] shifts x by 3: x[n] * δ[n - 3] = x[n - 3]. This is a delay system, and its h is a single shifted impulse. Convolving with 2δ[n] + δ[n - 1] gives 2x[n] + x[n - 1]. So any FIR system is just a sum of scaled delays.

Real-life example 1, smoothing daily COVID-style case counts: Health dashboards often show a '7-day moving average' instead of raw daily counts. Raw counts jump around because of weekends and reporting delays: a low Friday, a big Sunday. Convolving the daily list with h = {1/7, 1/7, ..., 1/7} (seven values) smooths out the weekly pattern and shows the real trend. That one line on the chart is a convolution sum computed every day.

Real-life example 2, an echo in a recorded announcement: A railway station announcement in Kamalapur is recorded in a hall that adds one echo 0.25 seconds later at 40 percent strength. If the audio is sampled at 8000 samples per second, 0.25 seconds is 2000 samples, so h[n] = δ[n] + 0.4δ[n - 2000]. The recorded signal is the clean voice convolved with this h: y[n] = x[n] + 0.4x[n - 2000]. Knowing h exactly, an engineer can design a system to remove the echo.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to flip h in the slide method, which gives a wrong answer whenever h is not symmetric. Losing track of where n = 0 is when signals start at negative indices. Getting the wrong output length; always check Lx + Lh - 1. Adding the carries in the multiplication trick; convolution never carries. Forgetting the u[n] in answers to infinite convolutions, which says the output is zero for negative n.

What exams ask: 'Find y[n] = x[n] * h[n] for x[n] = {1, 2, 1} and h[n] = {1, -1}, both starting at 0.' (Answer: {1, 1, -1, -1}.) 'Find the step response of h[n] = (0.8)^n u[n].' (Answer: (1 - 0.8^(n + 1))/0.2 for n ≥ 0, which approaches 5.) 'Show graphically the flip and slide for n = 2.' Draw neatly with labelled k axes.

Recap: The convolution sum can be computed by rows of copies, by flip and slide, or by long multiplication without carrying (polynomial multiplication). The output starts at the sum of the start indices and has length Lx + Lh - 1. For infinite signals, use the formula and the geometric series. Convolving with δ[n - n0] shifts a signal, and the moving average smooths it. Always check the start index, the length, and the sum test.
key_points: y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n - k] = Σ h[k]x[n - k]: convolution is commutative.
Rows of copies: each x[k] launches x[k] times h starting at k; add columns.
Flip and slide: flip h to h[-k], shift it by n, multiply overlaps and add for each n.
Convolution of finite lists equals long multiplication without carrying, or polynomial multiplication.
Output starts at the sum of the start indices and has length Lx + Lh - 1.
For infinite signals use the geometric series: 1 + r + ... + r^N = (1 - r^(N+1))/(1 - r).
x[n] * δ[n - n0] = x[n - n0]; a moving average h = {1/N, ..., 1/N} smooths data.
lessons.tip: Use two methods on every exam convolution: compute with rows or flip-and-slide, then check with the no-carry multiplication trick. It takes a minute and catches nearly every arithmetic slip.
lessons.task: Compute {2, 1, -1} * {1, 3} three ways: rows of copies, flip and slide, and no-carry multiplication. Then check the sum test (sum of output = sum of x times sum of h).

quiz.q: x[n] = {1, 2, 3} and h[n] = {1, 1}, both from n = 0. What is y[n]?
quiz.explain: Rows: {1, 1}, {2, 2} shifted by 1, {3, 3} shifted by 2. Columns: 1, 3, 5, 3.

quiz.q: x has 5 samples and h has 4 samples. How long is y = x * h at most?
quiz.explain: Length is Lx + Lh - 1 = 5 + 4 - 1 = 8.

quiz.q: x starts at n = -2 and h starts at n = 3. Where does y = x * h start?
quiz.explain: The output starts at the sum of the start indices: -2 + 3 = 1.

quiz.q: What is x[n] * δ[n - 4]?
quiz.explain: Convolving with a shifted impulse delays the signal by that shift.

quiz.q: What is the step response of h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] at n = 2?

lessons.title: The Convolution Integral (Continuous Time)
lessons.content:
Imagine pouring water into a clay pot with a tiny hole at the bottom. Each splash you pour does not leave at once; it drips out slowly, fast at first and then slower. If you keep pouring a little every moment, the water coming out at any instant is the sum of the leftover drips from every splash you ever poured. Recent splashes drip strongly, old ones barely at all. That is the convolution integral in everyday form: the output now is the input from every past moment, each weighted by how much of it is still coming out. This lesson takes the convolution sum you know and moves it into continuous time, where sums become integrals.

From sum to integral: In discrete time, y[n] = sum over k of x[k]h[n - k]. In continuous time, the input is not a row of separate taps but a smooth flow. Imagine chopping x(t) into very thin slices of width Δτ. Each slice at time τ is like an impulse of area x(τ)Δτ. By time invariance it launches a copy h(t - τ), and by linearity that copy is scaled by x(τ)Δτ. Adding all the copies and letting the slices become infinitely thin turns the sum into an integral: y(t) = integral over all τ of x(τ)h(t - τ) dτ. We write y(t) = x(t) * h(t).

Reading the formula: τ is the dummy variable, the time of each input slice. t is the time at which we want the output. For a fixed t, the integrand x(τ)h(t - τ) is a product of two functions of τ, and the integral is the area under that product. So to find y at one moment, you compute one area. To find the whole y(t), you repeat for every t, which usually means a few cases, because the overlap changes shape at certain points.

The graphical method, step by step: Step 1: draw x(τ) on a τ axis. Step 2: draw h(τ), then flip it to get h(-τ). Step 3: slide the flipped h by t to get h(t - τ); for positive t it moves right. Step 4: for each t, find where x(τ) and h(t - τ) overlap, multiply them there, and find the area. Step 5: the breakpoints, where the edges of the two shapes meet, split t into cases. Handle each case with its own integral limits.

Worked example 1, box with box: Let x(t) = h(t) = a box of height 1 from 0 to 1. Flip h: a box from -1 to 0. Slide by t: a box from t - 1 to t. Case t < 0: the sliding box is entirely left of x, no overlap, y = 0. Case 0 ≤ t ≤ 1: the sliding box covers from t - 1 to t, overlapping x from 0 to t. The product is 1 there, so the area is t: y = t. Case 1 ≤ t ≤ 2: overlap from t - 1 to 1, length 2 - t: y = 2 - t. Case t > 2: no overlap, y = 0. Result: a triangle starting at 0, peaking at height 1 when t = 1, ending at 2.

What the triangle teaches: Two boxes of width 1 gave a shape of width 2. In general, if x lives on [a, b] and h lives on [c, d], then y lives on [a + c, b + d]. Widths add, just like lengths add in discrete time (minus one sample). Also, convolution tends to smooth: two shapes with sharp corners produced a triangle with a gentler shape, and convolving the triangle with another box would give an even smoother curve. Repeat this many times and the result looks more and more like a bell curve.

Worked example 2, step into an exponential system: Let x(t) = u(t) and h(t) = e^(-at)u(t) with a > 0. For t < 0, the flipped and shifted h(t - τ) is non-zero only for τ < t < 0, while x(τ) is zero there, so y = 0. For t ≥ 0, the overlap is from τ = 0 to τ = t, and x(τ) = 1 there, so y(t) = integral from 0 to t of e^(-a(t - τ)) dτ. Substitute or integrate directly: e^(-at) times the integral of e^(aτ) from 0 to t = e^(-at)(e^(at) - 1)/a = (1 - e^(-at))/a. So y(t) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-at))u(t). It rises from 0 and settles at 1/a.

The RC circuit connection: In Electrical Circuits you met the RC low-pass circuit: a resistor in series, a capacitor across the output. Its impulse response is h(t) = (1/RC)e^(-t/RC)u(t). Using example 2 with a = 1/RC and multiplying by 1/RC, the step response is y(t) = (1 - e^(-t/RC))u(t). That is exactly the capacitor charging curve you learned: after one time constant RC it reaches about 63 percent of the final value, and after five time constants it is above 99 percent. Convolution reproduces the circuit result from a completely different direction.

Worked example 3, two exponentials: x(t) = e^(-t)u(t) and h(t) = e^(-2t)u(t). For t ≥ 0, y(t) = integral from 0 to t of e^(-τ)e^(-2(t - τ)) dτ = e^(-2t) times the integral from 0 to t of e^(τ) dτ = e^(-2t)(e^t - 1) = e^(-t) - e^(-2t). For t < 0, y = 0. Check at t = 0: 1 - 1 = 0, which makes sense since no input has arrived yet. The output rises, peaks and then decays, a typical shape for two sluggish stages in a row.

Which function to flip: Because convolution is commutative, x * h = h * x, so you may flip either one. A good habit is to flip and slide the simpler shape, usually a box, and keep the more complicated one, such as an exponential, fixed. Fewer edges move, so there are fewer cases to worry about. In example 2 you could also flip the step instead of the exponential: the answer is the same, but the integral looks slightly different, which makes a nice self-check.

How to choose the integral limits: The trickiest part of continuous convolution is the limits. Rule: the integral runs over the range of τ where both x(τ) and h(t - τ) are non-zero. If x is non-zero for τ ≥ 0 and h(t - τ) is non-zero for t - τ ≥ 0, that is τ ≤ t, then the overlap is 0 ≤ τ ≤ t, which exists only when t ≥ 0. Write these two conditions down every time; it removes most mistakes.

Convolving with an impulse: Because of the sifting property, x(t) * δ(t) = x(t), and x(t) * δ(t - t0) = x(t - t0). Convolving with a shifted impulse delays a signal. A system with h(t) = δ(t - 2) is a pure 2-second delay. A system with h(t) = δ(t) + 0.5δ(t - 0.1) adds an echo 0.1 seconds later at half strength. Echo systems in continuous time are just sums of impulses.

Convolving with a step: x(t) * u(t) = integral from minus infinity to t of x(τ) dτ, the running integral of x. So a system whose impulse response is u(t) is an integrator. Feed it a box of height 2 and width 3 and the output is a ramp rising to 6 and then staying flat. This matches the idea that the step response of any LTI system is the running integral of its impulse response.

A quick check using areas: The area under y(t) equals the area under x(t) times the area under h(t). In example 1, both boxes have area 1 and the triangle has area (1/2) times base 2 times height 1 = 1. Good. In example 3, the area of e^(-t)u(t) is 1 and of e^(-2t)u(t) is 1/2, so the output area should be 1/2: integral of (e^(-t) - e^(-2t)) from 0 to infinity = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2. Correct. Use this to catch errors.

Why smoothing happens, in plain words: Each output value is a weighted average of many nearby input values, because the flipped impulse response covers a stretch of the input at once. Averages cannot jump as suddenly as single values can. If a single input value suddenly changes, it only nudges the average a little. So sharp corners and sudden jumps in the input become gentle slopes in the output. The wider the impulse response, the more input values are averaged together, and the stronger the smoothing. A system with a very narrow impulse response, close to an impulse, changes the signal very little.

Real-life example 1, a mobile phone charging indicator: When you plug in a charger, the battery voltage does not jump; the charging circuit and battery respond gradually. A simple model treats the input (charger switched on) as a step and the system as having an exponential impulse response. The output, the rising voltage, is the convolution: a curve that rises quickly at first, then slows as it nears full. Real lithium battery charging has extra stages controlled by a chip, but the first idea of a smooth rise comes straight from convolution.

Real-life example 2, blurred motion in a moving bus photo: Take a photo of a sign from a moving bus on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway with the shutter open for a short time. During that time, each point of the sign moves across the sensor a short distance at steady speed. Along that direction, the camera's impulse response is a short box: light spread evenly over the motion length. The photo is the sharp image convolved with that box. Edges that were sharp steps become ramps, exactly like a step convolved with a box.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to flip h. Using t as the integration variable instead of τ; t is fixed inside the integral. Getting limits from only one function instead of the overlap of both. Forgetting the u(t) at the end to show the output is zero for negative time. Losing a factor when integrating exponentials; differentiate your answer to check it.

What exams ask: 'Find and sketch y(t) = x(t) * h(t) for x(t) = u(t) - u(t - 2) and h(t) = e^(-t)u(t).' Expect three cases: t < 0 gives 0; 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 gives 1 - e^(-t); t > 2 gives e^(-(t - 2)) - e^(-t). 'Find the step response of an RC circuit by convolution.' 'Show that convolving two equal boxes gives a triangle.'

Recap: The convolution integral y(t) = integral of x(τ)h(t - τ) dτ adds up scaled, shifted impulse responses from every slice of input. Compute it by flip, slide, multiply and find area, splitting t into cases at the breakpoints. Widths add, areas multiply, and convolution smooths. A step into an exponential system gives a rising exponential, the RC charging curve. Convolving with δ(t - t0) shifts and with u(t) integrates.
key_points: y(t) = ∫ x(τ)h(t - τ) dτ = x(t) * h(t): every slice of input launches a scaled, shifted impulse response.
Graphical method: flip h, slide by t, multiply where they overlap, find the area; split t into cases at breakpoints.
Box of width 1 convolved with itself gives a triangle of width 2 and peak 1.
If x lives on [a, b] and h on [c, d], y lives on [a + c, b + d]; area of y = area of x times area of h.
u(t) * e^(-at)u(t) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-at))u(t), which gives the RC charging curve 1 - e^(-t/RC).
x(t) * δ(t - t0) = x(t - t0); x(t) * u(t) is the running integral of x.
Integral limits come from where both x(τ) and h(t - τ) are non-zero.
lessons.tip: Draw the sliding picture for one value of t in each case before writing any integral. The picture gives you the limits, and the limits are where almost all marks are lost.
lessons.task: Convolve a box of height 1 on [0, 2] with a box of height 1 on [0, 1]. Find y(t) in every case, sketch it (it should be a trapezoid), and check that its area is 2 times 1 = 2.

quiz.q: A box of height 1 on [0, 1] is convolved with itself. What is y(1)?
quiz.explain: The result is a triangle from 0 to 2 with peak value 1 at t = 1.

quiz.q: x(t) lives on [0, 3] and h(t) lives on [1, 2]. Where does y = x * h live?
quiz.explain: The output lives on [a + c, b + d] = [0 + 1, 3 + 2] = [1, 5].

quiz.q: What is u(t) * e^(-2t)u(t) for t ≥ 0?
quiz.explain: Using (1/a)(1 - e^(-at)) with a = 2 gives (1 - e^(-2t))/2.

quiz.q: The areas of x(t) and h(t) are 3 and 4. What is the area of x * h?
quiz.explain: The area of a convolution is the product of the areas: 3 times 4 = 12.

quiz.q: A system has h(t) = u(t). What does it do?
quiz.explain: x(t) * u(t) equals the integral of x from minus infinity to t, so the system is an integrator.

lessons.title: Properties of Convolution and LTI Systems
lessons.content:
When you learned multiplication, you also learned its rules: 3 times 4 equals 4 times 3, (2 times 3) times 4 equals 2 times (3 times 4), and 2 times (3 + 4) equals 2 times 3 plus 2 times 4. Those rules let you rearrange problems to make them easier. Convolution has the same kind of rules, and each one has a meaning for real systems: swapping blocks, merging a chain of filters into one, or splitting a filter into simpler parallel parts. This lesson collects those rules and then uses the impulse response to answer the system questions from lesson 6: is it causal, is it memoryless, is it stable, is it invertible? For LTI systems, h answers all of them.

Commutative property: x * h = h * x. In the sum, substitute m = n - k, and sum over k of x[k]h[n - k] becomes sum over m of h[m]x[n - m]. The meaning: the input and the impulse response play symmetric roles. If you feed signal A into a system with impulse response B, you get the same output as feeding B into a system with impulse response A. Practically, it lets you flip whichever of the two is simpler.

Associative property: (x * h1) * h2 = x * (h1 * h2). The meaning: a cascade of two LTI systems, first h1 then h2, behaves exactly like one LTI system whose impulse response is h1 * h2. Example: h1 = {1, 1} and h2 = {1, -1}. Then h1 * h2 = (1 + z)(1 - z) = 1 - z squared, which is {1, 0, -1}. So a 2-point sum followed by a difference is the same as one system y[n] = x[n] - x[n - 2]. Check with an input: x = δ gives, after h1, {1, 1}, and after h2, {1, 0, -1}. It matches.

Order in a cascade does not matter: Combining associativity and commutativity: x * h1 * h2 = x * h2 * h1. So you can swap the order of LTI blocks in a cascade without changing the output. Engineers use this freely. For example, in a digital audio system, it might be cheaper to apply a simple gain first and a long filter afterwards, or to put a noise-reducing filter before an amplifier. The overall response is identical. Remember, this is not true for non-linear blocks.

Distributive property: x * (h1 + h2) = x * h1 + x * h2. The meaning: two LTI systems in parallel, with outputs added, behave exactly like one LTI system with impulse response h1 + h2. Example: h1 = δ[n] (pass straight through) and h2 = 0.5δ[n - 3] (a soft echo three steps later). The parallel connection has h = δ[n] + 0.5δ[n - 3], one echo system. Going the other way, a complicated h can be split into simple parts, each handled separately and the results added.

Identity and shifting: x * δ = x, so δ is the identity system, a wire that changes nothing. x[n] * δ[n - n0] = x[n - n0], a pure delay. These are simple, but they let you treat delays as convolutions, which is useful when combining them with other systems. A cascade of a delay of 2 and a delay of 3 is δ[n - 2] * δ[n - 3] = δ[n - 5], a delay of 5, as common sense says.

Memoryless from h: An LTI system is memoryless only if h[n] = Kδ[n] for some number K, that is, h is zero everywhere except at n = 0. Then y[n] = Kx[n], a pure gain. If h has any non-zero value at another n, the output at time n uses an input from a different time, so the system has memory. In continuous time, memoryless means h(t) = Kδ(t).

Causality from h: An LTI system is causal exactly when h[n] = 0 for all n < 0. Why? The output y[n] = sum of h[k]x[n - k]. If h[k] were non-zero for some negative k, say k = -2, then y[n] would include h[-2]x[n + 2], a future input. If h[k] is zero for all negative k, only x[n], x[n - 1], ... appear, which are present and past values. In plain words: the system must not respond to an impulse before the impulse arrives. Example: h[n] = {1, 2} at n = -1, 0 is non-causal. h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] is causal.

Stability from h, the rule: A discrete LTI system is BIBO stable exactly when the sum of |h[n]| over all n is finite. In continuous time, the integral of |h(t)| over all t must be finite. This is called absolute summability (or absolute integrability). It turns the stability question, which is about every possible input, into a single sum you can compute.

Why the rule works, sufficiency: Suppose |x[n]| ≤ M for all n, and S = sum of |h[k]| is finite. Then |y[n]| = |sum of h[k]x[n - k]| ≤ sum of |h[k]| |x[n - k]| ≤ M times sum of |h[k]| = M S. So the output is bounded by M S. A bounded input gives a bounded output.

Why the rule works, necessity: Suppose S is infinite. Choose the input x[n] = the sign of h[-n] (that is, +1 where h[-n] is positive, -1 where negative, 0 where zero). This input is bounded by 1. Then y[0] = sum of h[k]x[-k] = sum of h[k] times the sign of h[k] = sum of |h[k]| = infinite. A bounded input gave an unbounded output, so the system is not stable. Together, these two arguments prove the rule both ways.

Stability examples: h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]: the sum of |h| is 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + ... = 2, finite, stable. h[n] = (2)^n u[n]: grows without limit, unstable. h[n] = u[n] (the accumulator): the sum is 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = infinite, unstable, matching what you found in lesson 6. h[n] = (1/(n + 1))u[n]: the sum is 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., the harmonic series, which grows without limit (very slowly), so unstable even though h itself shrinks to zero. h(t) = e^(-2t)u(t): integral is 1/2, stable. Any FIR system is stable, because its sum has finitely many finite terms.

A useful pattern: For h[n] = a^n u[n], the system is stable when |a| < 1 and unstable when |a| ≥ 1. For h(t) = e^(at)u(t), stable when a < 0. Later, poles will generalise this: in discrete time all poles inside the unit circle, in continuous time all poles in the left half of the s-plane.

Invertibility from h: An LTI system with impulse response h has an LTI inverse with impulse response h_inv when h * h_inv = δ. Cascading the system and its inverse gives the identity. Example: the accumulator has h = u[n], and its inverse is the first difference with h_inv = δ[n] - δ[n - 1]. Check: u[n] - u[n - 1] = δ[n]. Another example: h = δ[n] - 0.5δ[n - 1] has the inverse (0.5)^n u[n]. Check: (0.5)^n u[n] - 0.5 times (0.5)^(n - 1) u[n - 1] = (0.5)^n (u[n] - u[n - 1]) = (0.5)^n δ[n] = δ[n]. This is how echo cancellers work: they convolve with an inverse of the echo system.

Step response from h: For an LTI system, the step response is s[n] = sum of h[k] for k ≤ n, and h[n] = s[n] - s[n - 1]. In continuous time, s(t) is the running integral of h(t), and h(t) = ds/dt. So measuring the step response, which is often easier, gives you h by differencing or differentiating.

FIR and IIR, summarised: An FIR (finite impulse response) system has h non-zero for only finitely many n. It is always stable, can be made with only feedforward (no feedback) and is easy to design with linear phase, which keeps the shapes of waveforms. An IIR (infinite impulse response) system has h that goes on forever, usually made with feedback. IIR filters can achieve sharp filtering with very few calculations, but they must be checked for stability. Digital Signal Processing, a later course, designs both.

A combined worked example: Consider h[n] = {1, 2, 1} at n = -1, 0, 1. Memoryless? No, it has values at n = -1 and 1. Causal? No, because h[-1] = 1 is non-zero, so the output at time n uses x[n + 1]. Stable? Yes, the sum of |h| is 4, and it is FIR. If we delay it by one step, h[n - 1] = {1, 2, 1} at n = 0, 1, 2, it becomes causal while staying stable. This trick, adding delay to make a non-causal filter causal, is used all the time in real-time audio, at the cost of a small lag.

Real-life example 1, a noise filter chain in a mobile phone: A phone's microphone signal might pass through three digital LTI filters: one removing a low hum, one removing high hiss, and one shaping the voice. Engineers can combine all three into one impulse response h = h1 * h2 * h3 and run one filter instead of three. Or they can reorder them to reduce rounding errors. Both are possible only because the filters are LTI and convolution is associative and commutative.

Real-life example 2, cancelling a hall echo on a Zoom class: If a teacher's room adds one echo, h = δ[n] + 0.5δ[n - 800], an echo canceller tries to build the inverse system. For this h, the inverse is an IIR system: y[n] = x[n] - 0.5y[n - 800], whose impulse response is δ[n] - 0.5δ[n - 800] + 0.25δ[n - 1600] - ... . Because the echo is weaker than the original (0.5 < 1), this inverse is stable. If the echo were stronger than the direct sound, the simple inverse would be unstable, and engineers would need other methods.

Common mistakes: Saying an LTI system is stable because h goes to zero; it must be absolutely summable (the harmonic example). Saying a system is causal because h is zero for n > 0; causality needs zero for n < 0. Thinking the parallel connection multiplies impulse responses; it adds them, and the cascade convolves them. Forgetting that these rules require LTI systems.

What exams ask: 'State and prove the condition for BIBO stability of an LTI system.' 'Find the overall impulse response of the given cascade/parallel connection.' 'Determine whether h[n] = (0.9)^n u[n + 2] is causal and stable.' (Not causal because h[-1] and h[-2] are non-zero; stable because the sum of |h| is finite.)

Recap: Convolution is commutative, associative and distributive, with δ as identity. Cascades convolve impulse responses and can be reordered; parallel connections add them. An LTI system is memoryless if h = Kδ, causal if h = 0 for negative time, BIBO stable if h is absolutely summable or integrable, and invertible if some h_inv gives h * h_inv = δ. FIR systems are always stable; IIR systems must be checked.
key_points: Convolution is commutative (x * h = h * x), associative and distributive; δ is the identity.
A cascade of LTI systems has impulse response h1 * h2, and the order can be swapped.
A parallel connection of LTI systems has impulse response h1 + h2.
An LTI system is memoryless iff h = Kδ and causal iff h[n] = 0 for all n < 0.
BIBO stable iff Σ|h[n]| (or ∫|h(t)| dt) is finite; e.g. (0.5)^n u[n] is stable, u[n] and 1/(n+1) u[n] are not.
An inverse system satisfies h * h_inv = δ; the accumulator's inverse is δ[n] - δ[n - 1].
FIR systems are always stable; IIR systems (usually with feedback) must be checked.
lessons.tip: For any h you meet, run a four-question checklist in under a minute: is it Kδ (memoryless)? Is it zero for negative n (causal)? Is the sum of |h| finite (stable)? Is it finite length (FIR)? Write the answers next to h.
lessons.task: For h[n] = {2, -1} at n = 0, 1, find the inverse system h_inv by guessing it is of the form c a^n u[n], and check that h * h_inv = δ. Is the inverse stable?

quiz.q: Two LTI systems with h1 and h2 are connected in series. What is the overall impulse response?
quiz.explain: By associativity, x * h1 * h2 = x * (h1 * h2), so a cascade convolves the impulse responses.

quiz.q: Which impulse response gives a BIBO stable system?
quiz.explain: The sum of |(0.5)^n| is 2, finite. The others have infinite absolute sums.

quiz.q: When is an LTI system causal?
options: When the sum of |h| is finite
quiz.explain: If h were non-zero for negative n, the output would depend on future inputs.

quiz.q: What is the inverse of the accumulator (h = u[n])?
h[n] = (1/(n + 1))u[n] shrinks to zero. Is the system stable?
options: Yes, because h goes to zero
No, because the harmonic sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... is infinite
quiz.explain: Stability needs the absolute sum to be finite; the harmonic series grows without limit.

lessons.title: Systems Described by Difference and Differential Equations
lessons.content:
Your mother keeps a small savings box. Every month she adds whatever she saved, and the bank-like rule she follows is: this month's total equals last month's total plus this month's saving. That one sentence is a difference equation. It does not give a formula for the total directly; it tells you how to get the next value from the previous one. Most real digital systems are described exactly this way: a rule that links the current output to past outputs and current and past inputs. In continuous time, the same idea becomes a differential equation, a rule about how fast the output changes. This lesson shows how to read, solve and draw both.

The linear constant-coefficient difference equation: The general form is a0 y[n] + a1 y[n - 1] + ... + aN y[n - N] = b0 x[n] + b1 x[n - 1] + ... + bM x[n - M]. The a's and b's are fixed numbers, which is why it is called constant-coefficient. Usually a0 = 1, so we can solve for y[n]: y[n] = b0 x[n] + ... + bM x[n - M] - a1 y[n - 1] - ... - aN y[n - N]. The number N, the largest delay on y, is the order of the equation.

Non-recursive equations: If all the a's after a0 are zero, the output depends only on inputs: y[n] = b0 x[n] + b1 x[n - 1] + ... + bM x[n - M]. There is no feedback. The impulse response is simply the list of b's: h[n] = {b0, b1, ..., bM}. This is an FIR system. The 3-point moving average y[n] = (x[n] + x[n - 1] + x[n - 2])/3 is one, with h = {1/3, 1/3, 1/3}.

Recursive equations: If some a's are non-zero, the output depends on past outputs too. This is feedback, and usually the impulse response never ends, so the system is IIR. Example: y[n] = 0.5y[n - 1] + x[n]. We found earlier that h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]. Recursive equations are powerful because a few numbers can create a long, smooth response.

The condition of initial rest: A difference equation alone does not fully define a system. You also need to know where the output starts. The usual assumption is initial rest: if the input is zero before some time n0, the output is also zero before n0. With initial rest, a linear constant-coefficient difference equation describes a system that is linear, time-invariant and causal. Without it, for example if y[-1] = 5 while the input is still zero, the output is not zero for zero input, so the system is not linear in the strict sense.

Solving by iteration: The simplest way to solve a recursive equation is to compute it step by step, exactly as a computer would. Example: y[n] = 0.5y[n - 1] + x[n], with x[n] = u[n] and initial rest. y[0] = 0.5(0) + 1 = 1. y[1] = 0.5(1) + 1 = 1.5. y[2] = 0.5(1.5) + 1 = 1.75. y[3] = 0.875 + 1 = 1.875. The values approach 2. Iteration always works, but it gives numbers, not a formula.

Solving for a formula, the homogeneous part: For a formula, we split the solution into two parts. First, the homogeneous solution, which is what the system does on its own with zero input: y[n] - 0.5y[n - 1] = 0. Try y = C r^n: C r^n - 0.5C r^(n - 1) = 0, so r - 0.5 = 0 and r = 0.5. The homogeneous solution is C(0.5)^n. The equation r - 0.5 = 0 is called the characteristic equation, and its roots tell you how the system behaves naturally.

Solving for a formula, the particular part: Second, the particular solution, a solution that matches the type of input. For a constant input of 1 (for n ≥ 0), try a constant K: K - 0.5K = 1, so K = 2. The full solution is y[n] = 2 + C(0.5)^n. Use the starting value y[0] = 1: 2 + C = 1, so C = -1. Result: y[n] = 2 - (0.5)^n for n ≥ 0. Check: n = 1 gives 1.5 and n = 2 gives 1.75, matching the iteration. Notice the two pieces: a steady part 2 that follows the input, and a transient part -(0.5)^n that dies away.

Zero-input and zero-state responses: Another useful split. The zero-input response is what the output does because of stored initial conditions alone, with the input set to zero. The zero-state response is what the input causes when the system starts at rest. The total response is their sum. Example: y[n] = 0.5y[n - 1] + x[n] with y[-1] = 4 and x = u[n]. Zero-input: y[n] = 4(0.5)^(n + 1) = 2(0.5)^n. Zero-state: 2 - (0.5)^n. Total: 2 + (0.5)^n. Check at n = 0: 0.5(4) + 1 = 3, and the formula gives 2 + 1 = 3. Good.

Second-order example: y[n] = y[n - 1] - 0.25y[n - 2] + x[n]. The characteristic equation is r squared - r + 0.25 = 0, which is (r - 0.5) squared = 0, a repeated root r = 0.5. Repeated roots give homogeneous solutions of the form (C1 + C2 n)(0.5)^n. Another: y[n] = y[n - 1] + y[n - 2] with no input and y[0] = 0, y[1] = 1 gives the Fibonacci numbers 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...; its characteristic roots are (1 ± square root of 5)/2, and since one root (about 1.618) has magnitude greater than 1, the sequence grows without bound. Root size predicts stability: all roots with magnitude less than 1 means the natural response dies out.

Differential equations in continuous time: The continuous version is a0 y(t) + a1 dy/dt + ... = b0 x(t) + b1 dx/dt + .... Here derivatives replace delays. The simplest example, from Electrical Circuits, is the RC low-pass circuit: RC dy/dt + y = x, where x is the input voltage and y is the capacitor voltage. The order is the highest derivative of y. Initial rest means that if the input is zero before t0, the output and its derivatives are zero before t0 too.

Solving the RC equation for a step: Homogeneous: RC dy/dt + y = 0. Try y = C e^(st): RC s + 1 = 0, so s = -1/RC, giving C e^(-t/RC). Particular for x = 1 (t ≥ 0): try y = K: 0 + K = 1, K = 1. Full: y = 1 + C e^(-t/RC). Initial rest means y(0) = 0, so C = -1, and y(t) = (1 - e^(-t/RC))u(t). It is the same answer you got from convolution in lesson 10, which is a reassuring check. Two completely different methods, one answer.

Block diagrams of difference equations, Direct Form I: Any difference equation can be drawn with adders, gains and delays. Direct Form I builds two parts in a row: first a chain of delays on x with gains b0, b1, ..., added together (the feedforward part); then a chain of delays on y with gains -a1, -a2, ..., fed back into the adder (the feedback part). It uses M delays for x and N delays for y.

Direct Form II: Because the two parts are LTI, their order can be swapped (from the convolution properties lesson). Put the feedback part first, then the feedforward part. Now both parts use delays on the same middle signal, so they can share them. Direct Form II needs only max(N, M) delays, the minimum possible, so it is called a canonical form. Fewer delays means less memory, which matters on small chips such as those in hearing aids.

From equation to code: A recursive equation is a short loop. For y[n] = 0.5y[n - 1] + x[n]: keep y_prev = 0; for each new x, compute y = 0.5*y_prev + x; output y; set y_prev = y. For a second-order equation, keep two previous outputs. This is how filters run inside phones, smartwatches and music software: a few multiplications and additions per sample, millions of times a second.

Why both forms exist: Difference equations are natural for computers, because a computer works one sample at a time and can only remember a few past values. Differential equations are natural for physics, because capacitors, springs and motors obey laws about rates of change. When an engineer replaces an analog RC filter with a digital one inside a chip, the job is to turn the differential equation into a difference equation that behaves almost the same at the chosen sampling rate. Methods for doing this conversion are a big part of the Digital Signal Processing course.

Real-life example 1, a loan from a microfinance group: Suppose a family in a village takes a loan and the balance grows by 2 percent each month while they pay 1000 taka monthly. Then b[n] = 1.02b[n - 1] - 1000. This is a first-order recursive difference equation with root 1.02, which is greater than 1. If payments stop, the balance grows forever, an unstable natural response. Banks and NGOs use exactly this kind of equation to plan payment schedules that bring the balance to zero.

Real-life example 2, a smartwatch step counter smoothing: Raw accelerometer readings jump around. Many devices use a simple recursive filter, y[n] = 0.9y[n - 1] + 0.1x[n], called an exponential moving average. It needs just one stored value, unlike a long moving average that stores many. Its impulse response is 0.1(0.9)^n u[n], so recent readings matter most and old ones fade smoothly. The root 0.9 has magnitude less than 1, so the filter is stable.

Common mistakes: Forgetting initial rest and getting a non-zero output with zero input. Mixing up the signs when moving the y terms to the right side (y[n] - 0.5y[n - 1] = x[n] means y[n] = 0.5y[n - 1] + x[n]). Applying the initial condition to the homogeneous part alone instead of to the full solution. Using a particular solution that is the same form as a homogeneous term; then you must multiply by n (or t).

What exams ask: 'Find the impulse response of y[n] - 0.6y[n - 1] = x[n]' (answer (0.6)^n u[n]). 'Solve y[n] - 0.5y[n - 1] = u[n] with y[-1] = 0.' 'Draw Direct Form I and II realisations of y[n] = 0.5y[n - 1] + x[n] + 2x[n - 1].' 'Find the step response of RC dy/dt + y = x.'

Recap: Difference equations link outputs to past outputs and inputs; differential equations link outputs to their derivatives. Non-recursive equations give FIR systems; recursive ones usually give IIR systems. With initial rest, they describe causal LTI systems. Solve by iteration, or by homogeneous plus particular solutions using the characteristic equation; roots smaller than 1 in magnitude (discrete) or with negative real parts (continuous) die out. Direct Form II realises any equation with the minimum number of delays.
key_points: A linear constant-coefficient difference equation links y[n] to past outputs and present/past inputs; its order is the largest delay on y.
Non-recursive (no feedback) equations give FIR systems with h = {b0, ..., bM}; recursive ones usually give IIR systems.
With initial rest, the equation describes a causal LTI system.
Solutions can be found by iteration, or as homogeneous (C r^n from the characteristic equation) plus particular solution.
Total response = zero-input response (from initial conditions) + zero-state response (from the input).
RC dy/dt + y = x has step response (1 - e^(-t/RC))u(t), matching convolution.
Direct Form II shares delays and needs only max(N, M) of them, the minimum.
lessons.tip: Always iterate the first three or four values by hand before trusting a formula. If the formula and the iteration disagree at n = 0 or n = 1, the mistake is almost always in the initial condition.
