lessons.task: Solve y[n] = 0.8y[n - 1] + x[n] for x[n] = u[n] with initial rest: first iterate n = 0 to 4, then find the formula y[n] = K + C(0.8)^n and check it against your iterated values. What value does y approach?

quiz.q: What is the impulse response of y[n] = 0.6y[n - 1] + x[n] with initial rest?
quiz.explain: Iterating with x = δ gives 1, 0.6, 0.36, ..., which is (0.6)^n u[n].

quiz.q: Which equation describes an FIR system?
quiz.explain: It has no feedback terms in y, so the impulse response is the finite list {1, 2, -1}.

quiz.q: For y[n] - 0.5y[n - 1] = u[n] with initial rest, what value does y[n] approach as n grows?
quiz.explain: The particular (steady) solution is K with K - 0.5K = 1, so K = 2; the transient (0.5)^n dies out.

quiz.q: What is the step response of RC dy/dt + y = x with initial rest?
quiz.explain: Homogeneous C e^(-t/RC) plus particular 1, with y(0) = 0, gives 1 - e^(-t/RC).

quiz.q: Why does Direct Form II use fewer delays than Direct Form I?
options: It only works for FIR systems
Swapping the LTI parts lets feedforward and feedback share the same delays
quiz.explain: With the feedback part first, both parts delay the same middle signal, so max(N, M) delays suffice.

lessons.title: Fourier Series: Periodic Signals as Sums of Harmonics
lessons.content:
When a harmonium plays a note at a Rabindra Sangeet class, you hear one note, but it is not one pure tone. It is a main tone plus quieter tones at two times, three times, four times that frequency, mixed in a special recipe. That recipe is why a harmonium sounds different from a flute playing the same note. The Fourier series is the mathematical way to find that recipe for any repeating signal. In Math III you learned how to compute Fourier series. In this lesson we use them as an engineer: to see what an LTI system does to a periodic signal, one harmonic at a time.

The key discovery, eigenfunctions: Feed a complex exponential x(t) = e^(jωt) into an LTI system with impulse response h(t). By convolution, y(t) = integral of h(τ)e^(jω(t - τ)) dτ = e^(jωt) times the integral of h(τ)e^(-jωτ) dτ. The integral does not depend on t; it is just a complex number that depends on ω. Call it H(jω). So y(t) = H(jω)e^(jωt). The output is the same complex exponential, multiplied by a number. A signal that passes through a system keeping its shape, only scaled, is called an eigenfunction of the system, and the scaling number is its eigenvalue.

Why this matters so much: Most signals change shape completely when they pass through a system: a box can come out as a smooth hump. But complex exponentials come out as complex exponentials of the same frequency. The system can only change their size (by the magnitude |H(jω)|) and shift them in time (by the angle of H(jω), called the phase). If we can write any signal as a sum of complex exponentials, then the system's effect on the whole signal is just a separate scaling of each piece. That is the whole idea behind Fourier analysis.

A worked eigenfunction example: Let h(t) = e^(-t)u(t). Then H(jω) = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-t)e^(-jωt) dt = 1/(1 + jω). At ω = 1, H(j1) = 1/(1 + j). Its magnitude is 1/square root of 2, about 0.707, and its angle is -45 degrees (-π/4). So if the input is cos(t), which is the real part of e^(jt), the output is 0.707 cos(t - π/4): the same frequency, about 71 percent of the height, shifted a little later. No convolution integral needed for the output; just one complex number.

What magnitude and phase look like: Picture two cosine waves on the same graph, the input cos(t) and the output 0.707 cos(t - π/4). The output's peaks are lower, because the magnitude 0.707 shrinks it. And each output peak arrives π/4 seconds after the matching input peak, because the phase of -45 degrees delays it. That is all an LTI system can ever do to a single sinusoid: make it bigger or smaller, and slide it earlier or later. It can never change its frequency or add new frequencies. If you ever see new frequencies appear at the output, the system is not LTI.

The Fourier series formula: A periodic signal with period T0 and fundamental angular frequency ω0 = 2π/T0 can be written as x(t) = sum over all integers k of a_k e^(jkω0t). The terms with k = ±1 are the fundamental, k = ±2 the second harmonic, and so on. k = 0 gives a_0, the average value of the signal, called the DC component. The coefficients are found by a_k = (1/T0) times the integral over one period of x(t)e^(-jkω0t) dt. This works because the different harmonics are orthogonal: the integral over one period of e^(jkω0t)e^(-jmω0t) is zero unless k = m.

Reading the coefficients: Each a_k is a complex number. Its magnitude |a_k| says how strong the k-th harmonic is. Its angle says how that harmonic is shifted. For a real signal, a_(-k) is the complex conjugate of a_k, so the positive and negative k terms pair up into real cosines: a_k e^(jkω0t) + a_(-k)e^(-jkω0t) = 2|a_k| cos(kω0t + angle of a_k). Negative frequencies are a book-keeping trick that makes the maths tidy; for real signals they always come in matching pairs.

Reading a series off directly: Sometimes you can write the coefficients without any integral. Take x(t) = 1 + 2cos(ω0t) + sin(2ω0t). Using Euler, 2cos(ω0t) = e^(jω0t) + e^(-jω0t), and sin(2ω0t) = (e^(j2ω0t) - e^(-j2ω0t))/(2j). So a_0 = 1, a_1 = a_(-1) = 1, a_2 = 1/(2j) = -j/2, a_(-2) = j/2, and all others are zero. Always look for this shortcut first.

The square wave: Take a square wave that is +1 for half a period and -1 for the other half, centred so it is an odd function. Its Fourier series in sine form is x(t) = (4/π)[sin(ω0t) + (1/3)sin(3ω0t) + (1/5)sin(5ω0t) + ...]. Only odd harmonics appear, and their sizes fall as 1/k. With just the first term you get a sine wave of height 4/π, about 1.27. Add the third harmonic and the top flattens. Add more and the corners sharpen. Sharp corners need high harmonics; smooth signals need few.

Which signals have Fourier series: The series works for practically every periodic signal an engineer meets. The usual sufficient conditions, called the Dirichlet conditions, ask that over one period the signal has finite area under its absolute value, a finite number of maxima and minima, and a finite number of jumps. At a jump, the series converges to the midpoint of the jump. For a square wave jumping from -1 to +1, the series gives exactly 0 at the jump instant, which you can check: every sine term in the series is zero there.

The Gibbs effect: When you add up a finite number of harmonics of a square wave, the sum always overshoots near each jump, by about 9 percent of the jump size. Adding more terms makes the overshoot narrower but does not make it smaller. This is called the Gibbs phenomenon. It shows up in real life as faint ringing around sharp edges in compressed images and audio.

The line spectrum: Plot |a_k| as vertical lines at frequencies kω0. This picture is the line spectrum, the frequency view of a periodic signal. A pure cosine has two lines (at ±ω0). A square wave has lines at odd multiples, shrinking as 1/k. A periodic train of very narrow pulses has many lines of almost equal height. The spectrum tells you at a glance how much bandwidth a signal needs: the range of frequencies holding most of its power.

Power in the harmonics, Parseval: The average power of a periodic signal equals the sum of |a_k| squared over all k. So each harmonic carries its own share of power, and you can see where the power lives. For x(t) = 1 + 2cos(ω0t) + sin(2ω0t), the power is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3.5. Check in time: the DC part contributes 1, 2cos contributes 4/2 = 2, and sin contributes 1/2, total 3.5. Same answer.

Passing a periodic signal through an LTI system: Now combine everything. If x(t) = sum of a_k e^(jkω0t), each term passes through separately, scaled by H(jkω0). So y(t) = sum of a_k H(jkω0) e^(jkω0t). The output is also periodic with the same period, and its Fourier coefficients are b_k = a_k H(jkω0). In words: multiply each harmonic by the system's response at that harmonic's frequency. No convolution integrals required.

Worked example, square wave into an RC low-pass: The RC circuit has H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC). Suppose ω0 RC = 1. Then for the fundamental (k = 1), |H| = 1/square root of 2, about 0.71. For k = 3, |H| = 1/square root of 10, about 0.32. For k = 5, |H| = 1/square root of 26, about 0.20. The fundamental is mildly reduced, while the higher harmonics, which form the sharp corners, are cut much more. The output looks like a square wave with rounded corners, which is exactly what you see on an oscilloscope when you feed a square wave into an RC circuit.

Filtering harmonics on purpose: If you want to turn a square wave into a pure sine wave, pass it through a system that keeps the fundamental and removes the 3rd, 5th and higher harmonics: a low-pass filter with its cut-off between ω0 and 3ω0. Cheap inverters that produce 'modified sine wave' power, and electronic organs, use this idea to shape tones.

Symmetry shortcuts: Even periodic signals have only cosine terms, so their a_k are real. Odd periodic signals have only sine terms, so their a_k are purely imaginary. A signal with half-wave symmetry, where the second half of each period is the negative of the first half, has only odd harmonics; the square wave is one such signal. Spotting symmetry before integrating tells you which coefficients are zero and saves half the work.

Real-life example 1, the IPS at home: Many homes in Bangladesh use an IPS (instant power supply) during load-shedding. Cheaper units produce a stepped or square-like wave instead of a smooth sine. Its Fourier series contains strong 3rd and 5th harmonics (150 Hz and 250 Hz on a 50 Hz base). Fans connected to such a supply can hum loudly and motors run warmer, because those extra harmonics push useless currents. Pure sine wave inverters filter the harmonics out, which is why they cost more and run fans quietly.

Real-life example 2, why voices sound different: When two people say the same vowel at the same pitch, the fundamental frequency is the same, but the strengths of the harmonics differ. Your throat and mouth act as an LTI-like filter that boosts some harmonics and weakens others. That changes the a_k recipe and gives each voice its own colour, called timbre. Voice recognition software in phones measures these harmonic strengths to tell vowels and speakers apart.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the 1/T0 factor in a_k. Thinking negative frequencies are 'real' separate tones; for real signals they pair with the positive ones. Expecting the Gibbs overshoot to disappear with more terms. Multiplying a_k by H(jω0) instead of H(jkω0); each harmonic uses its own frequency. Forgetting that only LTI systems keep frequencies unchanged.

What exams ask: 'Show that complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems.' 'Find the Fourier series coefficients of x(t) = 3 + cos(2t) + 4sin(6t)' (period π; a_0 = 3, a_(±1) = 1/2, a_3 = 2/j = -2j, a_(-3) = 2j). 'A periodic signal with coefficients a_k passes through H(jω); find the output coefficients.' 'Sketch the line spectrum of a square wave.'

Recap: Complex exponentials pass through LTI systems unchanged except for a complex scale factor H(jω). A periodic signal is a sum of harmonics a_k e^(jkω0t), with a_k = (1/T0) times the integral of x(t)e^(-jkω0t) over a period, and a_0 the average. The line spectrum shows |a_k| against frequency; Parseval says power is the sum of |a_k| squared. An LTI system multiplies each harmonic by H(jkω0), so filtering is simply turning harmonics up or down.
key_points: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: e^(jωt) gives H(jω)e^(jωt), with H(jω) = ∫ h(τ)e^(-jωτ) dτ.
A periodic signal is x(t) = Σ a_k e^(jkω0t) with a_k = (1/T0) ∫ over a period of x(t)e^(-jkω0t) dt; a_0 is the average (DC).
For real signals a_(-k) is the conjugate of a_k, so pairs combine into real cosines.
A square wave contains only odd harmonics, with sizes falling as 1/k; partial sums overshoot by about 9 percent (Gibbs).
The line spectrum plots |a_k| at kω0; Parseval: average power = Σ |a_k| squared.
An LTI system multiplies each harmonic: output coefficients b_k = a_k H(jkω0).
Low-pass systems weaken high harmonics, rounding sharp corners.
lessons.tip: Before integrating for a_k, always try rewriting the signal with Euler's formula. Any signal made of a few sines and cosines gives its coefficients in one line.
lessons.task: Take a square wave with period 2π (so ω0 = 1). Using its series (4/π)[sin t + sin(3t)/3 + sin(5t)/5], compute the partial sum at t = π/2 with one, two and three terms, and see how it approaches 1 (and passes it).

quiz.q: What happens to e^(jωt) when it passes through an LTI system?
options: It comes out as H(jω)e^(jωt): same frequency, scaled by a complex number
quiz.explain: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems, so only their size and phase change.

quiz.q: What does the coefficient a_0 of a Fourier series represent?
options: The average (DC) value of the signal
quiz.explain: a_0 = (1/T0) times the integral of x over a period, which is the average value.

quiz.q: Which harmonics are present in a symmetric square wave (±1, half and half)?
quiz.explain: The series is (4/π)[sin ω0t + (1/3)sin 3ω0t + (1/5)sin 5ω0t + ...], only odd k.

quiz.q: h(t) = e^(-t)u(t). What is H(jω)?
quiz.explain: The integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-t)e^(-jωt) dt equals 1/(1 + jω).

quiz.q: A periodic input has coefficients a_k. What are the output coefficients of an LTI system H(jω)?
quiz.explain: Each harmonic e^(jkω0t) is scaled by the system's response at its own frequency kω0.

lessons.title: Discrete-Time Fourier Series
lessons.content:
Think of the traffic light at a busy Dhaka junction that follows a fixed cycle: red for a while, green, yellow, then red again. If a camera records the light's state once per second, you get a list of numbers that repeats every cycle, a periodic discrete-time signal. Just as the harmonium note had a recipe of continuous harmonics, this repeating list also has a recipe of discrete harmonics. The discrete-time Fourier series finds it. And it has a lovely surprise: because everything is finite, the recipe has only a fixed, small number of ingredients, and you can compute all of them with plain arithmetic, no integrals at all. That is exactly why computers love it.

Why discrete makes things easier: In continuous time, a periodic signal has a value at infinitely many instants in each period, so its recipe can need infinitely many harmonics, and we must worry about whether the infinite sum really adds up to the signal. In discrete time, one period is just N numbers, like N cells in a spreadsheet. N numbers in, N numbers out. Finding the recipe is like solving N equations for N unknowns, and the orthogonality of the harmonics makes that solving trivially easy: each coefficient comes from one simple sum.

Periodic discrete signals: A discrete signal is periodic with period N if x[n + N] = x[n] for all n, where N is a positive integer. The fundamental frequency is ω0 = 2π/N radians per sample. For example, a pattern 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, ... has N = 4 and ω0 = π/2. Because one period has only N values, the whole signal is described by just N numbers.

Discrete harmonics: The building blocks are discrete complex exponentials e^(jkω0n) = e^(jk(2π/N)n), for integers k. Here comes the surprise. In continuous time, e^(jkω0t) for different k are all different signals, infinitely many. In discrete time, the harmonic with k + N is identical to the harmonic with k, because e^(j(k + N)(2π/N)n) = e^(jk(2π/N)n) times e^(j2πn), and e^(j2πn) = 1 for every integer n. So there are only N distinct harmonics: k = 0, 1, ..., N - 1. Any N consecutive values of k will do.

The synthesis equation: A periodic signal with period N can be written as x[n] = sum over k = 0 to N - 1 of a_k e^(jk(2π/N)n). This is a finite sum of N terms. No infinite series, no convergence questions, no Gibbs overshoot. With N coefficients you can rebuild the N values of one period exactly.

The analysis equation: The coefficients are found by a_k = (1/N) times the sum over n = 0 to N - 1 of x[n] e^(-jk(2π/N)n). Just as in continuous time, this works because the harmonics are orthogonal: the sum over one period of e^(jk(2π/N)n)e^(-jm(2π/N)n) is N if k = m (counting modulo N) and 0 otherwise. The coefficients are themselves periodic: a_(k + N) = a_k. That is the frequency-side echo of the fact that only N harmonics exist.

Worked example 1, a single pulse per period: Let x[n] = 1 at n = 0 and 0 at n = 1, 2, 3, repeating with N = 4. Then a_k = (1/4)(1 times e^0) = 1/4 for every k. All four harmonics have equal strength. This matches the continuous idea that a very narrow pulse contains all frequencies equally. Check by synthesis: x[0] = 1/4 times (1 + 1 + 1 + 1) = 1. At n = 1, the four harmonics are 1, j, -1, -j, which sum to 0, so x[1] = 0. Correct.

Worked example 2, two ones per period: x[n] = {1, 1, 0, 0}, repeating with N = 4. With ω0 = π/2, e^(-jkπ/2 n) at n = 1 is e^(-jkπ/2). So a_k = (1/4)(1 + e^(-jkπ/2)). k = 0: (1/4)(2) = 1/2, the average. k = 1: e^(-jπ/2) = -j, so a_1 = (1/4)(1 - j). k = 2: e^(-jπ) = -1, so a_2 = 0. k = 3: e^(-j3π/2) = j, so a_3 = (1/4)(1 + j). Notice a_3 is the conjugate of a_1, because x is real and a_3 = a_(-1).

Worked example 3, a ramp pattern: x[n] = {1, 2, 3, 4}, N = 4. a_0 = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)/4 = 2.5. a_1 = (1/4)(1 + 2(-j) + 3(-1) + 4(j)) = (1/4)(-2 + 2j) = -0.5 + 0.5j. a_2 = (1/4)(1 - 2 + 3 - 4) = -0.5. a_3 = conjugate of a_1 = -0.5 - 0.5j. Check x[0] = a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + a_3 = 2.5 - 0.5 - 0.5 - 0.5 + (0.5j - 0.5j) = 1. Correct.

Worked example 4, a cosine: x[n] = cos(πn/2), which is 1, 0, -1, 0, repeating with N = 4. Using Euler: cos(πn/2) = (e^(jπn/2) + e^(-jπn/2))/2. The term e^(-jπn/2) is the k = -1 harmonic, which is the same as k = 3. So a_1 = 1/2, a_3 = 1/2, and a_0 = a_2 = 0. Again, try Euler before summing.

Picturing the harmonics for N = 4: Write the four harmonics as rows of four numbers, for n = 0, 1, 2, 3. The k = 0 row is 1, 1, 1, 1: a constant. The k = 1 row is 1, j, -1, -j: one full turn around the circle in four steps. The k = 2 row is 1, -1, 1, -1: the fastest flip-flop. The k = 3 row is 1, -j, -1, j: one full turn the other way. Computing a_k is just taking the signal's four values, multiplying them by the conjugate of row k, adding, and dividing by 4. Seeing the rows like this makes the whole method feel like simple pattern matching: how much does my signal look like each row?

The highest discrete frequency: The harmonic with k = N/2 (when N is even) has frequency π, the fastest possible discrete oscillation: e^(jπn) = (-1)^n. In example 3, a_2 = -0.5 measures how much of the pattern flips sign every sample. Harmonics with k between N/2 and N are better thought of as negative frequencies, k - N. So k = 3 in a period of 4 really behaves like frequency -π/2.

Parseval for discrete periodic signals: The average power over one period, (1/N) times the sum of |x[n]| squared, equals the sum of |a_k| squared over the N coefficients. For {1, 1, 0, 0}: power = (1 + 1)/4 = 0.5. Coefficients: |a_0| squared = 1/4, |a_1| squared = 2/16 = 1/8, |a_2| squared = 0, |a_3| squared = 1/8. Sum = 0.25 + 0.125 + 0.125 = 0.5. Equal, as promised.

Discrete LTI systems and harmonics: The eigenfunction idea works in discrete time too. Feed x[n] = e^(jωn) into an LTI system with impulse response h[n]: y[n] = sum of h[k]e^(jω(n - k)) = e^(jωn) times the sum of h[k]e^(-jωk). Call that sum H(e^(jω)), the frequency response. So a periodic input with coefficients a_k gives an output with coefficients a_k H(e^(jk2π/N)). Each harmonic is scaled by the frequency response at its own frequency.

A filtering example: The 2-point average h[n] = {1/2, 1/2} has H(e^(jω)) = (1 + e^(-jω))/2. At ω = 0, H = 1: slow parts pass. At ω = π, H = (1 - 1)/2 = 0: the fastest flip-flop is removed completely. Feed in x[n] = {1, 2, 3, 4} repeating. The a_2 term, at frequency π, is wiped out; a_0 passes unchanged; a_1 at frequency π/2 is scaled by (1 - j)/2. That is why averaging smooths jagged data: it kills the fastest harmonics.

The link to the DFT and FFT: If you take one period of length N and compute N times a_k, you get exactly the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), written X[k] = sum over n of x[n]e^(-j2πkn/N). The DFT is the frequency tool computers actually use. Computing it directly takes about N squared multiplications; the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), popularised by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, does it in about N log N. For N = 1024, that is roughly a million operations versus about ten thousand. The DSP course covers the DFT and FFT in detail.

Real-life example 1, a phone's tuner app: A guitar tuner app records a short chunk of sound, often a power of two like 4096 samples, and computes its FFT. The strongest peak in the result shows the main frequency of the string. If you pluck the A string, the peak should sit near 110 Hz. The app compares the peak with the target and tells you to tighten or loosen. Under the hood, it treats the recorded chunk as one period of a periodic signal and computes its discrete Fourier coefficients.

Real-life example 2, weekly patterns in shop sales: A grocery shop in Mirpur records daily sales. Sales repeat roughly every 7 days, higher on Thursday and Friday, lower midweek. Treat a typical week as one period with N = 7 and compute a_0 to a_6. a_0 is the average daily sale. a_1 and a_6 (a conjugate pair) show the once-a-week rise and fall. a_2 and a_5 show a twice-a-week pattern. The shopkeeper does not need the maths, but data analysts use exactly this to plan stock.

Choosing N for real measurements: When you take a chunk of a real signal and treat it as one period, you are pretending the chunk repeats forever. If the chunk does not contain a whole number of cycles of the main tone, the pretend repetition has a jump at the joins, and that jump spreads energy into many harmonics. This effect, called spectral leakage, is why tuner apps and audio analysers multiply the chunk by a smooth 'window' shape before computing the FFT. You will meet windows properly in DSP.

Common mistakes: Using infinitely many k in discrete time; only N distinct harmonics exist. Forgetting the 1/N factor in a_k (some books put it in the synthesis equation instead; be consistent with your textbook). Mixing up the period N with the number of non-zero samples. Thinking e^(j(k + N)(2π/N)n) is a new harmonic. Forgetting that coefficients of real signals come in conjugate pairs a_(N - k) = conjugate of a_k.

What exams ask: 'Find the DTFS coefficients of x[n] = {1, 0, 1, 0} with N = 4' (a_0 = 1/2, a_2 = 1/2, a_1 = a_3 = 0). 'Show that a_k is periodic with period N.' 'Verify Parseval's relation for the given sequence.' 'Find the output of a given LTI system for a periodic input using the DTFS.'

Recap: A periodic discrete signal with period N is a finite sum of N harmonics e^(jk(2π/N)n). Coefficients a_k = (1/N) sum of x[n]e^(-jk(2π/N)n) are periodic in k with period N. a_0 is the average, a_(N/2) measures the fastest flip-flop, and real signals give conjugate pairs. Parseval holds, LTI systems scale each harmonic by H(e^(jω)), and N times a_k is the DFT, computed fast by the FFT.
key_points: A periodic discrete signal (period N) has only N distinct harmonics e^(jk(2π/N)n), because k and k + N give the same signal.
Synthesis: x[n] = Σ (k = 0 to N - 1) a_k e^(jk(2π/N)n); analysis: a_k = (1/N) Σ (n = 0 to N - 1) x[n]e^(-jk(2π/N)n).
The coefficients are periodic: a_(k + N) = a_k; for real x, a_(N - k) is the conjugate of a_k.
The sums are finite, so there are no convergence issues and no Gibbs overshoot.
Parseval: (1/N) Σ |x[n]| squared = Σ |a_k| squared.
An LTI system multiplies each harmonic by H(e^(jω)) = Σ h[n]e^(-jωn) at that harmonic's frequency.
N times a_k is the DFT; the FFT computes it in about N log N operations.
lessons.tip: For N = 4, memorise the four values of e^(-jπn/2): 1, -j, -1, j. Most small exam problems use N = 4 or 8, and knowing these makes the sums almost mental arithmetic.
lessons.task: Compute the DTFS coefficients of x[n] = {2, 0, 2, 0} (N = 4) by hand. Then check your answer by rebuilding x[0] and x[1] from the coefficients, and verify Parseval's relation.

quiz.q: How many distinct harmonics does a periodic discrete signal with period N have?
quiz.explain: e^(jk(2π/N)n) repeats when k increases by N, so only N distinct harmonics exist.

quiz.q: For x[n] = {1, 0, 0, 0} repeating with N = 4, what is a_k?
quiz.explain: Only x[0] = 1 contributes, giving a_k = (1/4)(1) for all k.

quiz.q: For x[n] = {1, 1, 0, 0} with N = 4, what is a_0?
quiz.explain: a_0 is the average: (1 + 1 + 0 + 0)/4 = 1/2.

quiz.q: The 2-point average h = {1/2, 1/2} has H(e^(jω)) = (1 + e^(-jω))/2. What is H at ω = π?
quiz.explain: e^(-jπ) = -1, so H = (1 - 1)/2 = 0; the fastest flip-flop is removed.

quiz.q: How are the DTFS coefficients related to the DFT X[k] of one period?
quiz.explain: The DFT omits the 1/N factor, so X[k] = N a_k.

lessons.title: The Continuous-Time Fourier Transform
lessons.content:
A single clap, a door slam, one beep of a rickshaw horn: these sounds happen once and do not repeat. The Fourier series needs a repeating signal, so it cannot describe them directly. Yet these one-off sounds also contain a mix of frequencies. A deep thud has mostly low frequencies; a sharp click has lots of high ones. The Fourier transform is the tool that finds the frequency recipe of a signal that does not repeat. In Math III you learned how to compute it. Here we focus on what it means for signals and systems: spectra, bandwidth and the deep trade-off between time and frequency.

From series to transform, the idea: Take a single pulse and pretend it repeats every T0 seconds. Then it has a Fourier series with lines at multiples of ω0 = 2π/T0. Now make T0 bigger and bigger, so the copies move farther apart. The lines get closer together, because ω0 shrinks. In the limit, when T0 is infinite, there is only one pulse and the lines merge into a continuous curve. That curve is the Fourier transform. Instead of separate harmonics, a non-repeating signal has a smooth spread of frequencies.

How to read the transform integral: For one chosen frequency ω, the integral multiplies the signal by e^(-jωt), a spinning arrow that turns at speed ω, and adds up the result over all time. If the signal contains a lot of wiggle at that same speed, the signal and the arrow keep 'agreeing' and the sum grows large. If the signal has nothing at that speed, the products point in all directions and cancel out, giving a small sum. So X(jω) is a measure of how much the signal resembles a wave of frequency ω. The transform repeats this question for every possible ω.

The definitions: The Fourier transform of x(t) is X(jω) = integral over all t of x(t)e^(-jωt) dt. The inverse transform rebuilds the signal: x(t) = (1/2π) times the integral over all ω of X(jω)e^(jωt) dω. Read the inverse as: x(t) is a continuous sum of complex exponentials e^(jωt), each with weight X(jω) dω/(2π). Some books use frequency f in hertz instead, with X(f) = integral of x(t)e^(-j2πft) dt and no 1/(2π) in the inverse. Both are correct; just stay consistent.

Magnitude and phase spectrum: X(jω) is a complex number for each ω. Its magnitude |X(jω)| is the magnitude spectrum: how much of each frequency is present. Its angle is the phase spectrum: how each frequency is shifted in time. Plots usually show the magnitude, because that is what our ears and most measurements notice first. For a real signal, |X(-jω)| = |X(jω)|, so the magnitude plot is symmetric and we often draw only positive ω.

Transform 1, the decaying exponential: x(t) = e^(-at)u(t) with a > 0. X(jω) = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-at)e^(-jωt) dt = 1/(a + jω). Its magnitude is 1/square root of (a squared + ω squared). At ω = 0 it equals 1/a, the area under x(t). At ω = a it is 1/(a times square root of 2), about 71 percent of the peak, which is the half-power point. For large ω it falls off like 1/ω. So a fast-decaying exponential (large a) has a wide spectrum, and a slow one (small a) has a narrow spectrum.

Transform 2, the rectangular pulse: x(t) = 1 for -T/2 < t < T/2, zero elsewhere. X(jω) = integral from -T/2 to T/2 of e^(-jωt) dt = 2 sin(ωT/2)/ω. At ω = 0 this equals T, the pulse's area. It crosses zero when ωT/2 is a multiple of π, that is at ω = 2π/T, 4π/T, and so on. The shape is called a sinc: a tall central lobe with smaller ripples on both sides that slowly die out. The width of the main lobe, from -2π/T to 2π/T, is 4π/T.

The great trade-off: Look at the pulse result. If the pulse gets shorter (T smaller), the first zero 2π/T moves out: the spectrum gets wider. If the pulse gets longer, the spectrum gets narrower. A signal cannot be both very short in time and very narrow in frequency. This is a fundamental law, sometimes called the time-bandwidth or uncertainty principle of signals. A camera flash, which is very short, has a very wide spectrum. A long steady whistle has a very narrow spectrum.

Transform 3, the impulse: x(t) = δ(t). By sifting, X(jω) = e^0 = 1 for every ω. An impulse contains every frequency in equal amount. This is the extreme case of the trade-off: zero width in time, infinite width in frequency. It also explains why a clap is a good test signal for a room: it excites all frequencies at once, so the response shows how the room treats each frequency.

Transform 4, a constant and a pure tone: The opposite extreme is x(t) = 1 for all time: infinitely wide in time. Its transform is 2πδ(ω), a single spike at zero frequency. Similarly, e^(jω0t) has transform 2πδ(ω - ω0), one spike at ω0, and cos(ω0t) has transform π[δ(ω - ω0) + δ(ω + ω0)], two spikes. A pure tone that lasts forever has all its energy at exactly one frequency. These impulse-shaped spectra also let the Fourier transform handle periodic signals: a Fourier series becomes a row of spikes at the harmonics.

A small table of pairs to remember: δ(t) gives 1. 1 gives 2πδ(ω). e^(-at)u(t) gives 1/(a + jω). A box of width T gives 2 sin(ωT/2)/ω. cos(ω0t) gives π[δ(ω - ω0) + δ(ω + ω0)]. e^(-a|t|) gives 2a/(a squared + ω squared). Most exam problems reduce to these plus the properties in the next lesson.

A worked example with two exponentials: Compare x1(t) = e^(-t)u(t) and x2(t) = e^(-10t)u(t). The first dies out in a few seconds; the second in a few tenths of a second. Their spectra are 1/(1 + jω) and 1/(10 + jω). At ω = 0 the magnitudes are 1 and 0.1, the two areas. The half-power points are at ω = 1 and ω = 10. So x2, ten times shorter, has a spectrum ten times wider and ten times lower at the centre. Shrinking in time by a factor spreads in frequency by the same factor, a rule that the next lesson states in general as the scaling property.

What bandwidth means: The bandwidth of a signal is the range of frequencies holding most of its energy. Definitions vary: the first zero of the spectrum, the range where the magnitude stays above 71 percent (the 3 dB bandwidth), or the range holding 99 percent of the energy. Whatever definition, bandwidth tells you how much of the frequency range a signal occupies, which decides how many signals can share a cable or the airwaves.

Bandwidth examples: Traditional telephone voice was limited to about 300 to 3400 hertz, enough to understand speech. Human hearing covers roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz, so music needs more. FM radio stations are spaced 200 kilohertz apart in many countries so their spectra do not overlap. A data signal sending faster pulses needs more bandwidth, by the trade-off: shorter pulses mean wider spectra. This is why faster internet needs wider frequency channels.

When does the transform exist: A sufficient condition is that the signal is absolutely integrable (the integral of |x(t)| is finite) and is reasonably well behaved: finitely many jumps and wiggles in any finite range. Signals like e^(-at)u(t) with a > 0 and boxes qualify. Growing signals like e^(t)u(t) do not have a Fourier transform. Constants, steps and sinusoids are not absolutely integrable, but we still give them transforms using impulses, as above. For growing signals we will use the Laplace transform instead.

The frequency response is a Fourier transform: For an LTI system, H(jω) from the eigenfunction lesson is exactly the Fourier transform of the impulse response h(t). So the system's frequency response is the spectrum of its fingerprint. A system whose h(t) is short in time has a wide H(jω): it passes many frequencies. A system whose h(t) is long and smooth has a narrow H(jω): it passes only low frequencies. Next lesson shows the central fact: the output spectrum is Y(jω) = X(jω)H(jω).

Real-life example 1, Wi-Fi and channel widths: A home Wi-Fi router in the 2.4 GHz band typically uses channels about 20 megahertz wide. Newer routers can use 40, 80 or even 160 megahertz channels in the 5 GHz band to carry data faster. That is the time-frequency trade-off at work: to send more, shorter symbols per second, the signal must occupy a wider band. When many flats in a Dhaka building run wide channels, their spectra overlap and everyone slows down, which is why routers offer a choice of channels.

Real-life example 2, a thunderclap vs a temple bell: A nearby thunderclap is a short, violent event: its spectrum is broad, from a deep rumble to sharp cracks. Far away thunder sounds like a low rumble because air absorbs high frequencies more over long distances, leaving only the low part of the spectrum. A temple or school bell rings for a long time at a few steady pitches: its spectrum has a few sharp, narrow peaks. Same physics, two shapes in time, two very different spectra.

Energy in the spectrum: The total energy of a signal can be computed in either domain: the integral of |x(t)| squared over time equals (1/2π) times the integral of |X(jω)| squared over frequency. This is Parseval's relation for the transform, and |X(jω)| squared is called the energy spectral density, which shows how the energy is spread across frequencies. Engineers read bandwidth from this picture: where does most of the area under |X| squared sit? Lesson 25 returns to this idea.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the 1/(2π) in the inverse when using ω. Mixing ω (radians per second) and f (hertz); ω = 2πf. Thinking a short pulse has a narrow spectrum; it is the opposite. Trying to find the Fourier transform of a growing exponential. Forgetting that the value X(0) equals the area under x(t), a quick check on any answer.

What exams ask: 'Find the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse and sketch its magnitude.' 'Find X(jω) for x(t) = e^(-2|t|)' (answer 4/(4 + ω squared)). 'Explain the time-frequency trade-off with an example.' 'Find the 3 dB bandwidth of e^(-at)u(t)' (answer ω = a).

Recap: The Fourier transform X(jω) = integral of x(t)e^(-jωt) dt gives the continuous frequency recipe of a non-repeating signal, and the inverse rebuilds x(t). Magnitude shows how much of each frequency, phase shows the shifts. Key pairs: δ gives 1, a box gives a sinc, e^(-at)u(t) gives 1/(a + jω), a pure tone gives spikes. Short signals have wide spectra and long ones narrow spectra. X(0) is the area of x(t). The frequency response H(jω) is the Fourier transform of h(t).
key_points: X(jω) = ∫ x(t)e^(-jωt) dt; inverse x(t) = (1/2π) ∫ X(jω)e^(jωt) dω.
The transform is the limit of a Fourier series as the period goes to infinity: lines merge into a continuous spectrum.
Key pairs: δ(t) gives 1; e^(-at)u(t) gives 1/(a + jω); a box of width T gives 2 sin(ωT/2)/ω; cos(ω0t) gives π[δ(ω - ω0) + δ(ω + ω0)].
Short in time means wide in frequency and long in time means narrow in frequency (time-bandwidth trade-off).
X(0) equals the area under x(t), a quick check.
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies holding most of a signal's energy; faster data needs more bandwidth.
The frequency response H(jω) is the Fourier transform of the impulse response h(t).
lessons.tip: For every transform you compute, check X(0) against the area under x(t), and check that shorter signals gave wider spectra. These two checks catch most algebra slips.
lessons.task: Compute the Fourier transform of a box of height 1 from -1 to 1 (T = 2), and of a box from -0.5 to 0.5 (T = 1). For each, find X(0) and the first zero crossing. Sketch both magnitude spectra on one graph and describe the trade-off you see.

quiz.explain: The integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-(a + jω)t) dt is 1/(a + jω).

lessons.title: Fourier Transform Properties in Action
lessons.content:
Imagine you have a translator who can turn any Bangla sentence into English and back. Some sentences are long and awkward in Bangla but short and simple in English, and the other way round. A smart writer chooses the language where the job is easiest, does the work there, and translates back. The Fourier transform is that translator between the time world and the frequency world. Its properties are the dictionary: they tell you what happens in frequency when you do something in time. With them, hard problems like convolution become easy multiplication. This lesson goes through the most useful properties with worked examples.

Why properties matter more than integrals: You could compute every Fourier transform from the definition, but that is slow and error-prone. Instead, engineers memorise a few basic pairs and a handful of properties. Then they build new transforms by combining them, like using a few LEGO bricks and a few joining rules to build anything. In exams, using a property is usually much faster than integrating, and examiners expect it.

Linearity: If x1 has transform X1 and x2 has transform X2, then a x1 + b x2 has transform a X1 + b X2. The transform of a sum is the sum of the transforms. Example: x(t) = 3e^(-t)u(t) + 2δ(t) has transform 3/(1 + jω) + 2. Linearity is why we can split signals into simple pieces, transform each, and add.

Time shift: x(t - t0) has transform e^(-jωt0)X(jω). Delaying a signal does not change its magnitude spectrum at all, because |e^(-jωt0)| = 1. It only adds a phase of -ωt0, a straight line in ω with slope -t0. This makes sense: delaying a song does not change which notes are in it, only when they arrive. Example: e^(-2(t - 3))u(t - 3), the exponential delayed by 3, has transform e^(-j3ω)/(2 + jω).

A numeric look at the shift: Take x(t) = e^(-t)u(t), with X(j1) = 1/(1 + j) at ω = 1: magnitude about 0.707, phase -45 degrees. Delay it by 2 seconds. Now the transform at ω = 1 is e^(-j2) times 1/(1 + j). The magnitude is still 0.707, but the phase is -45 degrees minus 2 radians (about 115 degrees), roughly -160 degrees in total. At ω = 2 the extra phase would be -4 radians, twice as much. Higher frequencies get more phase for the same delay, because one second is more of their cycles.

Linear phase means pure delay: The time-shift property tells us something important about filters. If a system's phase is a straight line, -ωt0, every frequency is delayed by the same amount t0, so the waveform arrives intact, just late. If the phase is curved, different frequencies are delayed differently and the waveform's shape gets smeared. That is why audio and data engineers like linear-phase filters.

Time scaling: x(at) has transform (1/|a|)X(jω/a). If a = 2, the signal is squeezed into half the time, and its spectrum is stretched to twice as wide (and half as tall). This is the time-frequency trade-off as an exact rule. Example: playing a recording at double speed doubles every frequency in it, which is why voices sound high and squeaky. Playing at half speed halves every frequency, and voices sound deep.

Time reversal and real signals: x(-t) has transform X(-jω). For a real signal, X(-jω) is the complex conjugate of X(jω), so the magnitude spectrum is even (symmetric) and the phase spectrum is odd. That is why we usually plot only positive frequencies for real signals: the negative side is a mirror image and carries no new information.

Differentiation: dx/dt has transform jωX(jω). Differentiating multiplies the spectrum by jω, which grows with frequency, so it boosts high frequencies. That fits intuition: derivatives highlight sudden changes, and sudden changes live at high frequencies. Edge-detection filters in image processing are built on this idea. Integration does the opposite: it divides by jω (plus an extra term at ω = 0 for the average), so it boosts low frequencies and smooths things.

The convolution property, the star of the show: x(t) * h(t) has transform X(jω)H(jω). Convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency. For an LTI system, Y(jω) = X(jω)H(jω). This is why frequency analysis is so powerful: instead of computing a convolution integral, you multiply two functions, then transform back. It also gives the cleanest view of filtering: the output spectrum is the input spectrum shaped by H.

Worked example of the convolution property: In lesson 10 we convolved e^(-t)u(t) with e^(-2t)u(t) and got e^(-t) - e^(-2t) for t ≥ 0. With transforms: X = 1/(1 + jω), H = 1/(2 + jω), so Y = 1/((1 + jω)(2 + jω)). Split into partial fractions: 1/((1 + jω)(2 + jω)) = 1/(1 + jω) - 1/(2 + jω). Check: putting the right side over a common denominator gives ((2 + jω) - (1 + jω))/((1 + jω)(2 + jω)) = 1/((1 + jω)(2 + jω)). Transforming back each piece gives y(t) = (e^(-t) - e^(-2t))u(t). Same answer, no integral needed.

Why multiplication is so much easier: Convolution needs flipping, sliding, finding limits and integrating for every output time. Multiplication needs one product at each frequency. For a cascade of five filters, convolution in time means four long integrals, while in frequency it means multiplying five functions together. Computers exploit this too: for long signals, it is faster to take the FFT of both signals, multiply, and take the inverse FFT than to convolve directly. This 'fast convolution' is used in audio reverb and image processing.

Cascades in frequency: Two LTI systems in series have overall frequency response H1(jω)H2(jω), the product. In parallel, H1(jω) + H2(jω), the sum. That matches the convolution rules from lesson 11, now in a simpler form. If one filter passes 80 percent at some frequency and the next passes 50 percent, together they pass 40 percent.

The multiplication property: The mirror of the convolution property: x(t)p(t) has transform (1/2π) X(jω) * P(jω). Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency. This is the basis of two big ideas in the coming lessons: sampling, where we multiply a signal by a train of impulses, and modulation, where we multiply a signal by a cosine.

Frequency shift and modulation: e^(jω0t)x(t) has transform X(j(ω - ω0)): multiplying by a complex exponential slides the whole spectrum to the right by ω0. Since cos(ω0t) = (e^(jω0t) + e^(-jω0t))/2, x(t)cos(ω0t) has transform (1/2)[X(j(ω - ω0)) + X(j(ω + ω0))]: two half-height copies of the spectrum, centred at +ω0 and -ω0. This is how AM radio lifts a voice spectrum up to the station's frequency. Lesson 20 explores it.

Why the multiplication property creates copies: Multiplying by a cosine is like switching the signal's sign smoothly back and forth ω0 times per 2π seconds. In frequency, the convolution with the cosine's two spikes places a copy of X at each spike. Convolving with a spike just moves a shape to the spike's location, exactly as convolving with δ(t - t0) moved a signal in time. Once you see 'convolution with spikes means copying', sampling in lesson 19 will feel obvious: a train of many spikes makes many copies.

Duality: The forward and inverse transform formulas look almost the same; only a sign and a 2π differ. So if x(t) has transform X(jω), then a signal shaped like X, as a function of time, has a transform shaped like x, flipped and scaled by 2π. Example: a box in time gives a sinc in frequency, so a sinc in time gives a box in frequency. This tells us the impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter (a box in frequency) is a sinc in time, which matters in lesson 18.

Parseval's relation: The energy of a signal is the same measured in time or frequency: the integral of |x(t)| squared dt equals (1/2π) times the integral of |X(jω)| squared dω. Example: x(t) = e^(-t)u(t). In time, energy = integral of e^(-2t) from 0 to infinity = 1/2. In frequency, |X| squared = 1/(1 + ω squared), and the integral over all ω is π, so (1/2π) times π = 1/2. Same. Parseval lets you compute energy in whichever domain is easier, and lets you say what fraction of energy lies in a band.

A property-chain example: Find the transform of x(t) = t e^(-t)u(t). One way: the property 'multiplying by t corresponds to j d/dω in frequency'. Another way: notice that e^(-t)u(t) * e^(-t)u(t) = t e^(-t)u(t) (convolve and check), so by the convolution property, X = 1/(1 + jω) squared. Both routes agree. Recognising signals as convolutions or shifts of known ones is the key exam skill.

Using the properties to design: Suppose you need a system that delays a signal by 1 millisecond and removes everything above 5 kilohertz. In frequency, you just write the target: H(jω) = e^(-jω(0.001)) for frequencies below 5 kHz and 0 above. The shift property gives the delay as linear phase, and the multiplication by a box in frequency gives the cut-off. Then you ask how close a real, causal system can get to this ideal. That is precisely how filter design starts in practice.

Real-life example 1, slowing down a lecture recording: Many students in Bangladesh speed up recorded lectures to 1.5x on YouTube. Simple speed-up is x(1.5t), which by the scaling property multiplies every frequency by 1.5, so the teacher would sound squeaky. Good players use extra processing that changes the speed while shifting the spectrum back to the original pitch, so the voice stays natural. Without understanding the scaling property, this problem would not even be clear.

Real-life example 2, a bass boost on a Bluetooth speaker: A bass boost is an LTI filter whose H(jω) is bigger than 1 at low frequencies and about 1 elsewhere. By the convolution property, the speaker's output spectrum is the song's spectrum multiplied by H. So the low drums get louder while the singer stays the same. Designing H in frequency is far easier than designing h(t) in time, which is why every equaliser app shows sliders for frequency bands.

Common mistakes: Thinking a delay changes the magnitude spectrum; it only changes phase. Forgetting the 1/|a| factor in scaling. Writing x * h in time as X * H in frequency; convolution becomes multiplication. Forgetting the 1/(2π) in the multiplication property. Using properties for growing signals that have no Fourier transform.

What exams ask: 'Using properties, find the transform of x(t) = e^(-3(t - 2))u(t - 2)' (answer e^(-j2ω)/(3 + jω)). 'Prove the convolution property.' 'An LTI system has H(jω) = 1/(2 + jω); find y(t) for x(t) = e^(-t)u(t)' (answer (e^(-t) - e^(-2t))u(t)). 'State Parseval's theorem and verify it for a given signal.'

Recap: Linearity adds transforms. A time shift multiplies by e^(-jωt0), changing phase only. Scaling by a stretches the spectrum by a and divides its height by |a|. Differentiation multiplies by jω. Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency, so Y = XH, and multiplication in time is convolution in frequency, the basis of sampling and modulation. Duality swaps the roles of time and frequency, and Parseval says energy is the same in both worlds.
key_points: Linearity: a x1 + b x2 transforms to a X1 + b X2.
Time shift: x(t - t0) gives e^(-jωt0)X(jω): same magnitude, linear phase; linear phase means pure delay.
Scaling: x(at) gives (1/|a|)X(jω/a): squeezing in time stretches the spectrum.
Differentiation multiplies by jω (boosting high frequencies); for real signals |X| is even.
Convolution property: x * h gives XH, so an LTI output is Y(jω) = X(jω)H(jω).
Multiplication property: x p gives (1/2π)X * P; x(t)cos(ω0t) gives half-copies of X at ±ω0.
Parseval: ∫|x(t)|² dt = (1/2π) ∫|X(jω)|² dω; duality swaps box and sinc.
lessons.tip: Before integrating any transform, ask: is this signal a shift, scale, derivative, sum or convolution of a pair I already know? Nine times out of ten, a property finishes the job in two lines.
lessons.task: Use the convolution property and partial fractions to find y(t) when x(t) = e^(-2t)u(t) passes through a system with h(t) = e^(-3t)u(t). Then check y(0) and the area of y(t) (which should equal (1/2) times (1/3)).

quiz.explain: The convolution property: x * h has transform X(jω)H(jω).

quiz.explain: x(at) gives (1/|a|)X(jω/a), so with a = 2 every frequency component moves to twice its value.

lessons.title: The Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT)
lessons.content:
Imagine a weather station in Cox's Bazar that records the wind speed once every minute. After a storm passes, the list of readings rises, wobbles and calms down. It does not repeat, so the discrete Fourier series cannot describe it. Yet the meteorologist wants to know: was the storm's wind mostly slow gusts or fast flutters? For a non-repeating list of samples, the tool that answers this is the discrete-time Fourier transform, or DTFT. It is the discrete cousin of the continuous Fourier transform, and it has one striking feature: its spectrum repeats forever, every 2π. This lesson explains what the DTFT is, why it repeats, and how to use it for discrete systems.

The definition: For a discrete signal x[n], the DTFT is X(e^(jω)) = sum over all n of x[n]e^(-jωn). The input is a list of numbers; the output is a continuous function of the frequency ω. The inverse rebuilds the samples: x[n] = (1/2π) times the integral over any interval of length 2π of X(e^(jω))e^(jωn) dω. The strange-looking notation X(e^(jω)) reminds us that the result depends on ω only through e^(jω), which will connect to the Z-transform later.

How to read the sum: For one chosen ω, the sum multiplies each sample by a unit arrow pointing at angle -ωn, then adds. If the signal wiggles at the same rate as the arrow turns, the products line up and the sum is large. If not, they point in different directions and largely cancel. So X(e^(jω)) measures how much the signal looks like a discrete wave of frequency ω, exactly the same idea as the continuous transform, but with a sum instead of an integral.

Why the spectrum repeats every 2π: Replace ω with ω + 2π. Each term becomes x[n]e^(-j(ω + 2π)n) = x[n]e^(-jωn)e^(-j2πn). But e^(-j2πn) = 1 for every integer n. So X(e^(j(ω + 2π))) = X(e^(jω)). The DTFT is always periodic with period 2π. This is the frequency-side version of the fact from lesson 5 that discrete sinusoids at ω and ω + 2π are identical. Only one period of the spectrum carries information; we usually draw it from -π to π.

Low and high frequency in discrete time: In the range from -π to π, frequencies near 0 are low: the samples change slowly. Frequencies near ±π are high: the samples flip sign almost every step. The very highest is ω = π, the signal (-1)^n. Because of the periodicity, frequencies near 2π are low again. Remember the picture of a clock hand turning ω radians per tick: a small ω turns slowly; ω = π flips back and forth; ω just under 2π looks like a slow turn backwards.

Connecting ω to real hertz: When x[n] comes from sampling at fs samples per second, the discrete frequency ω relates to real frequency f by ω = 2πf/fs. So ω = π corresponds to f = fs/2, half the sampling rate. For audio sampled at 48,000 samples per second, ω = π means 24,000 hertz, and ω = π/2 means 12,000 hertz. This half-sampling-rate limit will be the star of the sampling lesson.

Pair 1, the impulse: x[n] = δ[n]. Only n = 0 contributes, so X(e^(jω)) = 1 for every ω. Just like the continuous impulse, the discrete impulse contains all frequencies equally. A delayed impulse δ[n - n0] gives e^(-jωn0): magnitude 1, linear phase.

Pair 2, the decaying exponential: x[n] = a^n u[n] with |a| < 1. X(e^(jω)) = sum from n = 0 to infinity of (a e^(-jω))^n = 1/(1 - a e^(-jω)), using the geometric series (it converges because |a e^(-jω)| = |a| < 1). Take a = 0.5. At ω = 0, X = 1/(1 - 0.5) = 2. At ω = π, e^(-jπ) = -1, so X = 1/(1 + 0.5) = 2/3. The spectrum is bigger at low frequencies: this signal is mainly slow. Now take a = -0.5, which alternates in sign. At ω = 0, X = 1/1.5 = 2/3; at ω = π, X = 1/0.5 = 2. Mainly fast. The sign of a decides whether the signal is low-frequency or high-frequency.

Pair 3, the rectangular pulse: x[n] = 1 for n = 0, 1, ..., N - 1. The sum is a finite geometric series: X(e^(jω)) = (1 - e^(-jωN))/(1 - e^(-jω)). After some algebra, its magnitude is |sin(ωN/2) / sin(ω/2)|. At ω = 0 it equals N, the sum of the samples. It is zero at ω = 2π/N, 4π/N, and so on (except multiples of 2π). This is the discrete version of the sinc, sometimes called the Dirichlet kernel. A longer pulse (larger N) has a narrower main lobe: the time-frequency trade-off again.

A quick check for any DTFT: X(e^(j0)) equals the sum of all samples, because e^0 = 1. And X(e^(jπ)) equals the alternating sum x[0] - x[1] + x[2] - ..., because e^(-jπn) = (-1)^n. For x = {1, 2, 3}: X at 0 is 6 and X at π is 1 - 2 + 3 = 2. These two numbers instantly tell you how much 'slow' and 'fastest' content a signal has.

A tiny worked DTFT: Take x[n] = {1, 1} at n = 0, 1. Then X(e^(jω)) = 1 + e^(-jω). At ω = 0 it is 2. At ω = π/2 it is 1 - j, with magnitude about 1.41. At ω = π it is 1 - 1 = 0. So two equal neighbouring samples contain no content at the fastest frequency at all, which makes sense: nothing in the pair flips sign.

When does the DTFT exist: If the sum of |x[n]| is finite (absolutely summable), the DTFT exists and is a nice continuous function. That covers every finite-length signal and decaying signals like (0.5)^n u[n]. Growing signals like 2^n u[n] have no DTFT. Signals like constants and sinusoids are not absolutely summable but are given DTFTs with impulses, for example a constant 1 gives 2πδ(ω) repeated every 2π.

Properties, the same family: The DTFT has the same useful properties as the continuous transform. Linearity. Time shift: x[n - n0] gives e^(-jωn0)X(e^(jω)). Frequency shift: e^(jω0n)x[n] gives X(e^(j(ω - ω0))). Convolution: x[n] * h[n] gives X(e^(jω))H(e^(jω)). Multiplication: x[n]p[n] gives a periodic convolution of the spectra over one period, divided by 2π. Parseval: the sum of |x[n]| squared equals (1/2π) times the integral over one period of |X(e^(jω))| squared.

The frequency response of a discrete system: For a discrete LTI system with impulse response h[n], its frequency response is H(e^(jω)), the DTFT of h. A discrete exponential e^(jωn) passes through and comes out as H(e^(jω))e^(jωn). And for any input, Y(e^(jω)) = X(e^(jω))H(e^(jω)). So all the filtering ideas of continuous time carry over, with the one twist that every response repeats every 2π.

Example, the 2-point average: h[n] = {1/2, 1/2}. H(e^(jω)) = (1 + e^(-jω))/2. Factor out e^(-jω/2): H = e^(-jω/2)(e^(jω/2) + e^(-jω/2))/2 = e^(-jω/2)cos(ω/2). So |H| = |cos(ω/2)|: 1 at ω = 0, about 0.707 at ω = π/2, and 0 at ω = π. It is a gentle low-pass filter with linear phase -ω/2, which means a delay of half a sample. Change the sign to h = {1/2, -1/2} and |H| = |sin(ω/2)|: 0 at ω = 0 and 1 at π, a high-pass filter that removes the average and keeps the changes.

Example, a sinusoid through the average: Input x[n] = cos(πn/2) = 1, 0, -1, 0, .... At ω = π/2, H = (1 + e^(-jπ/2))/2 = (1 - j)/2, magnitude 0.707 and phase -π/4. So the output is 0.707cos(πn/2 - π/4). Check directly: y[1] = (x[1] + x[0])/2 = 0.5, and the formula gives 0.707cos(π/2 - π/4) = 0.707 times 0.707 = 0.5. It works.

Example, a recursive system: y[n] = 0.5y[n - 1] + x[n] has h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n], so H(e^(jω)) = 1/(1 - 0.5e^(-jω)). As computed above, |H| = 2 at ω = 0 and 2/3 at ω = π. This one-line recursive filter is a low-pass filter that boosts slow content three times more than the fastest content. With 0.9 instead of 0.5, the ratio becomes 19, a much stronger low-pass effect.

The DTFT and the DFT: A computer cannot store a continuous function of ω. The DFT from lesson 14 solves this: for a finite signal of length N, the DFT values X[k] are exactly samples of the DTFT at the N frequencies ω = 2πk/N. So when you run an FFT on a chunk of samples, you are looking at N evenly spaced points on the DTFT curve. Padding the chunk with zeros gives more points on the same curve, a smoother picture, but not more real detail.

Real-life example 1, a heart-rate app reading an ECG: A phone app samples an ECG signal 250 times per second. A normal heart beats about once per second, which is 1 hertz, so ω = 2π(1)/250, a very low discrete frequency. Muscle noise from shivering appears at much higher frequencies, and the mains hum appears at 50 hertz, ω = 2π(50)/250 = 0.4π. The app's designers look at the DTFT of typical recordings, see where the heartbeat lives and where the noise lives, and design H(e^(jω)) to keep one and cut the other.

Real-life example 2, a moving average on stock prices: Traders on the Dhaka Stock Exchange often plot a 10-day moving average of a share price. Its impulse response is a box of 10 samples, each 1/10. By pair 3, its frequency response is |sin(5ω)/(10 sin(ω/2))|, which is 1 at ω = 0 and first reaches 0 at ω = 2π/10. Day-to-day jitters (high ω) are strongly reduced, slow trends (low ω) pass. The ripples beyond the first zero mean some fast wiggles still leak through, which is why some analysts prefer weighted averages.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the DTFT is periodic and drawing it only once without saying so. Thinking ω = 2π is a high frequency; it is the same as 0. Mixing up ω in radians per sample with Ω in radians per second; they are linked by the sampling period. Forgetting that the DTFT of a^n u[n] only exists for |a| < 1. Confusing the DTFT (continuous in ω) with the DFT (N samples of it).

What exams ask: 'Find the DTFT of x[n] = (0.8)^n u[n] and evaluate its magnitude at ω = 0 and π' (5 and 1/1.8, about 0.556). 'Show that the DTFT is periodic with period 2π.' 'Find the frequency response of y[n] = x[n] - x[n - 1] and state what kind of filter it is' (|H| = 2|sin(ω/2)|, high-pass). 'Find the output for a sinusoidal input using H(e^(jω)).'

Recap: The DTFT X(e^(jω)) = sum of x[n]e^(-jωn) turns a non-repeating sequence into a continuous spectrum that repeats every 2π. Low frequencies are near 0, the highest is π, and ω = 2πf/fs links it to hertz. Key pairs: δ gives 1, a^n u[n] gives 1/(1 - a e^(-jω)), a box gives a discrete sinc. Properties mirror the continuous transform, so Y = XH. X at 0 is the sum of samples, X at π is the alternating sum. The DFT samples the DTFT at N points.
key_points: DTFT: X(e^(jω)) = Σ x[n]e^(-jωn); inverse: x[n] = (1/2π) ∫ over 2π of X(e^(jω))e^(jωn) dω.
The DTFT is always periodic in ω with period 2π; we usually draw -π to π.
Low discrete frequencies are near 0, the highest is ω = π; ω = 2πf/fs, so π matches fs/2.
Pairs: δ[n] gives 1; a^n u[n] (|a| < 1) gives 1/(1 - a e^(-jω)); a length-N box gives magnitude |sin(ωN/2)/sin(ω/2)|.
X at ω = 0 is the sum of samples; X at ω = π is the alternating sum.
Properties match the continuous transform: shift gives e^(-jωn0), convolution gives Y = XH, Parseval holds.
The DFT of a length-N signal samples its DTFT at ω = 2πk/N.
lessons.tip: For any discrete filter, compute H at just two points first: ω = 0 (sum of h) and ω = π (alternating sum of h). That alone tells you whether it is low-pass, high-pass or something in between.
lessons.task: For h[n] = {1, 2, 1}/4, compute H(e^(jω)) and its magnitude at ω = 0, π/2 and π. Decide whether it is low-pass or high-pass, then check the ω = 0 and ω = π values using the sum and alternating-sum shortcuts.

quiz.q: What is the period of the DTFT X(e^(jω)) in ω?
quiz.explain: e^(-j(ω + 2π)n) = e^(-jωn) for integer n, so the DTFT repeats every 2π.

quiz.q: What is the DTFT of (0.5)^n u[n]?
quiz.explain: The geometric series sum of (0.5e^(-jω))^n gives 1/(1 - 0.5e^(-jω)).

quiz.q: Which discrete frequency is the highest possible?
quiz.explain: ω = π gives (-1)^n, which flips every sample; 2π is the same as 0.

quiz.q: For x[n] = {1, 2, 3}, what is X(e^(jπ))?
quiz.explain: At ω = π, X is the alternating sum: 1 - 2 + 3 = 2.

quiz.q: h[n] = {1/2, -1/2}. What kind of filter is it?
quiz.explain: |H| = |sin(ω/2)| is 0 at ω = 0 and 1 at ω = π, so it passes fast changes and blocks the average.

lessons.title: Frequency Response and Filters
lessons.content:
Think of a tea strainer. You pour tea with leaves through it: the liquid passes, the leaves stay behind. A filter in signals does the same thing, but with frequencies instead of tea leaves. It lets some frequencies through and holds others back. Your phone uses filters to remove wind noise from calls, your radio uses them to pick one station out of dozens, and your earphones use them to make bass sound richer. In this lesson you will learn how a system's frequency response describes its filtering, the four classic filter types, why perfect filters are impossible, and how simple real filters like the RC circuit and the moving average behave.

Frequency response, the full picture: For a continuous LTI system, the frequency response H(jω) is the Fourier transform of its impulse response. For a discrete system it is H(e^(jω)), the DTFT of h[n]. At each frequency, H is a complex number. Its magnitude |H| is the gain: how much that frequency is amplified (bigger than 1) or weakened (smaller than 1). Its angle is the phase shift: how much that frequency is delayed. Because Y = XH, the output spectrum is the input spectrum with each frequency scaled by the gain and shifted by the phase.

A worked gain-and-phase example: A system has H(jω) = 1/(1 + jω). Input: x(t) = 2cos(t) + 2cos(10t). At ω = 1, |H| = 1/square root of 2 ≈ 0.707 and phase = -45 degrees. At ω = 10, |H| = 1/square root of 101 ≈ 0.0995 and phase ≈ -84 degrees. Output: y(t) ≈ 1.41cos(t - 45°) + 0.20cos(10t - 84°). The slow component kept about 71 percent; the fast one kept less than 10 percent. That is a low-pass filter in action.

Decibels: Engineers often measure gain in decibels: gain in dB = 20 log10 |H|. A gain of 1 is 0 dB (no change). A gain of 0.707 is about -3 dB, which is half the power. A gain of 0.1 is -20 dB, and 0.01 is -40 dB. A gain of 2 is about +6 dB. Decibels are handy because the gains of filters in a cascade multiply, and their decibels simply add: -3 dB followed by -20 dB is -23 dB. Our ears also hear loudness roughly on a logarithmic scale, so decibels match how we perceive sound.

Building one type from another: An ideal high-pass is simply 1 minus an ideal low-pass with the same cut-off: whatever the low-pass keeps, the high-pass throws away. A band-pass can be made by cascading a low-pass (cut-off at the top of the band) with a high-pass (cut-off at the bottom). A band-stop is 1 minus a band-pass. So if you understand low-pass filters deeply, you understand all four types, which is why textbooks spend most of their time on low-pass design.

The four classic filter types: A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and blocks high ones; it smooths signals. A high-pass filter passes high frequencies and blocks low ones; it removes slow drifts and keeps sharp changes. A band-pass filter passes only a band in the middle; radios use it to select a station. A band-stop filter blocks only a band; a notch filter is a very narrow band-stop, for example to kill the 50 hertz mains hum while keeping everything else.

Filter vocabulary: The passband is the range of frequencies a filter lets through. The stopband is the range it blocks. Between them is the transition band. The cut-off frequency marks the edge, often defined as where the gain falls to 0.707 (-3 dB). Real filters are not perfectly flat in the passband; the small wobble is called ripple. How quickly the gain falls after the cut-off is called the roll-off, often measured in dB per decade (a decade is a factor of 10 in frequency).

The ideal low-pass filter: The dream filter has H(jω) = 1 for |ω| < ωc and 0 for |ω| > ωc: a perfect box. Everything below the cut-off passes untouched, everything above vanishes completely. Sounds perfect. But what is its impulse response? By duality, the inverse transform of a box is a sinc: h(t) = sin(ωc t)/(πt). This sinc stretches forever in both directions, including negative time.

Why ideal filters are impossible: Because the ideal low-pass h(t) is non-zero for t < 0, the filter is non-causal: it would have to react before the input arrives. And because h(t) never ends, you would need infinite time and memory. So no real-time system can be a perfect box. Real filters approximate it: they are causal, have a finite transition band and some ripple. The art of filter design is getting as close as needed, at an acceptable cost. Famous designs like Butterworth (as flat as possible in the passband) and Chebyshev (sharper roll-off, with ripple) are studied in DSP.

The ideal discrete low-pass: In discrete time, an ideal low-pass has H(e^(jω)) = 1 for |ω| < ωc and 0 for ωc < |ω| ≤ π, repeating every 2π. Its impulse response is h[n] = sin(ωc n)/(πn) (with h[0] = ωc/π). Again infinite and non-causal. A practical trick is to cut it to a finite length, shift it to make it causal, and smooth the cut with a window. That gives a real FIR low-pass filter, the basic 'window method' you will meet in DSP.

The RC low-pass filter: The simplest real low-pass filter is the resistor-capacitor circuit. Its frequency response is H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC). At ω = 0, the gain is 1. At ω = 1/RC, the gain is 0.707 (-3 dB): this is the cut-off, ωc = 1/RC, or fc = 1/(2πRC) in hertz. Well above the cut-off, the gain is about 1/(ωRC), so every tenfold increase in frequency reduces the gain tenfold: a roll-off of -20 dB per decade. Example: R = 1000 ohms and C = 1 microfarad give RC = 0.001 seconds, ωc = 1000 radians per second and fc ≈ 159 hertz.

The RC high-pass filter: Swap the positions of R and C and take the output across the resistor. Now H(jω) = jωRC/(1 + jωRC). At ω = 0 the gain is 0: steady (DC) signals are blocked. At high ω the gain approaches 1. The cut-off is again ωc = 1/RC. This is the 'coupling capacitor' trick used in audio amplifiers to block a DC offset while passing the music.

The moving average as a discrete low-pass: A 4-point moving average h[n] = {1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4} has |H(e^(jω))| = |sin(2ω)/(4 sin(ω/2))|. At ω = 0 it is 1; at ω = π/2, sin(π) = 0, so the gain is 0; at ω = π it is |sin(2π)|/4 = 0. It is a simple low-pass with zeros at specific frequencies. It is easy, cheap and has linear phase, but its stopband is not very deep between the zeros: some high frequencies leak through.

Phase matters too: A filter with a straight-line phase, -ωt0, delays every frequency by the same t0, so a waveform keeps its shape. A filter with curved phase delays different frequencies by different amounts, which can smear sharp pulses. For music this is usually not noticed much, but for data pulses and for heartbeat shapes in an ECG it can matter a lot. Symmetric FIR filters, like the moving average, have exactly linear phase, one reason they are popular.

Bode plots: Engineers usually draw frequency responses as Bode plots: frequency on a logarithmic axis (so 10, 100, 1000 hertz are equally spaced) and gain in dB. On such a plot, the RC low-pass looks like a flat line at 0 dB until the cut-off, then a straight line sloping down at -20 dB per decade. A second-order filter slopes at -40 dB per decade. These straight-line approximations make it easy to sketch and combine filters by hand.

Filtering in action with a cascade: Two identical RC low-pass stages in series (buffered so they do not load each other) have H = 1/(1 + jωRC) squared. At the old cut-off, the gain is 0.707 squared = 0.5, which is -6 dB. Far above, the roll-off becomes -40 dB per decade. Cascading sharpens a filter, at the cost of more parts and a little more delay.

Real-life example 1, FM radio on a mobile phone: Many phones can tune FM stations like Radio Foorti or Radio Today. The antenna (usually your earphone cable) picks up all stations at once, each in its own band around 88 to 108 megahertz. To hear one station, the receiver uses band-pass filtering to keep only the band around that station's frequency and reject its neighbours. A poor band-pass filter lets a strong neighbouring station bleed in, which you hear as two programmes at once.

Real-life example 2, a notch filter for an ECG in a rural clinic: In clinics where wiring is old, the ECG trace often shows a regular wavy pattern at 50 hertz from the mains supply, hiding the small features of the heartbeat. A notch filter centred at 50 hertz removes that single frequency while leaving the heartbeat, which mostly lives below about 40 hertz, almost untouched. Many ECG machines have a '50 Hz filter' switch for exactly this.

Filters in your own code: You can try filtering in a few lines of Python or a spreadsheet. Take a list of noisy readings, apply y[n] = 0.8y[n - 1] + 0.2x[n] row by row, and plot both columns. The output is visibly smoother: a low-pass filter. Then try y[n] = x[n] - x[n - 1] and watch the steady parts vanish while the jumps stand out: a high-pass filter. Seeing the effect on real numbers makes the frequency-response formulas feel much more concrete.

Common mistakes: Thinking a gain of 0.5 is -3 dB; -3 dB is 0.707, while 0.5 is about -6 dB. Using 20 log10 for power instead of 10 log10 (for power ratios, use 10 log10). Believing an ideal brick-wall filter can be built in real time. Forgetting that a discrete filter's response repeats every 2π, so a 'low-pass' also passes frequencies near 2π. Ignoring phase when the waveform's shape matters.

What exams ask: 'Find the cut-off frequency of an RC low-pass with R = 10 kilohms and C = 0.1 microfarad' (RC = 0.001 s, fc ≈ 159 Hz). 'Show that the ideal low-pass filter is non-causal.' 'Classify a filter from its H(e^(jω)) at 0 and π.' 'Find the output for a sum of sinusoids passed through a given H(jω).' 'Convert gains of 0.707, 0.1 and 2 to decibels.'

Recap: The frequency response H gives each frequency a gain |H| and a phase shift. Gains in dB, 20 log10|H|, add in cascades; 0.707 is -3 dB. Filters are low-pass, high-pass, band-pass or band-stop, with passband, stopband, cut-off, ripple and roll-off. The ideal box filter has a sinc impulse response that is non-causal and infinite, so real filters only approximate it. The RC low-pass has cut-off 1/RC and rolls off at -20 dB per decade; the moving average is a simple discrete low-pass with linear phase.
key_points: Frequency response H(jω) or H(e^(jω)) gives each frequency a gain |H| and a phase shift; output spectrum is Y = XH.
Gain in dB = 20 log10|H|: 0.707 is -3 dB, 0.1 is -20 dB, 2 is about +6 dB; dB values add in a cascade.
Four filter types: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop (notch).
The ideal low-pass has a sinc impulse response that is non-causal and infinitely long, so it cannot be built in real time.
RC low-pass: H = 1/(1 + jωRC), cut-off ωc = 1/RC (fc = 1/(2πRC)), roll-off -20 dB per decade.
Moving averages are simple discrete low-pass filters with linear phase; linear phase keeps waveform shape.
Bode plots use a log frequency axis and dB gain, turning filter curves into near-straight lines.
lessons.tip: When you see any H(jω), evaluate |H| at three places: ω = 0, the suspected cut-off, and a very large ω. Those three numbers tell you the filter type and roughly where it cuts.
