quiz.q: What gain in decibels corresponds to |H| = 0.707?
quiz.explain: 20 log10(0.707) ≈ -3 dB, the half-power point.

quiz.q: Why can't an ideal low-pass (brick-wall) filter be built for real-time use?
options: Its impulse response is a sinc that is non-zero for negative time and infinitely long
quiz.explain: The sinc impulse response makes the filter non-causal and infinitely long.

quiz.q: An RC low-pass has R = 1 kilohm and C = 1 microfarad. What is its cut-off in radians per second?
quiz.explain: ωc = 1/RC = 1/0.001 = 1000 radians per second (about 159 Hz).

quiz.q: Which filter would remove a 50 Hz mains hum but keep nearby frequencies?
quiz.explain: A notch filter blocks a narrow band around one frequency and passes the rest.

quiz.q: Two filter stages give gains of -3 dB and -20 dB. What is the total gain?
quiz.explain: Gains multiply in a cascade, so their decibel values add: -3 + (-20) = -23 dB.

lessons.title: The Sampling Theorem and Aliasing
lessons.content:
Have you ever watched a video of a moving car and noticed the wheels seem to spin slowly backwards, or even stand still? The wheel is really spinning forwards very fast. The camera takes pictures at a fixed rate, maybe 30 per second, and if the wheel turns almost a full circle between pictures, each new picture shows it slightly behind where it was. Your brain joins the pictures and sees a slow backward spin. This illusion is called aliasing, and it is exactly what happens to any signal sampled too slowly. The sampling theorem tells us how fast we must sample so that this never happens, and so that the original signal can be rebuilt perfectly. It is one of the most important results in all of engineering.

The problem: In lesson 2 we saw that a computer stores a continuous signal x(t) as samples x[n] = x(nT), taken every T seconds, at a rate fs = 1/T. Between samples, the computer knows nothing. So a natural question arises: is it possible to lose nothing? Can the samples ever contain all the information of the continuous signal? Surprisingly, yes, if the signal does not change too fast and we sample fast enough.

Sampling as multiplication: To analyse sampling, model it as multiplying x(t) by an impulse train p(t), a row of impulses one every T seconds. The product xs(t) = x(t)p(t) is a row of impulses whose areas are the sample values x(nT). It is a continuous-time picture of the discrete list, which lets us use the continuous Fourier transform.

What sampling does to the spectrum: The impulse train p(t) is periodic, and its Fourier transform is also an impulse train, with spikes every ωs = 2π/T in frequency, each of height 2π/T. By the multiplication property, multiplying in time means convolving in frequency, and convolving with spikes makes copies. So the sampled signal's spectrum is (1/T) times the sum over all k of X(j(ω - kωs)): the original spectrum copied and repeated at every multiple of the sampling frequency. This matches the DTFT's periodicity from lesson 17, seen from the continuous side.

Band-limited signals: A signal is band-limited if its spectrum is zero above some highest frequency ωM (or fM in hertz). Real speech, music and sensor signals are approximately band-limited, especially after filtering. If X(jω) lives only between -ωM and ωM, each copy in the sampled spectrum occupies a band of width 2ωM, centred at kωs.

The key picture, copies that do or do not overlap: The copies are spaced ωs apart. If ωs > 2ωM, there is a gap between neighbouring copies: the copy centred at 0 ends at ωM, and the next one starts at ωs - ωM, which is bigger than ωM. Then we can recover the original by keeping only the central copy with a low-pass filter. If ωs < 2ωM, the copies overlap and add together, and in the overlap region the original spectrum is corrupted. No filter can separate them afterwards. That corruption is aliasing.

The sampling theorem: A band-limited signal with highest frequency fM is completely determined by its samples if the sampling frequency fs is greater than 2fM. The minimum rate 2fM is called the Nyquist rate, and half the sampling rate, fs/2, is called the Nyquist frequency, the highest frequency that can be represented without aliasing. The theorem is usually credited to Harry Nyquist and Claude Shannon, whose work in 1928 and 1949 established it for engineering, with related results by others such as Whittaker and Kotelnikov.

Why the samples can hold everything: It feels impossible that a few points per second describe every in-between value. The trick is the band limit. A signal with no frequencies above fM cannot wiggle faster than a certain rate; between two closely spaced samples it simply has no room to do anything surprising. So knowing enough points pins down the whole smooth curve, a bit like how knowing three points pins down a circle. Without the band limit, the signal could do anything between samples, and no sampling rate would be enough.

Reconstruction: To get x(t) back from its samples, pass the impulse train xs(t) through an ideal low-pass filter with gain T and a cut-off between ωM and ωs - ωM (often ωs/2). This keeps exactly the central copy, which is X(jω). In time, the ideal low-pass filter's impulse response is a sinc, so reconstruction means placing a sinc at each sample, scaled by the sample value, and adding them all up. This is called sinc interpolation. Each sinc is 1 at its own sample time and 0 at every other sample time, so the sum passes exactly through all the samples while filling in the smooth curve between them.

A worked example of the Nyquist rate: A signal is x(t) = cos(2π 100t) + sin(2π 300t). The highest frequency is 300 hertz. The Nyquist rate is 600 samples per second, so we must sample faster than 600 per second. At 1000 samples per second it is safe. At 500 per second, the 300 hertz part will alias.

Where does an aliased frequency land: When a frequency f is sampled at fs, it looks identical to frequencies f + k fs and to -f + k fs for any integer k. The apparent frequency is the one that lands between 0 and fs/2. Simple recipe: subtract the nearest multiple of fs and take the absolute value. Example: f = 7 kilohertz sampled at fs = 10 kilohertz. 7 - 10 = -3, absolute value 3: the 7 kilohertz tone appears as 3 kilohertz. Example: f = 300 hertz at fs = 500 hertz: 300 - 500 = -200, so it appears as 200 hertz.

Checking aliasing with actual samples: Take x(t) = cos(2π 3t), a 3 hertz cosine, sampled at fs = 4 hertz, so T = 0.25 seconds. The samples are cos(2π 3n/4) = cos(3πn/2). Since cos(3πn/2) = cos(2πn - πn/2) = cos(πn/2), these are exactly the samples of a 1 hertz cosine, cos(2π n/4). The values are 1, 0, -1, 0, 1, .... From the samples alone, nobody can tell whether the original was 3 hertz or 1 hertz. The recipe agrees: |3 - 4| = 1 hertz.

Why exactly 2fM is not enough: Sample sin(2π f t) at exactly fs = 2f, starting at t = 0. The samples are sin(πn) = 0 for every n. The sine vanishes completely! With other starting points you might catch peaks, but the result depends on luck. That is why the theorem says strictly greater than 2fM, and in practice engineers choose a comfortable margin above it.

The anti-aliasing filter: Real signals are never perfectly band-limited; there is always some noise or overtone above the Nyquist frequency. Any such content would alias down and pollute the useful band. So before every analog-to-digital converter, engineers put an analog low-pass filter, the anti-aliasing filter, that removes everything above fs/2 (as well as a real filter can). Once aliasing has happened, it cannot be undone, so it must be prevented before sampling.

Practical reconstruction, the zero-order hold: Real digital-to-analog converters do not produce sincs. The simplest ones hold each sample value constant until the next sample: a staircase, called a zero-order hold. The staircase contains the right spectrum plus unwanted high-frequency copies and a slight droop. A smoothing low-pass filter after the DAC removes most of the copies. Sampling well above the Nyquist rate (oversampling) makes this smoothing much easier, because the copies are pushed far away.

CD audio, a classic case: Human hearing reaches up to roughly 20,000 hertz. CDs use fs = 44,100 hertz, so the Nyquist frequency is 22,050 hertz, just above hearing. The gap between 20,000 and 22,050 hertz gives room for the anti-aliasing filter to go from passing to blocking. Telephone systems historically sampled voice at 8000 hertz, with a Nyquist frequency of 4000 hertz, enough for the 300 to 3400 hertz voice band. Many video and audio standards use 48,000 hertz for a little more margin.

Real-life example 1, a video of a ceiling fan: Record a ceiling fan on your phone at 30 frames per second. The fan has three blades, so the picture looks the same after a third of a turn. If the fan turns 10 times a second, the blade pattern repeats 30 times a second, exactly the frame rate. Each frame catches the blades in the same position, and the fan appears to stand still. A little faster and it seems to creep forward; a little slower and it seems to creep backward. Your phone is sampling the fan's motion, and the 'frozen fan' is aliasing at zero frequency.

Real-life example 2, digital temperature logging in a cold storage: A cold storage in Munshiganj keeps potatoes and logs the temperature. If the cooling system switches on and off every 10 minutes, the temperature wiggles with a period of 10 minutes. A logger that records only once every 15 minutes is sampling too slowly to see those wiggles properly; the record might show a slow fake wave, an alias, instead. Logging every minute or two, well above twice the wiggle frequency, shows the real behaviour.

Aliasing in images: Sampling also happens in space. A phone camera's sensor samples a scene with a grid of pixels. If the scene has a pattern finer than two pixels per stripe, such as a striped shirt or a distant brick wall, the camera produces strange wavy bands called moiré patterns. These are spatial aliases. Many cameras use a slight blur filter in front of the sensor, an optical anti-aliasing filter, for the same reason audio converters use one.

Common mistakes: Using the lowest frequency instead of the highest to find the Nyquist rate. Thinking fs = 2fM is enough; it must be greater. Believing aliasing can be fixed after sampling. Forgetting the anti-aliasing filter goes before the ADC, not after. Confusing the Nyquist rate (2fM, a property of the signal) with the Nyquist frequency (fs/2, a property of the sampler).

What exams ask: 'State and prove the sampling theorem using spectra.' 'Find the Nyquist rate of x(t) = 3cos(200πt) + 5sin(600πt)' (frequencies 100 and 300 hertz, Nyquist rate 600 hertz). 'A 9 kilohertz tone is sampled at 12 kilohertz; what frequency is heard after reconstruction?' (3 kilohertz). 'Explain the purpose of the anti-aliasing filter and the zero-order hold.'

Recap: Sampling multiplies a signal by an impulse train, which copies its spectrum at every multiple of fs. If fs is greater than twice the highest frequency, the copies do not overlap and an ideal low-pass filter (sinc interpolation) rebuilds the signal exactly. If not, copies overlap and high frequencies fold down as aliases, which cannot be removed later. An anti-aliasing filter before the ADC and a smoothing filter after the DAC make sampling work in practice, as in CDs at 44.1 kilohertz and phones at 8 kilohertz.
key_points: Sampling = multiplying by an impulse train; the spectrum is copied at every multiple of ωs = 2π/T (scaled by 1/T).
Sampling theorem: a signal band-limited to fM is fully recoverable if fs > 2fM; 2fM is the Nyquist rate, fs/2 the Nyquist frequency.
Reconstruction uses an ideal low-pass filter: a sum of sincs centred at the samples (sinc interpolation).
Aliasing: if fs is too low, copies overlap and a frequency f appears as |f - k fs| folded into 0 to fs/2.
Example: 3 Hz sampled at 4 Hz gives the same samples as 1 Hz; 7 kHz at 10 kHz appears as 3 kHz.
An anti-aliasing low-pass filter must come before the ADC because aliasing cannot be undone.
DACs use a zero-order hold (staircase) plus a smoothing filter; CDs use 44.1 kHz for hearing up to about 20 kHz.
lessons.tip: For any aliasing question, draw a frequency line from 0 to fs/2 and 'fold' it like a paper fan at every multiple of fs/2. Where your frequency lands after folding is what you will hear.
lessons.task: Write down the samples of cos(2π 5t) taken at fs = 8 Hz for n = 0 to 8. Then find which frequency below 4 Hz gives exactly the same samples, and check by computing that lower-frequency cosine at the same instants.

quiz.q: A signal contains frequencies up to 4 kHz. What is its Nyquist rate?
quiz.explain: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency: 2 times 4 kHz = 8 kHz; sampling must be faster than this.

quiz.q: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. At what frequency does it appear?
quiz.explain: |7 - 10| = 3 kHz, which lies between 0 and the Nyquist frequency of 5 kHz.

quiz.q: What does sampling do to a signal's spectrum?
options: Shifts it by fs only once
Copies it at every multiple of the sampling frequency
quiz.explain: Multiplying by an impulse train convolves the spectrum with spikes at multiples of ωs, making copies.

quiz.q: Where must the anti-aliasing filter be placed?
quiz.explain: Aliasing happens at the moment of sampling and cannot be undone, so high frequencies must be removed before the ADC.

quiz.q: Why is sampling a sine at exactly fs = 2f not safe?
options: The samples may all be zero, depending on the starting phase
quiz.explain: Sampling sin(2πft) at 2f starting at t = 0 gives sin(πn) = 0 for every n, so the tone is lost.

lessons.title: Modulation: Moving Spectra Around
lessons.content:
Imagine many people in a crowded Gulistan bus terminal all shouting at once. Nobody can understand anyone, because all the voices sit in the same range of frequencies and pile on top of each other. Now imagine each person could magically lift their voice to a different, private range of pitches, one person very high, another higher still, and each listener carried a tuner that listens only to one range. Suddenly everyone can talk at the same time without confusion. That magic is modulation, and it is how dozens of radio stations, TV channels and mobile calls share the same air. In signals terms, modulation simply means moving a signal's spectrum to a new place. This lesson shows how multiplying by a cosine does that, how the receiver moves it back, and why it matters.

Why we cannot just send voice directly: Voice and music live at low frequencies, from tens of hertz to a few kilohertz. To radiate efficiently, an antenna must be a decent fraction of the wavelength. At 3 kilohertz, the wavelength is the speed of light divided by 3000, which is 100 kilometres. An antenna kilometres long is absurd. At 100 megahertz the wavelength is 3 metres, so an antenna under a metre works fine. Also, if every station sent its raw audio, all of them would overlap in the same low band, like the bus terminal. Modulation solves both problems by lifting each signal to its own high frequency.

The key tool, multiplying by a cosine: From the Fourier properties lesson, multiplying x(t) by cos(ωc t) gives the spectrum (1/2)[X(j(ω - ωc)) + X(j(ω + ωc))]. The original spectrum, centred at zero, is copied to +ωc and -ωc at half height. The cosine is called the carrier, and ωc is the carrier frequency. The message x(t) is the modulating signal. This is called double-sideband suppressed-carrier modulation, DSB-SC.

Sidebands: If the message has frequencies up to ωM, then after modulation the positive copy occupies ωc - ωM to ωc + ωM. The part above ωc is the upper sideband and the part below is the lower sideband. They are mirror images of each other and carry the same information. The total bandwidth needed is 2ωM, twice the message bandwidth. Example: a message tone of 1 kilohertz on a carrier of 100 kilohertz produces two tones, at 99 and 101 kilohertz. You can see this with a trig identity: cos(a)cos(b) = (1/2)[cos(a - b) + cos(a + b)].

Getting the message back, synchronous demodulation: The receiver gets y(t) = x(t)cos(ωc t). It multiplies again by the same carrier: y(t)cos(ωc t) = x(t)cos squared(ωc t) = x(t)/2 + (x(t)/2)cos(2ωc t), using cos squared = (1 + cos 2θ)/2. The first term is the message at half size, back at low frequencies. The second is a copy of the message up at 2ωc. A low-pass filter keeps x(t)/2 and removes the high copy. In frequency terms: the second multiplication shifts the copies at ±ωc back to 0 (and also to ±2ωc), and the filter keeps the one at 0.

Demodulation with numbers: Let x(t) = cos(2π 1000t) and the carrier be cos(2π 100,000t). The transmitted DSB signal has tones at 99 and 101 kilohertz. The receiver multiplies by the carrier again. The 99 kilohertz tone times the 100 kilohertz carrier creates tones at 1 kilohertz and 199 kilohertz. The 101 kilohertz tone creates tones at 1 kilohertz and 201 kilohertz. A low-pass filter with a cut-off of, say, 10 kilohertz keeps the two 1 kilohertz pieces, which add up to the original tone at half strength, and removes everything near 200 kilohertz. The message is back.

Why it must be synchronous: The receiver's cosine must match the transmitter's in both frequency and phase. Suppose the receiver's carrier has a phase error θ: it uses cos(ωc t + θ). Then after filtering you get (x(t)/2)cos θ. With θ = 60 degrees the message is halved again; with θ = 90 degrees it vanishes completely. If the frequency is slightly off, cos θ drifts slowly with time and the sound fades in and out. Keeping the receiver locked to the carrier needs extra circuitry, which made early DSB receivers expensive.

Conventional AM, adding the carrier: Broadcast AM (amplitude modulation) avoids the synchronisation problem by sending the carrier too: y(t) = (A + x(t))cos(ωc t), with A large enough that A + x(t) is never negative. Now the outline, or envelope, of the high-frequency wave traces exactly A + x(t). The spectrum is the DSB spectrum plus two spikes for the carrier at ±ωc.

The envelope detector: Because the envelope follows the message, a very simple circuit recovers it: a diode that passes only the positive half, followed by a resistor and capacitor that smooth the peaks into a curve following the envelope. Remove the constant A (with a capacitor) and you have x(t). No local oscillator, no synchronisation. This is why cheap AM radios with a handful of parts were possible a century ago, and why AM spread everywhere.

Modulation index: For AM, define the modulation index m as the peak of |x(t)| divided by A. If m ≤ 1, A + x(t) never goes negative and the envelope detector works. If m > 1, called over-modulation, the envelope crosses zero and folds, and the detector output is distorted. Example: A = 2 and x(t) = 1.5cos(ωm t) gives m = 0.75, which is fine. A = 1 with the same x gives m = 1.5, over-modulated.

The price of simplicity, power: In AM, a large part of the transmitted power goes into the carrier, which carries no information. For a single tone with m = 1, the carrier takes two thirds of the total power and the two sidebands share one third. DSB-SC wastes none on the carrier but needs a harder receiver. Single-sideband (SSB) goes further: it sends only one sideband, halving the bandwidth. It is used by ham radio and some long-distance links. Engineers trade power, bandwidth and receiver cost.

A power worked example: An AM transmitter has carrier amplitude A = 10 volts and a single message tone with m = 0.5. The carrier power (into a 1 ohm load) is A squared over 2 = 50 watts. Each sideband has amplitude mA/2 = 2.5 volts, so each carries 2.5 squared over 2 = 3.125 watts, 6.25 watts for both. Out of 56.25 watts in total, only about 11 percent carries the message. This is the main reason modern systems prefer suppressed-carrier and digital schemes.

Frequency-division multiplexing: Now the bus terminal solution. Give each message its own carrier: station 1 at ωc1, station 2 at ωc2, and so on, spaced more than the signal bandwidth apart. Add all the modulated signals together and send them through the same air or cable. Their spectra sit side by side without overlapping. A receiver uses a band-pass filter to select one station's band, then demodulates it. This is frequency-division multiplexing (FDM), used in radio, TV broadcasting, and as a basis for parts of modern systems.

A worked FDM example: Three voice channels, each limited to 4 kilohertz, are to share a cable using DSB-SC. Each needs 8 kilohertz of bandwidth. If we add 2 kilohertz of guard space between channels to make filtering easier, carriers could be placed at, for example, 20, 30 and 40 kilohertz, giving bands of 16 to 24, 26 to 34, and 36 to 44 kilohertz. No overlap, so each can be separated.

Other kinds of modulation, briefly: Instead of the amplitude, a carrier's frequency can carry the message (frequency modulation, FM) or its phase (phase modulation, PM). FM resists amplitude noise, which is why FM radio usually sounds cleaner than AM. Digital systems such as WiFi and 4G vary amplitude and phase together to send several bits per symbol. The details belong to the Data Communication course; the core idea, moving spectra with carriers, is what you learned here.

Modulation and sampling are cousins: Sampling multiplies by an impulse train, and the spectrum is copied at every multiple of the sampling frequency. Modulation multiplies by a single cosine, and the spectrum is copied at plus and minus one carrier frequency. Both are applications of the same property: multiplication in time is convolution in frequency, and convolution with spikes makes copies. Seeing this link makes both topics easier.

Real-life example 1, Bangladesh Betar on medium wave: Bangladesh Betar has long broadcast on AM medium-wave frequencies, roughly in the range of 530 to 1600 kilohertz. Each transmitter uses its own carrier, and voice and music modulate its amplitude. A simple pocket radio in a village tea stall uses a tuned band-pass circuit to pick one carrier and an envelope detector to recover the audio, exactly the cheap, robust chain described above. Because medium-wave signals can travel far, especially at night, AM reached places where other services did not.

Real-life example 2, FM stations in Dhaka: FM stations in Dhaka sit at different carrier frequencies between 88 and 108 megahertz. Your phone's FM receiver tunes to one carrier, filters out the neighbours, and demodulates. Because each station is assigned a separate band, dozens can broadcast at once in the same city, which is FDM at work. If two stations were placed too close in frequency, listeners between them would hear both mixed, which is why regulators assign frequencies carefully.

Where modulation hides in everyday devices: Your WiFi router lifts data up to 2.4 or 5 gigahertz carriers. A TV remote flashes its infrared light on and off at a carrier of a few tens of kilohertz, so the TV's sensor can ignore steady sunlight and lamp light. Even an ultrasound scan at a hospital sends pulses on a carrier of a few megahertz. Each time, the same signals idea is at work: put the information on a carrier that suits the medium, then move it back at the receiver.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the factor 1/2 in the modulated spectrum. Thinking AM and DSB-SC are the same; AM includes the carrier. Writing the DSB bandwidth as ωM instead of 2ωM. Forgetting that synchronous detection needs matching phase as well as frequency. Using an envelope detector on DSB-SC, which fails because the envelope is |x(t)|, not x(t).

What exams ask: 'Sketch the spectrum of x(t)cos(ωc t) given X(jω).' 'Show how synchronous demodulation recovers x(t) and what happens with a phase error θ.' 'For AM with A = 4 and x(t) = 2cos(ωm t), find the modulation index' (0.5). 'Three 5 kHz signals share a channel using DSB; find the minimum total bandwidth' (30 kHz, without guard bands).

Recap: Modulation moves a message's spectrum up to a carrier frequency so that antennas are practical and many signals can share a channel. Multiplying by cos(ωc t) copies the spectrum to ±ωc at half height, creating two sidebands and needing bandwidth 2ωM. Synchronous demodulation multiplies again and low-pass filters, but needs matching phase. AM adds the carrier so a simple envelope detector works, if the modulation index is at most 1, at the cost of power. FDM places many signals at different carriers side by side.
key_points: Modulation moves a message spectrum up to a carrier frequency ωc, making antennas practical and allowing many signals to share a channel.
x(t)cos(ωc t) has spectrum (1/2)[X(j(ω - ωc)) + X(j(ω + ωc))]: two sidebands, total bandwidth 2ωM (DSB-SC).
Synchronous demodulation: multiply again by cos(ωc t) and low-pass filter to get x(t)/2; a phase error θ scales it by cos θ.
Conventional AM sends (A + x(t))cos(ωc t); if modulation index m = max|x|/A ≤ 1, an envelope detector recovers the message.
AM spends much power on the carrier (two thirds for a single tone with m = 1); SSB halves bandwidth by sending one sideband.
Frequency-division multiplexing places signals at different carriers so their spectra sit side by side.
Sampling and modulation both come from 'multiplication in time is convolution in frequency'.
lessons.tip: For any modulation problem, draw three spectrum pictures one under another: the message, after multiplying by the carrier, and after the receiver's multiplication. Shifting shapes by ±ωc on paper makes every formula obvious.
lessons.task: Let x(t) = cos(2π 500t) and the carrier be cos(2π 10,000t). Use cos(a)cos(b) = (1/2)[cos(a - b) + cos(a + b)] to find the frequencies in the DSB signal, then multiply by the carrier again and list the frequencies that appear before low-pass filtering.

quiz.q: What does multiplying a message by cos(ωc t) do to its spectrum?
options: Copies it to +ωc and -ωc at half height
quiz.explain: By the modulation property, the spectrum becomes (1/2)[X(j(ω - ωc)) + X(j(ω + ωc))].

quiz.q: A message with bandwidth 5 kHz is sent with DSB-SC. What bandwidth does it occupy?
quiz.explain: Both upper and lower sidebands are sent, so the bandwidth is 2 times 5 kHz.

quiz.q: In synchronous demodulation, the receiver's carrier has a 90 degree phase error. What is the output?
quiz.explain: The output is (x(t)/2)cos θ, and cos 90° = 0.

quiz.q: For AM with A = 4 and x(t) = 2cos(ωm t), what is the modulation index?
quiz.explain: m = max|x| / A = 2/4 = 0.5, so the envelope detector works.

quiz.q: Why can a cheap envelope detector demodulate conventional AM?
options: Because the envelope of the wave follows A + x(t), which stays positive
quiz.explain: Adding the carrier makes the envelope trace the message (plus a constant) when m ≤ 1.

lessons.title: The Laplace Transform for Systems
lessons.content:
The Fourier transform is like a camera that only works in daylight. It takes beautiful pictures of signals that settle down, but signals that grow, like e^(2t), or systems that are unstable, make it fail: the integral blows up. Engineers designing aeroplane controls or power circuits need to study exactly those growing and unstable cases, to make sure they never happen in practice. The Laplace transform is the night-vision camera. It adds a small damping factor that tames growing signals, so it works for a much bigger family. You met its maths in Math III. Here we use it the way signals and systems engineers do: with the s-plane, the region of convergence, poles and zeros.

The definition: The (bilateral) Laplace transform of x(t) is X(s) = integral over all t of x(t)e^(-st) dt, where s = σ + jω is a complex number. σ is the real part and ω the imaginary part. Notice that if we set σ = 0, then s = jω and the Laplace transform becomes exactly the Fourier transform. So the Fourier transform is a special case: the Laplace transform evaluated on the imaginary axis.

The damping view: Write e^(-st) = e^(-σt)e^(-jωt). So X(s) is the Fourier transform of x(t)e^(-σt). The factor e^(-σt) with σ > 0 shrinks the signal for large positive t. A signal like e^(2t)u(t) grows, so its Fourier integral diverges, but multiply it by e^(-3t) and you get e^(-t)u(t), which is perfectly fine. That is the whole trick: choose σ big enough to tame the growth, then take the Fourier transform of the tamed signal.

The s-plane: Because s is complex, we picture it as a plane: σ on the horizontal axis, ω on the vertical axis. The vertical line σ = 0 is the jω axis, where the Fourier transform lives. The left half (σ < 0) and right half (σ > 0) will turn out to describe decaying and growing behaviour. Engineers mark special points on this plane, poles and zeros, and read off a system's behaviour from the picture.

What history gives us: The transform is named after Pierre-Simon Laplace, a French mathematician who used similar integrals in probability around 1800. Its use in engineering grew in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when Oliver Heaviside invented an 'operational calculus' for solving circuit equations by treating the derivative as an algebraic symbol. Mathematicians later showed that the Laplace transform gives Heaviside's tricks a solid footing. Today it is the standard language of control engineering and circuit analysis.

Pair 1, the right-sided exponential: x(t) = e^(-at)u(t). X(s) = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-(s + a)t) dt = 1/(s + a), but only if the real part of s + a is positive, that is, Re(s) > -a. Otherwise the integral blows up. The set of s values where the integral converges is called the region of convergence, or ROC. Here the ROC is the half-plane to the right of the vertical line σ = -a.

Pair 2, the left-sided exponential: x(t) = -e^(-at)u(-t), which is non-zero only for negative time. X(s) = -integral from minus infinity to 0 of e^(-(s + a)t) dt = 1/(s + a), but now only if Re(s) < -a. Same formula, different ROC! This is a crucial lesson: the algebraic expression X(s) alone does not identify a signal. You must state the ROC. 1/(s + a) with Re(s) > -a is a causal, right-sided signal; with Re(s) < -a it is an anti-causal, left-sided one.

Rules for the ROC: The ROC is always made of vertical strips (it depends only on σ, not ω). It never contains a pole, because X(s) is infinite there. For a right-sided signal (zero before some time), the ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole. For a left-sided signal, it is to the left of the leftmost pole. For a two-sided signal, it is a strip between two poles, if it exists at all. For a finite-length signal, it is the whole s-plane (perhaps except s at infinity).

A two-sided example: x(t) = e^(-|t|), which decays on both sides. Split it: e^(-t)u(t) gives 1/(s + 1) with Re(s) > -1. e^(t)u(-t) gives the integral from minus infinity to 0 of e^((1 - s)t) dt = 1/(1 - s) with Re(s) < 1. Both must converge, so the ROC is the strip -1 < Re(s) < 1. Adding: X(s) = 1/(s + 1) + 1/(1 - s) = 2/(1 - s squared). The strip contains the jω axis, so the Fourier transform also exists, and setting s = jω gives 2/(1 + ω squared), matching the result from lesson 15.

A table of common pairs: δ(t) gives 1, ROC all s. u(t) gives 1/s, Re(s) > 0. t u(t) gives 1/s squared, Re(s) > 0. e^(-at)u(t) gives 1/(s + a), Re(s) > -a. e^(-at)cos(ω0t)u(t) gives (s + a)/((s + a) squared + ω0 squared), Re(s) > -a. e^(-at)sin(ω0t)u(t) gives ω0/((s + a) squared + ω0 squared), Re(s) > -a. Notice the step u(t), which has no ordinary Fourier transform, has a simple Laplace transform.

Linearity and the ROC: The transform of a sum is the sum of the transforms, but the ROC of the sum is at least the overlap of the two ROCs. Example: e^(-2t)u(t) + e^(-3t)u(t). The first converges for Re(s) > -2, the second for Re(s) > -3. Both converge where Re(s) > -2, so that is the ROC of the sum. If the two ROCs do not overlap at all, the sum has no Laplace transform, as happens for e^(t)u(-t) + e^(2t)u(t): the first needs Re(s) < 1 and the second Re(s) > 2.

Poles and zeros: Most transforms we meet are rational: X(s) = N(s)/D(s), a ratio of polynomials. The roots of N(s) are zeros, where X(s) = 0. The roots of D(s) are poles, where X(s) is infinite. Example: X(s) = (s + 1)/((s + 2)(s + 3)) has a zero at s = -1 and poles at s = -2 and s = -3. On the s-plane we mark poles with a cross and zeros with a small circle. Apart from a constant gain factor, the poles and zeros completely describe a rational X(s).

What a pole's position means: A pole at s = -a on the real axis corresponds to a time signal e^(-at). If the pole is on the left (a > 0), the signal decays; on the right, it grows; at the origin, it is constant. A pair of complex poles at s = -a ± jω0 corresponds to e^(-at)cos(ω0t): an oscillation inside an envelope. The distance to the left tells how fast it decays; the height above the axis tells how fast it oscillates. Poles on the jω axis itself give steady oscillations that never die.

A worked pole reading: X(s) = 1/(s squared + 2s + 5). The denominator roots are s = (-2 ± square root of (4 - 20))/2 = -1 ± j2. So the time signal (for a right-sided ROC) is a decaying oscillation: (1/2)e^(-t)sin(2t)u(t). It oscillates at 2 radians per second and the envelope e^(-t) halves roughly every 0.7 seconds. You can predict the shape just from the pole positions, before doing any inverse transform.

The unilateral Laplace transform: For circuits and control, where signals start at t = 0 and we know initial conditions, engineers often use the unilateral transform, integrating from 0 (just before zero) to infinity. Its derivative rule includes the initial value: dx/dt transforms to sX(s) - x(0-). This lets you solve differential equations with initial conditions in one go, as you did in Math III. For causal signals the bilateral and unilateral transforms are the same.

Why we need both Fourier and Laplace: Fourier gives the frequency response that we can measure and hear, but only for signals and systems that are stable enough. Laplace covers growing signals and unstable systems and turns differential equations into algebra, and its pole-zero picture makes stability easy to see. Engineers move between them: design and check stability in s, then look at the jω axis for the frequency response.

Real-life example 1, a motor speed controller: A small DC motor driving a conveyor in a garment factory is often modelled with a transfer function like K/(τs + 1), one pole at s = -1/τ. With τ = 0.5 seconds, the pole is at -2: after the voltage is switched on, the speed rises like 1 - e^(-2t), reaching about 86 percent in 1 second. Engineers add a controller and check, using pole positions, that the new system responds faster without oscillating too much.

Real-life example 2, a building swaying in wind: Engineers model a tall building in Dhaka as a mass on a spring with some damping. Its transfer function has two complex poles at -a ± jω0. ω0 is the natural swaying frequency and a sets how quickly swaying dies after a gust. If a is too small (poles very close to the jω axis), the building keeps swaying for a long time. Designers add dampers, which move the poles further left, so the sway dies quickly and occupants feel comfortable.

Seeing the s-plane as a map: A helpful picture is to imagine |X(s)| as the height of a rubber sheet stretched over the s-plane. At each pole, the sheet is pushed up into an infinitely tall tent pole. At each zero, it is pinned down to the floor. Walking along the jω axis on this sheet traces the magnitude of the frequency response: as you pass close to a pole, the height rises (a resonance peak); as you pass close to a zero, it dips. This is why pole and zero positions directly shape filters.

Common mistakes: Giving X(s) without its ROC. Assuming 1/(s + a) always means e^(-at)u(t); it depends on the ROC. Thinking the Fourier transform exists whenever the Laplace transform does; only if the ROC includes the jω axis. Putting poles inside the ROC; the ROC never contains poles. Mixing up a pole at s = -2 (decays as e^(-2t)) with a pole at s = 2 (grows as e^(2t)).

What exams ask: 'Find the Laplace transform and ROC of x(t) = e^(-2t)u(t) + e^(-3t)u(t)' (answer (2s + 5)/((s + 2)(s + 3)), Re(s) > -2). 'Find X(s) and ROC of e^(-3|t|).' 'Sketch the pole-zero plot of (s + 1)/(s squared + 4s + 13)' (zero at -1, poles at -2 ± j3). 'Explain why the same X(s) can correspond to different signals.'

Recap: The Laplace transform X(s) = integral of x(t)e^(-st) dt with s = σ + jω extends Fourier by damping the signal with e^(-σt). It equals the Fourier transform on the jω axis when that axis is in the ROC. The ROC is made of vertical strips, contains no poles, lies right of the poles for right-sided signals and left for left-sided ones. Rational transforms are described by poles and zeros: poles on the left mean decay, on the right mean growth, complex pairs mean oscillation. Always state the ROC.
key_points: Laplace: X(s) = ∫ x(t)e^(-st) dt with s = σ + jω; on the jω axis (σ = 0) it equals the Fourier transform.
Laplace is the Fourier transform of x(t)e^(-σt), so it works for growing signals like e^(2t)u(t).
The region of convergence (ROC) is where the integral converges; the same X(s) with different ROCs gives different signals.
ROC rules: vertical strips, no poles inside; right-sided signals have ROC right of the rightmost pole, left-sided left of the leftmost.
Pairs: δ gives 1; u(t) gives 1/s; e^(-at)u(t) gives 1/(s + a) for Re(s) > -a.
Poles (denominator roots) and zeros (numerator roots) plotted on the s-plane describe a rational X(s).
Left-half-plane poles mean decay, right-half-plane poles mean growth, complex pole pairs mean oscillation.
lessons.tip: Write the ROC next to every X(s) you compute, every single time, as if it were part of the answer. Most exam traps in this topic are about a missing or wrong ROC.
lessons.task: Find the Laplace transform and ROC of x(t) = e^(-t)u(t) - e^(2t)u(-t). Mark the poles on an s-plane sketch, shade the ROC, and decide whether this signal has a Fourier transform.

quiz.q: What is the Laplace transform of e^(-3t)u(t), with its ROC?
quiz.explain: The integral of e^(-(s + 3)t) from 0 to infinity converges to 1/(s + 3) when Re(s) > -3.

quiz.q: When does the Fourier transform equal the Laplace transform at s = jω?
options: When the ROC includes the jω axis
quiz.explain: The Fourier transform is X(s) evaluated on σ = 0, which is valid only if that line is inside the ROC.

quiz.q: Which statement about the ROC is true?
options: It is the same for every signal with the same X(s)
quiz.explain: X(s) is infinite at a pole, so the integral cannot converge there.

quiz.q: A right-sided signal has poles at s = -1 and s = -4. What is its ROC?
quiz.explain: For right-sided signals the ROC lies to the right of the rightmost pole, here -1.

quiz.q: Poles at s = -1 ± j2 (right-sided) correspond to what kind of time signal?
quiz.explain: Real part -1 gives decay e^(-t); imaginary part 2 gives oscillation at 2 rad/s.

lessons.title: Transfer Functions and Stability
lessons.content:
When a lift in a building stops at your floor, a good one slows smoothly and stops level. A badly tuned one overshoots, bounces up and down a few times, and then settles. A really broken one might never settle at all. Engineers predict which of these will happen before the lift is ever built, using one compact object: the transfer function. It is the Laplace transform of the impulse response, and its poles tell you at a glance whether a system is stable, how fast it responds, and whether it will oscillate. This lesson shows how to get transfer functions, how to read stability from them, and how first- and second-order systems behave.

The transfer function: For a continuous LTI system with impulse response h(t), the transfer function is H(s), the Laplace transform of h(t). Because convolution becomes multiplication, Y(s) = H(s)X(s), so H(s) = Y(s)/X(s): output over input. On the jω axis, H(jω) is the frequency response. So one function gives you the impulse response (by inverse Laplace), the frequency response (by setting s = jω), and the stability (from the poles).

From a differential equation to H(s): Take an LTI system described by a2 y'' + a1 y' + a0 y = b1 x' + b0 x, starting at rest. The Laplace transform turns each derivative into multiplication by s (with zero initial conditions): (a2 s squared + a1 s + a0)Y(s) = (b1 s + b0)X(s). So H(s) = (b1 s + b0)/(a2 s squared + a1 s + a0). Example: y'' + 3y' + 2y = 2x gives H(s) = 2/(s squared + 3s + 2) = 2/((s + 1)(s + 2)), with poles at -1 and -2.

Causality from the ROC: A causal system has h(t) = 0 for t < 0, so h is right-sided, and its ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole. For rational H(s), causal means the ROC is a right half-plane.

Stability from the ROC: BIBO stability needs the integral of |h(t)| to be finite. This happens exactly when the ROC of H(s) includes the jω axis, because that is where the Fourier transform of h exists in the ordinary sense. So stable means the jω axis is inside the ROC.

The golden rule, causal and stable: Put the two facts together. For a causal system, the ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole. For it to include the jω axis, the rightmost pole must be to the left of the axis. So a causal LTI system with rational H(s) is stable if and only if all its poles have negative real parts, that is, all poles lie in the left half of the s-plane. This one rule is the basis of stability analysis in control engineering.

Why left-half poles mean stable, intuitively: Each pole contributes a term to h(t). A pole at -a gives e^(-at), which dies out if a > 0. A complex pair at -a ± jω0 gives e^(-at)cos(ω0t), which also dies out if a > 0. A pole with positive real part gives a growing term, which makes the system unstable. A pole exactly on the jω axis gives a term that never dies and never grows: a constant or a steady oscillation. Such a system is called marginally stable, and it is not BIBO stable: for example, the integrator 1/s (pole at 0) turns a bounded step into an unbounded ramp.

Stability examples: H(s) = 1/(s + 2): pole at -2, stable. H(s) = 1/(s - 1): pole at +1, unstable (h(t) = e^t u(t)). H(s) = 1/(s squared + 4): poles at ±j2, on the axis, marginally stable, not BIBO stable; an input at 2 radians per second makes the output grow without limit, which is resonance. H(s) = (s - 3)/((s + 1)(s + 5)): poles at -1 and -5, stable. The zero at +3 does not affect stability; only poles do.

The first-order system: H(s) = 1/(τs + 1) has one pole at s = -1/τ. Its impulse response is (1/τ)e^(-t/τ)u(t), and its step response is (1 - e^(-t/τ))u(t). τ is the time constant: after τ the output reaches about 63 percent of its final value, after 3τ about 95 percent, and after 5τ more than 99 percent. Example: an RC low-pass with RC = 2 milliseconds has τ = 2 ms, so it settles in roughly 10 ms. A smaller τ means a pole further left and a faster system.

The second-order system: Many systems, like a mass on a spring, an RLC circuit or a car suspension, follow H(s) = ωn squared/(s squared + 2ζωn s + ωn squared). ωn is the natural frequency and ζ (zeta) is the damping ratio. The poles are at -ζωn ± ωn times the square root of (ζ squared - 1). The value of ζ decides the behaviour.

The four damping cases: If ζ > 1, the poles are two separate real negative numbers: overdamped, the step response rises slowly with no overshoot, like a heavy door closer. If ζ = 1, there is a double real pole: critically damped, the fastest rise without overshoot. If 0 < ζ < 1, the poles are a complex pair -ζωn ± jωn times the square root of (1 - ζ squared): underdamped, the step response overshoots and rings before settling, like a plucked ruler. If ζ = 0, the poles are on the jω axis at ±jωn: undamped, the system oscillates forever.

A worked second-order example: An RLC series circuit with output across the capacitor has H(s) = 1/(LCs squared + RCs + 1). Take L = 1 henry, C = 0.25 farad and R = 1 ohm. Then H(s) = 1/(0.25s squared + 0.25s + 1) = 4/(s squared + s + 4). So ωn squared = 4, ωn = 2, and 2ζωn = 1, giving ζ = 0.25. Underdamped: the poles are at -0.5 ± j times the square root of 3.75, about -0.5 ± j1.94. A step input makes the capacitor voltage overshoot and ring at about 1.94 radians per second, fading like e^(-0.5t). Increasing R raises ζ and calms the ringing.

Step response by partial fractions: For H(s) = 2/((s + 1)(s + 2)) and a unit step input X(s) = 1/s, Y(s) = 2/(s(s + 1)(s + 2)). Split: A/s + B/(s + 1) + C/(s + 2). Cover-up method: A = 2/((1)(2)) = 1 at s = 0; B = 2/((-1)(1)) = -2 at s = -1; C = 2/((-2)(-1)) = 1 at s = -2. So y(t) = (1 - 2e^(-t) + e^(-2t))u(t). Check: y(0) = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0 (starts at rest) and y(infinity) = 1. Overdamped, as two real poles predict.

The final value theorem: For a stable system, the final value of y(t) is the limit of sY(s) as s goes to 0. For a unit step input, that is just H(0), the DC gain. Above, H(0) = 2/2 = 1, matching y(infinity) = 1. Warning: the theorem gives nonsense for unstable systems, so check the poles first.

How fast and how much overshoot: For an underdamped second-order system, two numbers describe the step response. The percent overshoot depends only on ζ: it is 100 times e^(-πζ / square root of (1 - ζ squared)). For ζ = 0.5 that is about 16 percent; for ζ = 0.25 about 44 percent; for ζ = 0.7 under 5 percent. The settling time, to stay within 2 percent of the final value, is roughly 4/(ζωn), which is 4 divided by the distance of the poles from the jω axis. So moving poles left speeds settling, and moving them closer to the real axis reduces overshoot.

Feedback can fix or break stability: Consider an unstable plant G(s) = K/(s - 1), with a pole at +1, like balancing a broomstick. Put it in a negative feedback loop with unity feedback. The closed-loop transfer function is G/(1 + G) = K/(s - 1 + K). Its pole is at s = 1 - K. If K > 1, the pole moves into the left half-plane, and the closed loop is stable. Feedback can tame an unstable system, which is how self-balancing scooters and rockets stay upright. Too much gain in other systems, however, can push poles to the right and cause instability, like microphone howl.

Checking stability without finding roots: For high-order denominators, finding poles by hand is hard. A quick necessary condition: for all poles to be in the left half-plane, all coefficients of the denominator polynomial must be non-zero and have the same sign. s squared + 3s + 2 passes. s cubed + s squared - s + 1 fails (a negative coefficient), so it is unstable. For a full test, the Routh-Hurwitz method, covered in control courses, decides stability from the coefficients alone.

Real-life example 1, a car's suspension on a Dhaka road: Hitting a pothole gives the car a sudden input. The suspension is a mass-spring-damper, a second-order system. With worn-out shock absorbers, the damping ratio drops, and the car bounces several times after each pothole: an underdamped response. New shock absorbers bring ζ back to the value the designers chose, a compromise between comfort and control, so the car settles quickly with only a small bounce.

Real-life example 2, a voltage stabiliser at home: Many homes in Bangladesh use automatic voltage stabilisers for fridges and TVs. The stabiliser senses the output voltage and adjusts it through feedback. If the designer chose too high a loop gain, the closed-loop poles would move towards or across the jω axis, and the output would oscillate or hunt up and down. A well-designed stabiliser has its poles comfortably in the left half-plane, so it corrects a sudden dip quickly without overshooting into a damaging surge.

Common mistakes: Thinking zeros in the right half-plane make a system unstable; only poles decide stability. Calling a system with poles on the jω axis stable; it is only marginally stable, not BIBO stable. Using the final value theorem on an unstable system. Forgetting that 'causal and stable means all poles in the left half-plane' assumes the system is causal.

What exams ask: 'Find H(s) for y'' + 5y' + 6y = x and determine stability' (poles -2 and -3, stable). 'For H(s) = 25/(s squared + 4s + 25), find ωn, ζ and classify the response' (ωn = 5, ζ = 0.4, underdamped). 'Find the step response by partial fractions.' 'For what K is K/(s - 2) with unity feedback stable?' (K > 2).

Recap: The transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) is the Laplace transform of h(t) and comes straight from a differential equation. A causal system is stable exactly when all poles are in the left half-plane; poles on the jω axis mean marginal stability, on the right mean instability. First-order systems rise with time constant τ. Second-order systems are overdamped, critically damped, underdamped or undamped depending on ζ. Partial fractions give time responses, the final value theorem gives steady states, and feedback moves poles.
key_points: The transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) is the Laplace transform of h(t); from a differential equation, replace each derivative by s.
A system is stable when its ROC includes the jω axis; a causal system's ROC lies right of its rightmost pole.
Golden rule: a causal LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if all poles are in the left half of the s-plane.
Poles on the jω axis give marginal stability (not BIBO stable); right-half-plane poles give instability; zeros do not decide stability.
First order 1/(τs + 1): step response 1 - e^(-t/τ), about 63% at τ and over 99% at 5τ.
Second order ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²): ζ > 1 overdamped, ζ = 1 critical, 0 < ζ < 1 underdamped (overshoot), ζ = 0 undamped.
Final value of a step response is H(0) for a stable system; feedback can move poles to stabilise or destabilise.
lessons.tip: Before calculating any response, find the poles and mark them on an s-plane sketch. Their positions tell you stability, speed and oscillation, so you know the shape of the answer before the algebra.
lessons.task: For the system y'' + 2y' + 5y = 5x: find H(s), its poles, ωn and ζ. Predict the shape of the step response, then compute H(0) to find its final value.

quiz.q: When is a causal LTI system with rational H(s) BIBO stable?
options: When all zeros are in the left half-plane
When all poles are in the left half-plane
quiz.explain: Causal means the ROC is right of the rightmost pole; including the jω axis requires all poles to have negative real parts.

quiz.q: What is H(s) for y'' + 3y' + 2y = 2x (at rest)?
quiz.explain: Each derivative becomes a power of s: (s squared + 3s + 2)Y = 2X.

quiz.q: For H(s) = 4/(s squared + s + 4), what is the damping ratio ζ?
quiz.explain: ωn squared = 4 so ωn = 2; 2ζωn = 1 gives ζ = 0.25, an underdamped system.

quiz.q: H(s) = 1/(s squared + 9) has poles at ±j3. What kind of system is it?
options: Marginally stable: it oscillates forever and is not BIBO stable
quiz.explain: Poles on the jω axis give a steady oscillation; an input at 3 rad/s makes the output grow (resonance).

quiz.q: A stable system has H(s) = 6/((s + 2)(s + 3)). What is the final value of its unit step response?
quiz.explain: By the final value theorem the step response settles at H(0) = 6/(2 times 3) = 1.

lessons.title: The Z-Transform
lessons.content:
In the last two lessons the Laplace transform gave continuous-time systems a superpower: differential equations became algebra, and the poles on the s-plane told us stability at a glance. Computers, phones and digital filters live in discrete time, and they deserve the same superpower. The z-transform is exactly that: the discrete-time cousin of the Laplace transform. It turns difference equations into algebra, turns convolution into multiplication, and draws a map, the z-plane, where a single circle decides stability. Every engineer who designs a digital filter, a digital controller or an audio effect uses it.

The definition: The z-transform of a sequence x[n] is X(z) = the sum over all n of x[n]z^(-n), where z is a complex number. Each sample x[n] is attached to a power z^(-n), like a label saying 'I belong to time n'. For example, x[0] = 3, x[1] = 2, x[2] = 1 and zero elsewhere gives X(z) = 3 + 2z^(-1) + z^(-2). You can read the sequence straight back from the coefficients.

The link to the DTFT: Write z in polar form, z = re^(jω). Then X(z) = sum of x[n]r^(-n)e^(-jωn), which is the DTFT of x[n]r^(-n). The factor r^(-n) plays the same damping role as e^(-σt) in Laplace: choosing r large enough tames sequences that grow. When r = 1, z = e^(jω) lies on the unit circle, and X(z) becomes exactly the DTFT X(e^(jω)). So the DTFT is the z-transform evaluated on the unit circle, just as the Fourier transform is the Laplace transform on the jω axis.

The z-plane: We draw z on a plane with real and imaginary axes. The unit circle, |z| = 1, plays the role that the jω axis played in the s-plane. Going around the circle once, from ω = 0 at z = 1 through ω = π at z = -1 and back, sweeps through all discrete frequencies. Low frequencies are near z = 1, high frequencies near z = -1. Inside the circle corresponds to decaying behaviour, and outside to growing behaviour.

Why a polynomial picture helps: Think of X(z) as a storage box where each sample sits in its own labelled drawer. Drawer z^0 holds x[0], drawer z^(-1) holds x[1], drawer z^(-2) holds x[2], and so on. Adding two sequences adds what is in matching drawers. Delaying a sequence by one step moves every sample one drawer along, which is the same as multiplying the whole box by z^(-1). And multiplying two boxes like polynomials combines drawers exactly the way convolution combines samples. That single picture explains every property in this lesson.

Pair 1, the impulse: x[n] = δ[n]. Only n = 0 contributes, so X(z) = 1 times z^0 = 1, for every z. A delayed impulse δ[n - k] gives z^(-k). This is why z^(-1) is called the unit delay: multiplying by z^(-1) shifts a sequence one step later.

Pair 2, the right-sided exponential: x[n] = a^n u[n]. X(z) = sum from n = 0 to infinity of (az^(-1))^n. This is a geometric series, which converges only if |az^(-1)| < 1, that is, |z| > |a|. Then X(z) = 1/(1 - az^(-1)) = z/(z - a). The region of convergence (ROC) is everything outside the circle of radius |a|. With a = 1 this gives the unit step: u[n] has transform 1/(1 - z^(-1)) with |z| > 1.

Pair 3, the left-sided exponential: x[n] = -a^n u[-n - 1], non-zero only for n ≤ -1. Working through the sum gives the same formula 1/(1 - az^(-1)), but now with ROC |z| < |a|, inside the circle. Exactly as with Laplace, the formula alone is not enough: you must give the ROC to know which sequence you mean.

ROC rules: The ROC is a ring (annulus) centred at the origin, because convergence depends only on |z|. It contains no poles. A right-sided sequence has an ROC outside the outermost pole, possibly including infinity if the sequence is causal. A left-sided one has an ROC inside the innermost pole. A two-sided one has a ring between poles. A finite-length sequence has an ROC of the whole plane, except possibly z = 0 or z = infinity.

A worked sum example: x[n] = (1/2)^n u[n] + (-1/3)^n u[n]. First term: 1/(1 - (1/2)z^(-1)), |z| > 1/2. Second term: 1/(1 + (1/3)z^(-1)), |z| > 1/3. Both must converge, so the ROC is |z| > 1/2. Adding them: X(z) = (2 - (1/6)z^(-1))/((1 - (1/2)z^(-1))(1 + (1/3)z^(-1))). Poles at z = 1/2 and z = -1/3, both inside the unit circle, and the ROC includes the unit circle, so the DTFT exists.

When the ROC exists and when it does not: x[n] = (1/2)^n u[n] - 2^n u[-n - 1]. The first part needs |z| > 1/2. The second, a left-sided sequence with a = 2, needs |z| < 2. The overlap is the ring 1/2 < |z| < 2, which exists. But if the second part were -(1/4)^n u[-n - 1], it would need |z| < 1/4, which does not overlap |z| > 1/2, so the sum would have no z-transform at all.

A table of common pairs: δ[n] gives 1, all z. δ[n - k] gives z^(-k). u[n] gives 1/(1 - z^(-1)), |z| > 1. a^n u[n] gives 1/(1 - az^(-1)), |z| > |a|. n a^n u[n] gives az^(-1)/(1 - az^(-1)) squared, |z| > |a|. cos(ω0n)u[n] gives (1 - cos(ω0)z^(-1))/(1 - 2cos(ω0)z^(-1) + z^(-2)), |z| > 1. Many exams give this table; know how to use it rather than memorising it blindly.

Property 1, linearity: The transform of ax[n] + by[n] is aX(z) + bY(z), with ROC at least the overlap of the two ROCs. This lets you split complicated sequences into pieces from the table, as in the examples above.

Property 2, time shift: x[n - k] has transform z^(-k)X(z). Delaying by one sample multiplies by z^(-1). This one property is why the z-transform turns difference equations into algebra: y[n - 1] becomes z^(-1)Y(z), y[n - 2] becomes z^(-2)Y(z), and so on. In block diagrams, a box labelled z^(-1) is a one-sample delay, often a single memory register in hardware.

Property 3, convolution: If y[n] = x[n] * h[n], then Y(z) = X(z)H(z). Convolution becomes multiplication, as in every transform we have met. Example: x[n] = δ[n] + δ[n - 1] and h[n] = δ[n] - δ[n - 1]. X(z) = 1 + z^(-1), H(z) = 1 - z^(-1). The product is 1 - z^(-2), so y[n] = δ[n] - δ[n - 2]. Direct convolution gives y = [1, 0, -1], which matches.

Property 4, multiplication by a^n: a^n x[n] has transform X(z/a). This scales the z-plane: every pole and zero moves by a factor of a. It is the discrete version of multiplying by e^(at) in continuous time, which shifts poles in the s-plane. For example, from u[n] with pole at 1 we can get a^n u[n] with pole at a.

Property 5, initial value: For a causal sequence, x[0] is the limit of X(z) as z goes to infinity, because every term with z^(-n), n ≥ 1, disappears. For X(z) = z/(z - 0.5), the limit is 1, so x[0] = 1, matching (0.5)^n u[n] at n = 0.

Poles and zeros in the z-plane: Rational X(z) can be written as a ratio of polynomials in z. Roots of the numerator are zeros, roots of the denominator are poles. A pole at z = a on the real axis corresponds to a^n: if |a| < 1 it decays, if |a| > 1 it grows, and if a is negative it alternates sign each step. A complex pair at re^(±jθ) corresponds to r^n cos(θn + φ): an oscillation at frequency θ inside an envelope r^n. The distance from the origin, not from an axis, decides decay.

The mapping from s to z: If you sample a continuous signal e^(s0 t) every T seconds, you get (e^(s0T))^n, so a pole at s0 in the s-plane becomes a pole at z0 = e^(s0T). The left half of the s-plane (negative real part) maps inside the unit circle, the jω axis maps onto the unit circle, and the right half maps outside. This explains why the unit circle plays the role of the jω axis.

A note on history and names: The idea of using generating functions, sums of sequence values times powers of a variable, goes back to mathematicians such as Abraham de Moivre in the 1700s. Engineers working on sampled-data control systems in the late 1940s and early 1950s, including John Ragazzini and Lotfi Zadeh, developed it into the z-transform for sampled systems. Today it is built into tools such as MATLAB and Python's SciPy, where filters are specified by their z-domain numerator and denominator coefficients.

Real-life example 1, a moving average in a sales app: A shop in Chattogram uses a small app that smooths daily sales with y[n] = (x[n] + x[n - 1] + x[n - 2])/3. Its z-transform is H(z) = (1 + z^(-1) + z^(-2))/3. The zeros are the roots of z squared + z + 1, which are at e^(±j2π/3), on the unit circle. So any pattern repeating every 3 days is completely cancelled, which is exactly why a 3-day average hides a 3-day cycle.

Real-life example 2, a digital audio echo: An app that adds an echo uses y[n] = x[n] + 0.5x[n - D], where D is the delay in samples. Its transfer function is H(z) = 1 + 0.5z^(-D). With a sample rate of 48,000 per second and a 0.25 second echo, D = 12,000. The z-transform turns this whole effect into one compact expression, and its zeros, spread evenly around a circle of radius 0.5 to the power 1/D, explain the comb-like frequency response that gives echoes their colour.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the ROC. Writing a^n u[n] as 1/(1 - az) instead of 1/(1 - az^(-1)). Thinking poles inside the unit circle always mean stable, without checking that the system is causal. Confusing the s-plane rule (left half) with the z-plane rule (inside the unit circle). Treating z^(-1) as an advance instead of a delay.

What exams ask: 'Find the z-transform and ROC of x[n] = (0.8)^n u[n] - (0.5)^n u[n].' 'Find the z-transform of x[n] = {2, 1, 0, 3} starting at n = 0' (2 + z^(-1) + 3z^(-3)). 'Using the convolution property, find y[n] for given x and h.' 'Explain the relationship between the z-transform and the DTFT.' 'Sketch the pole-zero plot of H(z) = (1 - z^(-1))/(1 - 0.9z^(-1))' (zero at 1, pole at 0.9).

Recap: The z-transform X(z) = sum of x[n]z^(-n) is the discrete cousin of Laplace. On the unit circle it equals the DTFT. Its ROC is a ring with no poles, outside the outermost pole for right-sided sequences and inside the innermost pole for left-sided ones; the same formula with different ROCs gives different sequences. z^(-1) is a unit delay, so shifts become powers of z and difference equations become algebra. Convolution becomes multiplication. Poles at a give a^n; the distance from the origin decides decay or growth.
key_points: Z-transform: X(z) = Σ x[n]z^(-n); with z = re^(jω), on the unit circle (r = 1) it equals the DTFT.
Key pairs: δ[n] gives 1; δ[n - k] gives z^(-k); a^n u[n] gives 1/(1 - az^(-1)) with ROC |z| > |a|.
The ROC is a ring centred at the origin with no poles; right-sided: outside outermost pole; left-sided: inside innermost pole.
The same X(z) with different ROCs gives different sequences, so always state the ROC.
Time shift: x[n - k] gives z^(-k)X(z); z^(-1) is a unit delay, which turns difference equations into algebra.
Convolution becomes multiplication: Y(z) = X(z)H(z).
A pole at a gives a^n: decays if |a| < 1, grows if |a| > 1; sampling maps s to z = e^(sT), so the left half-plane maps inside the unit circle.
lessons.tip: Always write transforms in powers of z^(-1) rather than z when working with sequences and difference equations. Then each z^(-1) is literally a one-step delay, and you can read sequences and block diagrams straight off the formula.
lessons.task: Find the z-transform and ROC of x[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] + 2δ[n - 1]. Mark the poles and zeros on a z-plane sketch, draw the unit circle, and decide whether the DTFT exists.

quiz.q: What is the z-transform of a^n u[n], with ROC?
quiz.explain: The geometric series Σ (az^(-1))^n converges to 1/(1 - az^(-1)) when |z| > |a|.

quiz.q: Where in the z-plane is the DTFT found?
quiz.explain: Setting z = e^(jω) (r = 1) makes the z-transform equal the DTFT.

quiz.q: What does multiplying X(z) by z^(-1) do to x[n]?
quiz.explain: The time-shift property: x[n - 1] has transform z^(-1)X(z).
